papers.abstract: Context windows have grown a thousand-fold, yet coding agents still start every session with no memory of their past work. They re-read files, retry failed approaches, and forget root causes they established hours earlier. This is not a context-length problem but a memory-architecture problem. Our hypothesis: coding agents need persistent, experience-aware repository memory, so that knowledge survives from one session to the next. Three measurements on real repositories motivate the design. First, mid-size projects already exceed the largest production context windows, and storing knowledge inside the model's key-value (KV) cache costs $10^4$ to $10^5$ times more bytes than storing it as indexed text. Second, across 752 real bug-fix commits, the median fix edits two files, and these files plus their direct imports amount to less than 10% of the repository; the bottleneck is selection, not capacity. Third, even with transitive import reachability and test links, 47% of co-edited file pairs remain structurally disconnected; the knowledge needed for selection must be mined from history and experience. We sketch Stratum, a tiered memory that lives with the repository and serves it through page-safe tools: every response states what was returned, what remains, and what it cost. Retrieval over a store of one million nodes takes 1.7 ms at the median. In a multi-session experiment on eight real bugs, a fresh agent that inherited a prior session's memory, written by a different model, identified the root-cause file in 21 of 24 trials versus 6 of 24 for a retrieval-only baseline (Fisher $p<10^{-4}$), at 4.5x lower median token cost. With the notes of all eight investigations pooled in one store, success remained 8/8.
authors: Yuvraj Sehgal, Mahsa Panahandeh, Naser Ezzati-Jivan
bullets: Coding agents repeatedly reread files, retry failed approaches, and lose established root causes because their memory does not persist between sessions.
The design uses tiered, repository-resident memory with page-safe tools that report returned information, remaining content, and access cost.
It combines repository structure with knowledge mined from history and prior experience, addressing the limits of import-based retrieval for selecting relevant files.
Retrieval over one million nodes took 1.7 ms at the median; inherited memory found root-cause files in 21/24 trials versus 6/24 for a retrieval-only baseline, with 4.5× lower median token cost.
Scope is limited to a multi-session experiment covering eight real bugs, though pooled investigation notes achieved 8/8 success.

papers.tldr: Stratum gives coding agents persistent, repository-level memory that helps them carry debugging knowledge across sessions while reducing retrieval cost.

papers.abstract: Financial institutions operating under data-residency constraints are restricted to open-weight models small enough to locally host, which trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning. On-policy distillation narrows such gaps by supervising a student on its own rollouts, but traditional OPD requires a strong external teacher, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions on a full reference solution. We ask how much of that signal is necessary. We present Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for multi-step reasoning. Given a problem the student fails, the student itself identifies the first incorrect reasoning step and writes a short critique of that step. We truncate the student's trajectory immediately before the error (aiming to obtain a correct prefix), condition a frozen copy of the student on the same prefix plus the hint, and distill that hint-conditioned teacher into the student over a short rollout under reverse KL. No external model contributes a gradient. We apply Fin-SD to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark that requires deriving formula inputs from realistic scenarios via accounting conventions. We find: (i) replacing the critique with a generic-feedback control matches Fin-SD's entire 3.03 pp accuracy gain over the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, suggesting the gain comes from where supervision is applied, not hint content; (ii) the model writing the hint does not need to be stronger than the model receiving it: hints from same-family GPT-OSS-120B, at roughly 6x the parameters, yield no materially greater benefits than self-written hints; and (iii) Fin-SD matches on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions on accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. With Fin-SD, general reasoning on MMLU-Pro and a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust show no material regression.
bullets: A generic feedback signal matches the full 3.03-point gain, indicating that supervision placement matters more than hint content.
Hints generated by a larger GPT-OSS-120B model provide no material benefit over self-written hints.
Fin-SD matches full-reference on-policy self-distillation while using 9.5% fewer tokens.
No material regression appears on MMLU-Pro or a 14-metric FinTrust compliance audit.
Scope: evaluated on GPT-OSS-20B and a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Fin-SD. The student is sampled on a training problem and judged against the ground truth. On failures, a frozen copy of the student receives the query, the failing trajectory, and the answer, and returns the first faulty step 𝑘 , a short critique ℎ, and an error type; pure arithmetic slips are dropped without a gradient. The trajectory is truncated immediately before k, so both policies condition on the on-policy prefix before the localized error, with the frozen teacher also receiving ℎ. The student minimizes the per-token KL between the two next-token distributions over an L = 100 rollout. At each epoch boundary, the failure set is re-mined and the teacher re-frozen.

papers.title: How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) to solve complex visual problems, but also exposes them to CoT hijacking: an adversary implants a backdoor through poisoned fine-tuning so that a visual trigger induces a hijacking turn, redirecting an otherwise faithful reasoning chain to an attacker-chosen answer. However, since the hijack acts within the reasoning chain, existing multimodal backdoor defenses designed for MLLMs that answer directly struggle to detect it. Moreover, inspecting the chain itself does not reliably expose the hijack, since the hijacking turn can resemble honest self-correction in form. In this paper, we find that honest reasoning tends to revise its answer at high-entropy "aha moments", whereas a hijack can overturn a confident answer through a near-deterministic turn. To quantify this contrast, we formalize this phenomenon as belief inertia, the cumulative next-token entropy of a reasoning span minus the answer-belief revision it induces, with markedly lower values for hijacked spans than for honest reasoning spans. Since hijacking tokens are also image-dependent, we further improve detection by restricting the measure to image-dependent spans, yielding visual belief inertia (VBI). Building on this, we propose InertiaGuard, a training-free, test-time detector that flags a trace when its VBI falls below a threshold calibrated on a small set of clean traces. Across various attacks and benchmarks, InertiaGuard achieves higher detection performance than existing baselines, while generalizing to different model architectures and trigger types.
bullets: CoT hijacking redirects a model’s reasoning and answer after an attacker implants a backdoor triggered by an image.
Existing defenses struggle because hijacks occur inside reasoning chains and can resemble honest self-correction.
The paper defines belief inertia as reasoning-span token entropy minus the resulting answer-belief revision.
Visual belief inertia (VBI) focuses this measure on image-dependent spans, improving sensitivity to visual hijacks.
InertiaGuard is a training-free, test-time detector calibrated on a small set of clean traces and performs better than existing baselines across attacks, benchmarks, architectures, and trigger types.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CoT hijacking combines low belief inertia with strong image dependence. Each dot is a reasoning step (gray: clean; red: hijacking) sampled from a validation set. (a, b) Hijacking steps induce large belief revisions B at low entropy cost H , resulting in lower belief inertia than clean reasoning. (c, d) Because hijacking steps also exhibit strong image dependence, adding this criterion filters out most low-inertia clean steps while retaining hijacking steps.

Figure 2: Illustration of INERTIAGUARD. Although the model initially recognizes the stop sign, a trigger-induced hijacking turn redirects its answer from (b) to (a). To detect this redirection, INERTIAGUARD first identifies image-dependent steps, then compares the belief revision across spans containing these steps with their cumulative entropy. Because the hijacking span induces a large revision at little entropy cost, its belief inertia falls below the calibrated threshold, causing the trace to be flagged.

papers.title: Detecting Chain-of-Thought Hijacking in Backdoored Multimodal Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: InertiaGuard detects visual trigger-induced chain-of-thought hijacking by identifying unusually deterministic answer revisions in multimodal reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: New words are invented every day. A human listener can learn a new word by hearing it clearly once and inferring its usage from sentence context. This paper proposes granting ASR a similar ability to learn the contextual representations and spellings of new words from unlabeled test data at test time. A frozen CTC acoustic model provides spellings, a frozen language model provides contextual evidence for out-of-vocabulary (OOV) word detection, and an adaptation module expands the vocabulary by learning the lexical token representations with distributions over CTC-generated candidates. The spelling model of each token is optimized by minimizing a Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) objective. We demonstrate that the CTC-weighted language model log likelihood ratio can be interpreted as the KLD between the unknown correct ASR and the unsupervised learned ASR, and that, using a Pinsker bound, the square root of KLD can be interpreted as an upper bound on the total variation distance between the true and estimated spelling of the unknown word. Experiments show relative OOV character-error-rate reductions of up to 14.97% on LibriSpeech and 6.67% on dysarthric Speech Accessibility Project data for recurring OOV words, relative to the corresponding rescoring system.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recognizing newly invented or unseen words during ASR inference.
Uses a frozen CTC acoustic model for spelling candidates and a frozen language model to detect OOV words from context.
Expands the vocabulary by learning lexical token representations and spelling distributions with a Kullback–Leibler divergence objective.
Provides a theoretical link between the weighted language-model likelihood ratio, KLD, and an upper bound on spelling-distribution error.
Reduces relative OOV character error rates by up to 14.97% on LibriSpeech and 6.67% on dysarthric speech data for recurring OOV words.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of proposed test-time adaptation framework. The CTC model generates N-best hypotheses for an input utterance. Word spans with strong CTC-LM preference disagreement are selected as potential OOV regions (one span here). Top-K CTC spellings are used to initialize a placeholder token with uniform spelling prior. For the first occurrence, the placeholder is added into the vocabulary and fine-tuned in context, while the utterance is buffered for potential final refinement. Otherwise, we retrieve the existing placeholder and re-transcribe the test utterance, possibly reducing errors. The retrieved placeholder is further updated using unsupervised model adaptation.

Table 1. Results on LibriSpeech (%). “OOV subset” denotes the set of test utterances that contain frequent OOV words. Parentheses indicate the relative error reduction (%) over the corresponding shallow fusion system. Asterisks denote statistically significant differences from the corresponding plain rescoring baselines: * denotes significance at p < 0.05 and ** at p ≤ 0.001, measured with the NIST sc stats tool.
Table 2. Results on SAP-dev OOV subset (%). Parentheses show relative error reduction (%) over the corresponding shallow fusion system. Significant reductions: * for p < 0.05 and ** for p ≤ 0.001.

papers.tldr: An ASR adaptation method learns spellings and contextual representations for recurring out-of-vocabulary words directly from unlabeled test speech, improving OOV recognition.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation helps a deployed model respond to changing inputs, but the same intervention can rescue one batch and damage the next. Updating normalization statistics, for example, can improve corrupted images yet fail when a batch contains mostly one class. Average accuracy hides these failures and cannot tell a model when to use an intervention. Target labels can guide this decision, but they are scarce and some choices are already clear. We introduce PORTAL, a controller that chooses when to deploy an intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying. Each available prediction rule is a candidate, and its predictions are fixed before current feedback arrives. Every acquired label therefore evaluates all candidates on the same input. PORTAL combines these shared comparisons and directs queries toward candidates that can still overtake the current leader. It stops when the remaining labels cannot change the choice or when the possible accuracy gain no longer justifies another query. Our analysis links the required feedback to accuracy gaps and shared mistakes, explaining why some choices need much less evidence. Experiments show that this control turns an intervention that loses accuracy overall into a useful choice on selected batches. It prevents severe failures caused by changes in arrival order and preserves gains across complete corruption streams. When a fixed rule already works well, PORTAL uses little feedback to retain its performance. Periodic label checks reveal when past evidence needs refreshing and help the controller recover as conditions change. The acquired labels also train stronger candidates for future batches, and selection brings nearly all of their accuracy gains into deployment. The same feedback therefore improves both the choice made now and the predictions available to later batches.
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Xinling Wen, Liangliang Li, Yu Chen
bullets: Test-time interventions can help some batches but hurt others, and average accuracy does not reveal when they are safe.
PORTAL treats each prediction rule as a candidate, uses shared labeled comparisons, and queries inputs that could change the current choice.
It stops querying when further labels cannot alter the decision or the expected gain no longer justifies the cost.
Experiments show it avoids severe order-dependent failures, retains effective fixed rules with little feedback, and adapts as conditions change.
Collected labels also improve future candidate models, bringing most of their gains into deployment.

papers.abstract: Streaming multimodal assistants must make response decisions while events are still unfolding. They need to recognize when the available evidence warrants a response, produce an appropriate continuation, and remain silent otherwise. Supervised fine-tuning learns from recorded assistant turns, but does not directly train on the response prefixes produced by the evolving policy itself. We introduce Live-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method that uses privileged hints available only during training to supervise the policy on its own outputs. The policy first generates a continuation from the streaming context alone. The same model then re-evaluates that continuation with a hint describing the relevant evidence, and the resulting distributions guide the unhinted policy. On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, Live-OPSD attains an average score of 59.64 on LiveProBench, 5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline, and stays competitive on OVO-Bench (65.84). These results indicate that guiding the policy on its own outputs with privileged hints improves both when and how a streaming assistant responds.
authors: Kaixuan Du, Xin Wan, Dai Guan, Ming Chen, Xiaoxi Jiang, Guanjun Jiang
bullets: Streaming assistants must decide whether to respond, what to say, or remain silent as events unfold.
The method addresses a gap in supervised fine-tuning, which does not train on prefixes generated by the evolving policy.
It generates a continuation from streaming context, then re-evaluates it with training-only privileged evidence hints.
On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, it scores 59.64 on LiveProBench—5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline—and remains competitive on OVO-Bench at 65.84.
The approach improves both response timing and content, within the evaluated streaming-assistant benchmarks.

papers.tldr: Live-OPSD improves proactive streaming video assistants by self-distilling hint-guided judgments onto their own unhinted outputs.

papers.abstract: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.
authors: XinYu Piao, Myunghoon Ryu, Joongheon Kim, Jong-Kook Kim
bullets: Addresses dialogue recall when no external storage or future question knowledge is available.
Generates varied questions for each dialogue turn and writes them with the turn content into model parameters.
Uses matching later user questions to retrieve and answer from parameter-stored content.
Evaluated on five language models, recalling most stored dialogue turns.
Scope: focused on parameter-only recall rather than external-memory systems.

papers.title: Self-Keyed In-Parameter Memorization for External Memory-Free Dialogue Recall in Frozen Language Models
papers.tldr: SKIM stores dialogue turns directly in frozen model parameters using self-generated question keys, enabling later recall without external memory.

papers.abstract: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. We present TALOR, a lightweight, backward-free rectification module that uses the source linear head as a geometric anchor. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.
authors: Yingkai Yang, Chaoqi Chen, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets open-set test-time adaptation under simultaneous covariate and semantic shifts.
Decomposes normalized features into principal and tail coordinates using the source linear head as an anchor.
Uses soft-routed weighted ridge regression to estimate and subtract principal-space drift conditioned on tail features.
On ImageNet-C with six csOOD datasets, it achieves 2.2% higher H-score than UniEnt and runs 2.5× faster with 12% of its GPU memory.
As a post-correction plug-in, it raises COME to 68.4% H-score with 2% additional memory overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Pipeline. papers.selection_reason: Open-set test-time adaptation via lightweight feature rectification, directly fitting test-time learning.
papers.title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: TALOR is a lightweight, backward-free plug-in that corrects open-set test-time feature drift using the source classifier’s geometry, improving accuracy while reducing adaptation cost.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.
authors: Marc Ziegler, Batu \"Ozen, Sami Mentes, Thomas Waschulzik, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses sensor corruption when the robot policy is frozen or inaccessible.
Separates periodic gait dynamics from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair.
On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis improved success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reached 382/640.
Produced no false triggers across 64 held-out fault-free episodes; a matched boosted-tree surrogate showed no repair benefit.
Separate surrogate fits helped Go1 and ANYmal C, while phase-aware gradients performed better.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Method overview: Diagnosis and input repair. MBD identifies the faulty sensor from the structured surrogate’s per-sensor contributions, and PRR repairs its input before the frozen policy acts. For a +0.3 rear-left thigh-encoder offset: (a) the sensor explains 49% of the abnormal correction across 16 diagnosis logs; (b) PRR supplies its phase-matched healthy value; and (c) repair removes the sideways drift and raises walking success from 3/16 to 16/16 fresh episodes.

Table 1: Results across three embodiments. For Go2, R2 measures action prediction on 16 clean trajectories, and Diagnosed reports top-1 sensor identification across 37 faults. Go2 Walk and Survive are counts over 640 episodes. Online MBD detects, diagnoses, and repairs faults within each episode. Go1 and ANYmal C report walking over 352 episodes per method. On these two robots, the GBM predicts actions directly and shares neither MBD’s gait model nor its input representation.

papers.selection_reason: The paper addresses sensor failure in robot foundation models by proposing a transparent surrogate for online diagnosis and repair of inputs to a frozen locomotion policy. This falls under robot learning (surrogate modeling) and test-time learning (online adaptation).
papers.title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
papers.tldr: A transparent, phase-aware surrogate can diagnose and repair sensor faults around a frozen robot policy, improving simulated locomotion but with limited validation.

papers.abstract: Controlling the personality of a language model usually relies on written profiles or named trait categories, so it can only express what an author writes down or what a taxonomy names. We instead propose Personality Latents (PL), which learn a latent for each person from their own writing, with no personality labels and no authored profile, and inject it into a frozen language model as a soft prefix. Following generative latent optimization, each training person receives a free latent that is optimized through the frozen model itself, while an encoder learns to predict these latents so that a new person needs only one forward pass, with optional refinement at test time. We evaluate on held-out people by having the conditioned model answer neutral and interview questions and reading personality from its answers with scorers trained on real human writing. On the MBTI axes PL reaches an AUC of , ahead of persona embedding and prompt-based baselines under identical settings, and the ranking holds when the answers are scored in three different embedding spaces. A latent learned with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct also transfers personality to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct through a new adapter alone.
bullets: Learns a separate latent for each person directly from their writing, without predefined traits or personality annotations.
Trains an encoder to predict a person’s latent in one forward pass, with optional test-time refinement.
Evaluates personality expression through answers to neutral and interview questions scored by models trained on human writing.
Outperforms persona-embedding and prompt-based baselines on MBTI-axis AUC under matched settings; the ranking holds across three embedding spaces.
Latents learned with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct transfer to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using only a new adapter.

During training, a free person-specific latent is optimized through a frozen LLM, while an amortizing encoder learns to predict it from the person’s posts. The latent is converted into soft prefix tokens by an adapter. For an unseen person, the encoder prediction is used directly or optionally refined at test time before generation.

papers.tldr: Personality Latents infer an individual’s writing-based personality without labels or profiles and condition frozen language models via a learned soft prefix.

papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.
authors: Yue Wu, Yang Zhang, Weinan Gan, Chongming Gao, Xinsen Guo, Xiaoyuan Li, Fuli Feng
bullets: In-Place TTT can lose its benefit on realistic web long-context QA because uniform writes let irrelevant content dilute useful information.
Select-TTT conditions each chunk’s write strength on its relevance to the user query.
Relevance is obtained without supervision or added parameters from the frozen output head’s probability mass on query tokens.
A temperature-scaled softmax converts relevance scores into learning-rate multipliers while preserving context-parallel computation.
The method consistently improves long-context QA across two benchmarks and two model backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Select-TTT. (1) The frozen LM head maps chunk hidden states to logit space, where query-token scores are aggregated by top-𝑘 mean pooling to assess chunk relevance. (2) Relevance scores are converted into learning-rate multipliers. (3) In-Place TTT computes the NTP-aligned fast-weight updates. (4) The multipliers rescale these updates to selectively write query-relevant information into fast-weight memory.
Figure 5: Efficiency analysis of Select-TTT. Prefill throughput (a) and peak GPU memory (b) are compared across the Baseline, IP-TTT, and Select-TTT on Qwen3-4B model.

The default In-Place TTT configuration uses 0.3 for both learning rates. The dashed line marks the zero-shot Baseline (33.4%).

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation updates a deployed model on an unlabeled test stream. In practice this stream often arrives one sample at a time, with the classes in no particular order. A single sample then provides limited information for estimating distribution-level statistics, and selecting samples by confidence can admit predictions that are wrong yet confident. A corruption, however, shifts the features while leaving the decision regions of the frozen classifier unchanged. We therefore propose Origin-recentered Test-Time Adaptation (OriTTA), which constructs fixed geometric targets from the source model and adapts selected features toward them. Seen from the origin of the feature space, the classes lean toward a common direction. We choose a new origin to bring class scores closer together while keeping it near the mean feature of one synthetic prototype per class. From this origin, prototype directions spread more evenly, and each class obtains an axis and an ideal point before any test data arrives. During adaptation, OriTTA aligns selected features with their predicted class axis and penalizes excessive radius, keeps one input per predicted class in memory to limit feature changes for classes absent from the stream, and resets the model when re-classifying this memory reveals collapse. Without tuning for each setting, OriTTA achieves the highest mean accuracy at batch size 1 on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C and ImageNet-C in all sixteen combinations of four backbones, two protocols and two stream orders. On ImageNet-C fog, recent methods collapse in up to two thirds of one hundred runs, while OriTTA never does.
authors: Jaeho Hwang, Yujin Oh, Juhyeon Shin, Juhye Lee, Sungroh Yoon, Uiwon Hwang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of adapting to unlabeled streams one sample at a time, where distribution statistics are unreliable and confident predictions may be wrong.
Constructs fixed class-specific geometric targets from the frozen source classifier using synthetic prototypes and a recentered feature-space origin.
Adapts selected features toward predicted class axes, penalizes excessive feature radius, and stores one sample per class to preserve absent-class behavior.
Detects adaptation collapse by reclassifying the stored memory and resets the model when necessary.
Achieves the highest mean accuracy at batch size 1 across the reported CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C settings; it avoids collapses observed by recent methods on ImageNet-C fog.

papers.abstract: Web fashion images support applications such as visual product search and consumer-to-shop matching, yet their visual heterogeneity makes reliable garment segmentation challenging. Despite advances in promptable segmentation, autonomously identifying and correcting garment-specific errors without human-provided spatial prompts remains difficult. We propose GarmentSegAgent, an autonomous framework that integrates semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation through iterative textual self-refinement. At its core, we introduce CAST (Constrained Attribution-guided Selective TextGrad), which connects visual error attribution with targeted textual optimization. CAST identifies instruction components responsible for segmentation errors, selectively updates them through textual gradients, and validates the resulting instructions against garment-specific constraints. This enables image-specific error correction at inference time while keeping the underlying foundation models frozen. Experiments on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia demonstrate consistent improvements in region overlap and boundary accuracy, alongside more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad. By enabling visual feedback to guide controlled instruction updates, GarmentSegAgent offers a promising direction for autonomous garment understanding, with potential applications in scalable fashion content analysis, visual retrieval, and consumer-to-shop matching on the Web.
authors: Jia Chen, Chao Huang, Xinrong Hu, Mingdi Huang, Ruyang Zhao, Jun Bai
bullets: Addresses unreliable garment segmentation caused by heterogeneous web fashion imagery and the need for spatial prompts.
Combines semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation in an iterative self-refinement framework.
Introduces CAST, which attributes errors to instruction components, selectively optimizes them, and checks garment-specific constraints.
Evaluations on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia show consistent gains in region overlap and boundary accuracy, with more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad.
Foundation models remain frozen; refinement occurs at inference time through image-specific instruction updates.

papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories couple a learned design surrogate to an instrument, and on every new target domain it must answer four questions: when it can be trusted, how many target measurements it needs, which to make first, and when to stop adapting, switch models or escalate. We state a framework making each measurable (a competence ratio, a budget $k^*(\varepsilon)$, a time-to-target and a priced decision) and instantiate it without wet experiments on six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables as offline laboratories: 107 leave-one-group tiers whose rows are hidden labels. A sealed, pre-registered programme (two sealed negative validations and a pre-registered test on three more tables) and seven frozen closed-loop protocols, each run twice, yield 23 findings. Shift cost is stratified by shift type; no label-free statistic certifies individual candidates; random-split model-family rankings predicted neither the sealed nor the loop rankings. Warm-start residual boosting returns a surrogate to $1.25\times$ its development reference within 20 target rows in 94% of chemistry tiers (27% under a strict noise-floor reading), 90% of laboratory and 40% of device tiers, and a budget planned from the shift type on other tables is not measurably worse on a new one. In the loop, one gain survives drift and shuffled-label controls on all tiers, carried by the sparsely sampled ones: proposing at once and warm-starting on every measurement reaches a 10% target in 2.80 measurements against 3.31 for the reference, and in 5.72 against 11.35 for random proposals on 301 hard units at a 3% tolerance. No label-free acquisition rule survives the shuffled-label control, no interval-aware proposal or other model family does better, and no threshold rule on the tested diagnostics beats always continuing once escalation is priced. No wet-lab validation is claimed.
bullets: Evaluated 107 leave-one-group tiers across six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables using sealed, preregistered offline protocols.
Formalized measurable trust, target-measurement budget, time-to-target, and cost-aware decisions for adapting, switching, or escalating a surrogate.
Warm-start residual boosting recovered near-reference performance within 20 target rows most often in chemistry tiers, less often in laboratory and device tiers.
Propose-then-update reached a 10% target in 2.80 versus 3.31 measurements for the reference, and 5.72 versus 11.35 for random proposals on hard units at 3% tolerance.
Shuffled-label controls invalidated label-free acquisition rules; no tested stopping threshold, interval-aware proposal, or alternative model family consistently improved decisions.

papers.title: When Can a Learned Design Surrogate Be Trusted in a Self-Driving Microfluidics Laboratory? An Offline Closed-Loop Framework Built and Tested on Six Public Tables
papers.tldr: An offline study defines and tests when learned surrogates can be trusted and adapted in self-driving microfluidics, finding that warm-start closed-loop updating helps on sparse, shifted settings but no label-free stopping or acquisition rule is reliable.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
authors: Xusheng Liang, Jianqiao Sun, Hao Zhang, Yulei Niu, Hengshuang Zhao, Jiawei Ma
bullets: Long-video QA is difficult because sparse frame sampling can miss decisive evidence, while spurious cues can still mislead models.
S-MME benchmarks shortcut-biased behavior from misleading language correlations and salient but irrelevant visual content.
CLEAR estimates bias using question-only and locally salient-clip views, then intervenes on hidden states at inference.
Experiments across five benchmarks show consistent gains in prediction and robustness across different MLLMs.
CLEAR is presented as a complementary test-time scaling approach; the abstract does not specify detailed limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of CLEAR. (a) The full-video path produces the final answer, while questiononly and salient-view probes reveal spurious linguistic correlations and salient-yet-misleading visual observations. The salient view is formed by selecting top-K locally relevant clips according to query-conditioned visual attention. (b) CLEAR extracts the hidden state of the shared decision token z at selected late decoder layers, and constructs residual vectors rql = hf l − hq l and rsl = hf l − hs l from the restricted-view probes to the full-video state. These residual vectors are injected into the full-video path to steer its hidden state away from shortcut anchors before final decoding.

papers.abstract: Test-time updating lets a language model change persistent state after training---such as model weights, adapter parameters, or a memory module---before or while answering queries. Existing evaluations often compare systems using update count or frequency and performance measured immediately afterward. These summaries omit what is updated, where, when, and in what order. The same total can therefore hide an important difference: one system may answer after one update while another answers after two. We introduce the Control Map, an evaluation framework that records the committed updates preceding each scored answer and separately evaluates behavioral changes, immediate learning (acquisition), later recall (retention), preservation of unrelated behavior (locality), and performance in new settings. We prove when counts alone determine final state and show, under stated assumptions, how differences between pre-answer histories limit differences in average scores. Using ControlMap, our experiments reveal three insights. First, update scheduling matters: at a 760M-parameter checkpoint, 24 schedules with the same update count yield 19.7%--34.2% accuracy. Second, learning an edit does not guarantee that it lasts or remains contained: all six selected CounterFact LoRA settings learn the new information, while ROME retains edits at all 13 operating points but fails locality at each. Third, no editor performs best consistently across models, benchmarks, and tests. Evaluations should therefore report update histories and assess acquisition, retention, and locality separately.
authors: Zehao Zhao, Shangjian Yin, Rui Liu, Chongyang Bai, Mark Ibrahim, Kavosh Asadi, Yuchen Lu, Hang Cui, Hamed Firooz
bullets: Update count alone can hide differences in what is updated, when, and in what order before an answer is scored.
The framework records committed pre-answer updates and evaluates behavioral change, immediate learning, later recall, preservation of unrelated behavior, and new-setting performance.
The authors prove when update counts suffice to determine final state and bound score differences caused by different update histories.
Experiments show scheduling strongly affects accuracy: 24 equal-count schedules at one checkpoint range from 19.7% to 34.2%.
Learning an edit may not imply durability or locality, and no editor is consistently best across models, benchmarks, and tests.

papers.abstract: Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning? Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA). Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.
bullets: Frozen latent world models can plan poorly when deployment conditions differ from training.
Prediction-only adaptation fits observed transitions but may remain inaccurate about goal-reaching actions.
OpTTA jointly minimizes observed-transition prediction loss and the planner’s goal-reaching cost on candidate rollouts.
Across manipulation, reaching, and navigation shifts, OpTTA improved final planning success by 13.5 percentage points on average, versus 6.9–7.5 for prediction-only adaptation.
The approach was evaluated with three JEPA world models and both CEM and gradient-based planners, without additional environment interaction.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies and language-model agents provide complementary capabilities, but completing a task also requires adapting their use to the consequences of physical interaction. We study execution as a locus of adaptation: feedback guides the current action and supplies evidence for revising subsequent decisions under fixed model weights. We introduce RoboDoctor, a training-free framework that connects diagnosis, grounded action, and persistent experience across three revision targets. The harness allocates control between policy and agent; intervention determines when to assist while preserving useful policy behavior; and operation refines physical methods through observed effects. Linked experience records retain the reason for a decision, the attempted method, its outcome, and conditions for reuse. On a curated archive of 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, RoboDoctor achieves a five-dimension mean score of 57.10, with a native success rate of 49.44%. Recorded interactions illustrate strategy changes, selective correction, and grasp revision. These findings characterize execution-time adaptation in the evaluated system; controlled trials remain necessary to isolate the contribution of cross-episode experience.
authors: Heyang Yu, Haomin Li, Sihang Li, Jixin Yan, Shiyun Peng, Wanqi Zhong, Tianyu Xin, Yuan Yao, Xiaoyu Tian, Yiming Li

On 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, it reports a five-dimension mean score of 57.10 and a native success rate of 49.44%.
The results demonstrate execution-time adaptation, but controlled trials are still needed to isolate the value of cross-episode experience.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) adapts large pretrained models to unseen target distribution shifts by updating only lightweight prompt tokens. Existing TPT methods are effective, but they mainly optimize each prompt update locally. Across test-time steps, prompts updated at the current step are reused for the corresponding predictions and updates, so noisy or biased unlabeled objectives can accumulate and destabilize the prompt-update trajectory. We identify two failure modes: magnitude expansion, where updates move the prompt too far, and directional drift, where consecutive updates point in inconsistent directions. To analyze and control these failures, we propose Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition ($\mathtt{TPD}$), which characterizes observed prompt-update trajectories from a dynamical-systems view and decomposes base prompt updates into magnitude and direction. $\mathtt{TPD}$ computes a spectral radius to measure update expansion and decomposes update directions into persistent, oscillatory, and residual components. Building on this decomposition, Adaptive Koopman Control ($\mathtt{AKC}$) regulates update magnitude by shrinking updates under expansive recent dynamics, while Hankel Update Router ($\mathtt{HUR}$) refines update direction by preserving persistent components and suppressing oscillatory and residual components. Together, $\mathtt{AKC}$ and $\mathtt{HUR}$ produce a stabilized prompt update. As a prompt-agnostic framework, $\mathtt{TPD}$ can be plugged into visual and text TPT methods without modifying the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss. Experiments on 15 datasets show that $\mathtt{TPD}$ consistently improves 10 baselines, with accuracy gains of $3$--$8\%$ for visual prompts and over $2\%$ for text prompts.
authors: Junze Wang, Lei Fan, Dezheng Zhang, Donglin Di, Yang Song, Sidong Liu, Cong Cong
bullets: Addresses two failure modes in test-time prompt tuning: excessive update magnitude and inconsistent directional drift.
Decomposes prompt-update trajectories into magnitude plus persistent, oscillatory, and residual directional components.
Uses Adaptive Koopman Control to shrink expansive updates and Hankel Update Router to preserve persistent directions while suppressing unstable components.
Prompt-agnostic: integrates with existing visual and text TPT methods without changing the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss.
Across 15 datasets, improves 10 baselines, with reported gains of 3–8% for visual prompts and over 2% for text prompts.

papers.abstract: Point cloud models are increasingly deployed through score-only black-box interfaces. Under this access model, test-time rotations outside the training distribution can substantially degrade performance. Although existing mitigations such as equivariant retraining and gradient-based adaptation are effective, they are infeasible without access to model weights or gradients. To address this limitation, we propose CanDO, a test-time canonicalization method that recovers lost performance using only forward queries. Specifically, CanDO searches for an input transformation that maximizes model confidence and uses derivative-free optimization to perform this search without gradients. We further identify three conditions for successful recovery: a training augmentation gap, an accuracy-aligned confidence surrogate, and global search over a multi-modal objective. Across multiple architectures and benchmarks, CanDO recovers 76% of the oracle gap under azimuthal misorientation and 51% under arbitrary SO(3) rotations for object part segmentation. These results show that frozen score-only point cloud models can recover from rotation-induced distribution shifts through post-deployment canonicalization alone.
bullets: Targets pose-induced performance degradation when only forward confidence scores—not weights or gradients—are accessible.
Searches for an input transformation that maximizes model confidence via derivative-free, global optimization.
Successful recovery depends on an augmentation gap, confidence aligned with accuracy, and handling a multimodal objective.
Recovers 76% of the oracle gap under azimuthal shifts and 51% under arbitrary SO(3) rotations for object part segmentation.
Scope: addresses rotation-induced shifts through post-deployment canonicalization of frozen models.

papers.abstract: Quadrotor trajectory tracking under unmodeled disturbances often relies on online residual adaptation, but short out-domain residuals can corrupt the learned disturbance model when constant-step updates treat every residual gradient uniformly. We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), an adaptive-learning method for mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances that retains the random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares adaptation of a prior domain-adaptive residual policy (DAPL) while modifying the online update step size. DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts. We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events. Compared with $L_1$-augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases.
bullets: Targets corruption of online disturbance learning caused by treating all residual gradients equally.
Retains DAPL’s random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares residual adaptation.
Compares current gradients with short- and long-term memories to classify adaptation regimes.
Uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates and recover after persistent domain shifts.
In numerical tests with four mixed disturbances, DGC achieved the lowest mean position RMSE among the evaluated baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of Dual Gradient Consensus for online adaptive learning under mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances. Left: the residual pipeline forms a packed gradient gt from the RFF predictor, a low-pass residual, and the least-squares loss. Center: Long-Term Gradient (LTG) and Short-Term Gradient (STG) memories classify gt into four regimes; only (0, 1) hands LTG over to STG. Right: a confidence map sets the step length of the (α̂, σ̂) update on mixed in-domain/out-domain residuals. Bottom: the applied learning step size remains high in-domain, drops on transients, and recovers after a completed domain shift.

Fig. 2. Representative rollouts for the four cases in Section IV-C. Columns: (a) step domain shift with out-domain pulse (Case 1); (b) stationary domain with out-domain pulses (Case 2); (c) periodic domain shift with out-domain pulse (Case 3); (d) ramp domain shift with out-domain pulse (Case 4). papers.abstract: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/
authors: Xuan He, Sining Zhoubian, Ruozhen Yang, Yuhao Wen, Zhineng Wang, Yuyang Hu, Ke Yang, Yuyu Zhang, Ping Nie, Jiawei Han, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Evaluates memory systems across multiple benchmarks and model backbones against naive RAG.

Advocates evaluating the net value and reliability of memory rather than standalone performance; code and results will be released.

papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection identifies inputs outside the training distribution. Rank-based analyses such as RankFeat and RankWeight suggest that OOD overconfidence is closely related to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces. Since weight averaging operates directly in parameter space and improves model generalization, we consider it for OOD detection from a dominant-component perspective. Trainable Weight Averaging (TWA) assigns a single coefficient to each checkpoint, limiting independent control of dominant weight components. We extend TWA with leading rank-one weight components extracted by Singular Value Decomposition as correction directions, whose contributions are learned through the in-distribution classification objective. On ResNet50, our method improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across the evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, both with and without Outlier Exposure. Mahalanobis-based evaluation yields mixed results, indicating that the benefit depends on the OOD scoring protocol. Target-layer analyses with MSP and Energy favor correction near the classifier.
bullets: OOD overconfidence is linked to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces.
The method extends Trainable Weight Averaging with SVD-derived rank-one weight corrections learned using the in-distribution classification objective.
On ResNet50, it improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, with and without Outlier Exposure.
Mahalanobis evaluation is mixed, and target-layer analyses favor applying corrections near the classifier.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can exploit shortcuts, i.e., correlations present in training data that may not hold at test time. This can lead to poor predictions when correlations shift. Most existing solutions for removing shortcuts operate at training time, requiring labeled training data, model weight access, and significant computational resources. Here, we study the problem of test-time shortcut removal. We propose a family of counterfactual test-time augmentation (CTTA) methods: given an example, each method uses an auxiliary model to generate counterfactual edits in which the shortcut value is changed, and then takes a weighted average of the LLM's predictions across these edits. We prove that the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor is a member of this CTTA family, and we characterize its weights. The weights depend on the training distribution, and therefore are, in general, not identifiable from the trained model and unlabeled test data. However, we present assumptions under which the weights can be obtained using the token probabilities of the trained LLM, and propose tests to detect violations of these assumptions. We use these tests to develop Select-CTTA, an aggregate method that selects among CTTA methods. Empirically, we find that Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches the performance of models fine-tuned on shortcut-balanced data.
authors: Katie Matton, Rosalind W. Picard, John Guttag, Maggie Makar
bullets: Addresses shortcut-induced failures under distribution shifts using only test-time intervention, avoiding labeled training data and model-weight access.
Uses an auxiliary model to create counterfactual edits and combines the LLM’s predictions with method-specific weights.
Proves the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor belongs to the CTTA family and characterizes its weights.
Introduces Select-CTTA, which chooses among CTTA methods using tests for assumptions needed to estimate weights from token probabilities.
Empirically, Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches shortcut-balanced fine-tuning performance.

papers.selection_reason: Develops test-time counterfactual augmentation to remove shortcuts in LLM predictions, fitting deployment-time adaptation.

papers.tldr: Counterfactual test-time augmentation reduces language-model shortcut reliance without retraining by averaging predictions over edited examples that change shortcut values.

papers.abstract: Skill learning enables web agents to reuse prior experience for long-horizon interactive tasks. However, learned skills are typically evaluated in closed environments, overlooking the fact that real-world web deployment involves continuous shifts in invocation context, perceptual grounding, and execution feasibility. To this end, we introduce SkillShift-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating skill learning with controlled open-environment shifts. SkillShift-Bench simulates Contextual Shift, Perceptual Shift, and Execution Shift across three self-hosted web systems, and evaluates agents with diagnostics covering task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure. Comprehensive experiments reveal systematic robustness degradation under controlled shifts, characterized by lower success rates, higher interaction costs, and more frequent skill failures, with Execution Shift exerting the strongest pressure. We further formulate shifted skill execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and provide both a dynamic-regret analysis and a practical test-time adaptation method, demonstrating the feasibility of improving learned-skill execution without relearning the skill library. Code, tasks, environments, documentation, and the leaderboard are available at https://skillshift-bench.github.io/.
authors: Bo-Yu Chen, Zhi Zhou, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Introduces controlled Contextual, Perceptual, and Execution Shifts across three self-hosted web systems.
Measures task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure under changing conditions.
Finds systematic robustness degradation, with Execution Shift producing the strongest impact.
Frames shifted execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and proposes test-time adaptation without relearning the skill library.
Provides code, tasks, environments, documentation, and a leaderboard.

papers.abstract: Visual effects are often easier to demonstrate via reference than to describe in words. We study effect-reference editing, where a reference image shows a desired visual effect and language identifies which properties should guide the edit. Existing single-pass editing techniques often fail to make fine-grained edits, resulting in unintended changes to source content or deviations from the reference effect. We introduce KINESYS, a test-time adaptation framework for effect-reference editing that combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback to transfer the desired effect while preserving the composition and content of the original shot. To ensure KINESYS can produce a diverse set of edits that preserve the source, we develop a robust optimization strategy in which the generative model is fine-tuned across multiple noise samples and optimization runs. Evaluation with VLM judges, source preservation metrics (LPIPS, TPIPS), and a user study shows that KINESYS outperforms state-of-the-art image editors in source preservation; on effect transfer, it remains competitive with Nano Banana 2 and outperforms open-weight editors.
authors: Noah Frahm, Luchao Qi, Haoze Li, Dan B Goldman, Sambit Bhattacharya, Roni Sengupta
bullets: Targets fine-grained effect-reference editing guided by both a reference image and language.
Combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback during optimization.
Fine-tunes across multiple noise samples and optimization runs to produce diverse, source-preserving edits.
Evaluations using VLM judges, preservation metrics, and a user study show stronger source preservation than existing editors.
Effect transfer is competitive with Nano Banana 2 and better than open-weight editors.

papers.abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.
authors: Yepeng Liu, Shengmai Chen, Xuandong Zhao, Chengzhi Liu, Dawn Song, Xin Eric Wang, Yuheng Bu
bullets: Motivation: Test-time training improves scientific discovery but incurs substantial computational cost from online model-weight updates.
Method: TTME continually distills experience into external memory to guide later discovery without changing model weights.
Evaluation: TTME and TTT are compared within the same discovery framework, differing only in their test-time adaptation method.
Results: TTME outperforms TTT on all five evaluated mathematical tasks while reducing FLOPs by 82.8–84.6% and runtime by 47.7–58.4%.
Scope: Findings are demonstrated in the evaluated scientific-discovery settings.

papers.abstract: Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time. It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://osheraz.github.io/RISE/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing among multiple valid recovery motions based on scene and task requirements.
Learns a recovery vocabulary linking intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback.
Uses a visual diffusion planner to predict future body-state intent and steer it with task costs.
Generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent to shape recovery execution.
Simulation shows diverse, terrain-adaptive, and steerable recoveries; real-world demonstrations are provided on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: Camera-trap species classification is dominated by large models from well-resourced organisations, which often lack the species-level distinctions regional conservation needs, such as native red versus invasive grey squirrels in the UK. We ask whether open weights let a small team with a modest dataset and a single GPU take a real part in AI development. We fine-tuned the open DeepFaune classifier on 28 UK classes, paired it with the unmodified MegaDetector v6, and compared the resulting DeepFaune-UK v1.2 with DeepFaune v1.5.0 and SpeciesNet on 20,212 hand-verified MammalWeb citizen-science images, after removing sequences sharing any of 1,039 images with our training archive. DeepFaune-UK achieved a strict image-level accuracy of 88.8%, including empty frames, against 56.5% and 59.0% for the baselines, but at DeepFaune's coarser label resolution DeepFaune v1.5.0 was more accurate, though not significantly under contributor resampling (91.4% vs. 88.8%). As DeepFaune v1.5.0 uses a newer DINOv3-based classifier, we applied the identical recipe, without new data, to that classifier. The resulting DeepFaune-UK v1.3 reached 90.6% strict accuracy, narrowed the like-for-like gap to 0.8 points and reduced roe deer misclassified as fallow deer by 69%. On 1,850 images from the 26 contributors with no overlapping images, the three DeepFaune-based models did not differ significantly (90.5%, 90.6%, 89.9% like-for-like). Fine-tuning on 10% of the training crops (about 150 per class) gave out-of-distribution accuracy similar to using all of them, and a DINOv2 run on this subset took about 22 minutes with under 4 GB of GPU memory. Open weights thus make regional model development feasible for small teams, but the largest like-for-like gain came from a newer base model trained by others, so this democratisation depends on large actors continuing to release open weights, under licences that may change.
bullets: A UK-specific model was fine-tuned for 28 classes, including native red and invasive grey squirrels, using an open DeepFaune classifier and unmodified MegaDetector.
DeepFaune-UK v1.2 reached 88.8% strict image-level accuracy, outperforming the reported baselines, but was less accurate at DeepFaune’s coarser label resolution.
Applying the same regional fine-tuning recipe to the newer DINOv3-based classifier produced 90.6% accuracy and reduced roe-deer/fallow-deer confusion by 69%.
Using only 10% of training crops produced similar out-of-distribution accuracy; one subset training run took about 22 minutes and under 4 GB of GPU memory.
The approach supports small-team regional model development, but its largest gain came from a newer model released by a larger organisation, with licensing remaining a limitation.

(b) Inference and evaluation: MegaDetector v6 localises animals, people and vehicles; only animal crops are classified, and the image label is that of the most confident animal detection. DeepFaune-UK and the two baselines are scored on the MammalWeb out-of-distribution set, which plays no part in training, classifier selection or threshold tuning (Sections 3.3 and 3.5).

papers.selection_reason: Investigates efficient fine-tuning of open-weight camera-trap models for regional wildlife classification with modest data. This is a relevant case study in test-time adaptation and continual learning for embodied perception.
papers.title: Standing on Open Shoulders: Regional Fine-Tuning of Open-Weight Camera-Trap Models for UK Wildlife with Modest Data and Compute
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning open-weight camera-trap models with modest UK data and compute can deliver strong regional species classification, though progress still depends on access to newer open base models.

papers.abstract: Adapting ASR to a domain with only untranscribed audio typically relies on pseudo-labeling, a strong teacher transcribes the audio and a student is fine-tuned on it. Because supervised fine-tuning (SFT) treats every pseudo-label token as a target, the student inherits the teacher's errors. We show that using the same pseudo-labels as a reward reference for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is more robust to label noise. In the banking domain, GRPO yields 29.3% to 56.2% relative WER improvements over SFT on Whisper-generated labels, and the advantage holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains and four languages. While SFT reproduces almost 100% of teacher errors verbatim, GRPO passes through only 27%. Rollout statistics explain why, erroneous pseudo-label words rarely appear in on-policy rollouts, so group-relative advantages stay aligned with the clean transcript, whereas SFT forces them into the policy's support and collapses the reward variance GRPO relies on.
authors: Shashi Kumar, Yanis Labrak, Sergio Burdisso, Esa\'u Villatoro-Tello, Petr Motlicek, Kadri Hacioglu, Andreas Stolcke
bullets: SFT makes students inherit nearly all teacher transcription errors, while GRPO passes through far fewer.
GRPO improves relative WER over SFT by 29.3%–56.2% in banking-domain adaptation using Whisper-generated labels.
The benefit holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains, and four languages.
On-policy rollouts rarely contain erroneous pseudo-label words, preserving useful group-relative reward signals.
Scope: results concern semi-supervised ASR adaptation with untranscribed audio and pseudo-label supervision.

papers.selection_reason: Applies Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to semi-supervised ASR, using pseudo-labels as rewards to improve robustness against label noise.
papers.title: Pseudo-Labels as Rewards, Not Targets: Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Semi-Supervised ASR
papers.tldr: Using pseudo-labels as reward references rather than hard targets makes GRPO substantially more robust to noisy ASR supervision than SFT.

papers.abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.
authors: Xiaopeng Ke, Zhixin Wang, Xuebo Liu, Xinyu Ma, Xing Zheng, Bowen Song, Weiqiang Wang, Min Zhang
bullets: Introduces a seven-dataset benchmark spanning domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and five independent human labels per instance.
Evaluates annotations against human labeling distributions using Fleiss kappa rather than single-label accuracy alone.
Proposes ANT-OR, which refines prompts by distilling contrastive rules from positive and negative feedback.
Improves agreement@≥2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves near-best distributional alignment, within 2 Fleiss-kappa points of the best result.
Targets complex, evolving guidelines and reasonable annotator disagreement, especially on boundary cases.

papers.abstract: Multi-task deep learning has been developed to ensure explainability in computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems. These systems simultaneously predict interpretable characteristics of findings in auxiliary tasks to help radiologists assess the reliability of the diagnostic prediction. However, the CAD's opinion would not be referred to when the auxiliary task prediction deviates from the radiologist's expectation. To further leverage CAD's knowledge in the above situation, we proposed a multi-task gradient assist (MGA) method that brings interactivity to multi-task models without additional training. MGA allows radiologists to give feedback to the CAD and ask for additional diagnostic suggestions. Using two datasets of mammography and CT, we show that MGA successfully improves diagnostic accuracy upon feedback on various auxiliary tasks. Compared to an existing method using forward propagation only, MGA performs more robustly and can be combined to further improve accuracy. Our method paves a promising way for integrating artificial intelligence into image diagnosis.
bullets: Addresses cases where CAD auxiliary predictions conflict with a radiologist’s expectations.
Introduces multi-task gradient assist (MGA), enabling interactive feedback without additional training.
Uses radiologist feedback to request updated diagnostic suggestions.
Improves diagnostic accuracy across auxiliary tasks on mammography and CT datasets.
MGA is more robust than a forward-propagation-only method and can be combined with it.

papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting plays an important role in real-world applications, where probabilistic approaches provide uncertainty estimates for decision-making. Real-world systems are inherently non-stationary, leading to distribution shifts between training and test data. However, existing probabilistic methods mainly focus on modeling data distributions under standard settings, while distribution shift methods often handle such shifts in a coarse manner, failing to characterize shift degree and adapt prediction strategy accordingly. As a result, they often produce miscalibrated and unreliable forecasts. To address this issue, we propose REMIND, a retrieval-guided probabilistic framework for spatiotemporal forecasting under distribution shift. REMIND leverages retrieval to estimate how well current observation are supported by historical patterns, enabling adaptive prediction under different shift regimes. It employs spatiotemporal retrieval to construct a memory bank and introduces a dual branch architecture, combining a memory-calibrated probabilistic branch for mild shifts with a deviation-aware probabilistic branch for severe shifts. A shift-adaptive gate, guided by retrieval similarity and memory dispersion, balances the two branches according to shift degree. We further design a hierarchical Gaussian mixture to capture heterogeneous uncertainty over the dual branch predictions, and introduce a memory perturbation training scheme to improve generalization. Experiments on real-world datasets with distribution shifts demonstrate that REMIND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both forecasting accuracy and probabilistic prediction quality.
authors: Haochen Lv, Jianhao Zhang, Zhichen Lei, Yang Jiang, Xiaowei Mao, Shengnan Guo, Youfang Lin, Huaiyu Wan
bullets: Addresses miscalibrated forecasts caused by non-stationary data and varying shift severity.
Builds a spatiotemporal memory bank to measure support from historical patterns.
Combines mild-shift memory-calibrated and severe-shift deviation-aware probabilistic branches.
Uses a retrieval- and dispersion-guided gate plus hierarchical Gaussian mixtures to model uncertainty.
Experiments on real-world shifted datasets show improved forecasting accuracy and probabilistic quality over existing methods.
