papers.abstract: This paper presents the engineering implementation methods of the SKG inference framework and provides complete case studies across four domains. Case 1, 2D Dissipative Mechanical System: OOD MSE is 1.69 to 4.12 times lower than the best neural baseline; the state-dependent metric yields a 10^8-order improvement under controlled conditions. Case 2, Target Detection Sim-to-Real: Real-machine mAP increases from 0.2564 to 0.4964 (+24.00 points, single-run experiment, 32 images, point estimate), and AP75 increases from 0.1736 to 0.5765 (+40.29 points), with no real-machine retraining required. Case 3, Sequence Modeling sine to square: OOD MSE is 0.0296 versus Transformer 0.0641 (mean of 5 seeds, p=0.024). Case 4, Molecular Dynamics MD17: ID@100 ADE is 0.0285 versus ESTAG 0.1467; OOD@100 is 0.0316 versus 0.1411 (single seed). For each case, we present the objective, applied SKG theory, parameter settings, baseline comparison protocol, data results, and sources of advantage. Following the cases, we provide the complete methodology: pre-validation, task invariant construction, three-stage training, residual training, and the four theorems and one proposition supporting these methods. This paper not only demonstrates effective configurations of SKG across four domains but also honestly reports the variance of single-run experiments, limitations of single-seed results, negative updates caused by parameterization mismatch, and practical experience of using engineering thresholds as diagnostic signals rather than hard constraints.
authors: Jian An, Chaoshi Wu, Xinpan Luo
bullets: Covers dissipative mechanics, sim-to-real target detection, sine-to-square sequence modeling, and MD17 molecular dynamics.
Methodology includes pre-validation, task-invariant construction, three-stage and residual training, plus supporting theoretical results.
Reported gains include lower OOD error in mechanics and sequence modeling, improved real-machine detection without retraining, and lower MD17 ADE than the cited baseline.
Results include single-run, single-seed, and small-sample experiments, so several findings have limited statistical reliability.
The paper discusses parameterization mismatch, experiment variance, and using engineering thresholds as diagnostics rather than hard constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Presents engineering implementations of the SKG inference framework for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across various domains, focusing on robustness.
papers.title: SKG in Practice: OOD Generalization Cases Across FourDomains
papers.tldr: SKG is implemented and evaluated across four domains, showing promising in- and out-of-distribution performance while documenting practical limitations and diagnostic lessons.

papers.abstract: Scientific, engineering, and mathematical reasoning tasks can admit multiple valid solutions, while exhaustive annotation of the full solution set is often prohibitively costly. Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) applies reinforcement learning to unlabeled test instances, offering a label-free approach to multiple-solution reasoning. In this setting, generation frequency serves two opposing objectives: correctness estimation favors frequent outcomes, whereas outcome-level diversity preservation favors less frequent outcomes. We term this tension the \textbf{Frequency Conflict}. To resolve this conflict, we propose MS-TTRL, which obtains frequency-independent correctness estimates through Outcome-Level Self-Verification while reserving generation frequency solely for diversity preservation. Three-State Outcome Cache and the Candidate State support verification reuse across repeated observations and confidence-aware handling of ambiguous outcomes, while Confidence-Gated Inverse Probability Scaling selectively strengthens the learning signals of rare, reliably verified outcomes. Experiments across two benchmarks, four multiple-solution tasks, and three backbone models, each evaluated with five random seeds, show that MS-TTRL improves Recovery Rate by 19.13 percentage points on average over the best-performing label-free baseline and approaches the performance of the supervised IPS-GRPO.
authors: Zhixia Zhang, Binqian Xu, Huaiyang Wang, Yikun Ban, Dianbo Liu
bullets: Multiple-solution reasoning lacks exhaustive labels, motivating reinforcement learning directly on unlabeled test instances.
The method uses outcome-level self-verification to estimate correctness independently of generation frequency.
A Three-State Outcome Cache and Candidate State reuse verification and handle ambiguous outcomes with confidence awareness.
Confidence-Gated Inverse Probability Scaling amplifies learning signals for rare outcomes that are reliably verified.
Across two benchmarks, four tasks, and three backbones, MS-TTRL improves Recovery Rate by 19.13 percentage points on average over the strongest label-free baseline and nears supervised IPS-GRPO.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task-specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.
authors: Dongki Kim, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Soyeong Jeong, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Addresses the expertise- and effort-intensive bottleneck of translating observations into scientific principles.
Forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships into inductive principles.

Outperforms baselines based on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while producing literature-consistent principles.

New observations are then used to revise the hypotheses involved, and the updated hypotheses support principle reconstruction, forming a continuous cycle of scientific knowledge construction and application.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly prediction (AP) aims to estimate future anomaly risks from current observations, providing early-warning signals for proactive intervention and maintenance in complex systems. Existing unsupervised AP methods follow a perturbation-based paradigm, where predefined or random perturbations are injected into historical windows to simulate abnormal future evolution. However, these methods share perturbations across different variables and contexts, and learn deterministic history-to-future evolution. In reality, anomaly evolution is variable- and context-dependent: the same perturbation may be amplified into abnormal future dynamics in one variable or context, while being absorbed as normal fluctuation in another. In addition, future evolution is not uniquely determined by a historical window, since similar histories may lead to multiple plausible trajectories, such as gradual degradation or abrupt changes. To address these problems, we propose EVOLVE, a unified framework that models unsupervised AP via variable- and context-conditioned perturbations and uncertainty-aware future reasoning. EVOLVE constructs context-specific anomaly perturbations through an adaptive anomaly prototype memory, which can dynamically update and retrieve relevant perturbations at the variable level. EVOLVE models uncertainty by sampling multiple latent historical states and decoding through complementary smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses, and the disagreement among decoded future trajectories is used to estimate future anomaly risk. Extensive experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that EVOLVE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art anomaly prediction baselines.
authors: Jianxin Jin, Kai Zhao, Shiyan Hu, Yang Shu, Peng Chen, Meng Wang, Zhongwen Rao, Yijie Li, Jing Wang, Bin Yang, Chenjuan Guo
bullets: Addresses the limitations of shared perturbations and deterministic history-to-future assumptions in unsupervised anomaly prediction.
Uses an adaptive anomaly prototype memory to retrieve and update variable- and context-specific perturbations.
Samples multiple latent historical states and decodes them with smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses.
Estimates future anomaly risk from disagreement among the resulting possible future trajectories.
Experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets show consistent improvements over existing anomaly-prediction baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture of EVOLVE. Given a historical window, EVOLVE first encodes the input into a normal historical representation Hn T . During training, Adaptive Anomaly Injection (AAI) retrieves variable-conditioned perturbations from the Anomaly Prototype Memory (APM) and constructs an anomaly-aware historical representation Ha T , while Anomaly Pattern Analysis (APA) progressively updates the dynamic prototype bank using residual-based anomaly-aware future representations. Both the normal and anomaly-aware historical views are then processed by Uncertainty-Aware Latent Modeling (UALM), which samples multiple latent semantic hypotheses and estimates their evolution-mode probabilities. The Dual-Structured Decoder (DSD) decodes these hypotheses through smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses to generate multiple plausible future trajectories. During inference, anomaly-aware injection, APA, and dynamic prototype updating are disabled, and future anomaly scores are computed from the predictive disagreement among decoded trajectories.

Fig. 1. Different impacts of similar historical perturbations on future evolution under time series heterogeneity. (a) Perturbations are amplified with abnormal evolution. (b) Perturbations are absorbed with normal evolution.

papers.abstract: Non-stationarity induces test-time distribution shifts in time series forecasting (TSF), resulting in forecast residuals between predictions and the corresponding ground truth. Recent works on test-time adaptation for TSF address this by introducing lightweight calibration modules around frozen forecasters, updated using observations that become incrementally available at test time. Existing approaches typically employ channel-wise adapters, implicitly assuming that forecast residuals are inherently channel-specific. However, we observe that forecast residuals often exhibit substantial shared structure across channels, suggesting that fully independent channel-wise parameterization may be redundant. Motivated by this observation, we propose the Dual-Branch Calibration Module (DBCM), which shares adaptation capacity across channels through a shared adapter while retaining limited channel-specific flexibility through a low-rank channel-wise adapter, further enhanced by channel mixing and nonlinear gated modulation. Extensive experiments show that DBCM consistently outperforms prior methods across diverse datasets, horizons, and backbones.
authors: Jaebyeong Jeon, Kunwoo Kang, Sang Yup Lee, Kibok Lee
bullets: Forecast residuals under distribution shift often share structure across channels, making fully independent channel-wise adaptation potentially redundant.
DBCM uses a dual-branch module: a shared adapter plus a low-rank channel-wise adapter.
Channel mixing and nonlinear gated modulation further refine the calibration process.
Experiments across diverse datasets, forecasting horizons, and backbones show consistent improvements over prior methods.

papers.abstract: This paper studies the problem of test-time robustness scaling for large vision-language models (LVLMs), which aims to mitigate language bias during inference. Existing approaches typically adopt test-time scaling techniques such as contrastive decoding to improve inference performance. Despite the progress, the performance of these approaches is far from satisfactory due to intentional evidence removal during perturbations and redundant inference cost. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Margin-gated Contrastive Debiasing with Evidence Restoration (MAGIC). The core of our MAGIC is to evaluate the decision margins of LVLMs to selectively activate textual and visual perturbation branches for efficient debiased inference. In particular, our MAGIC first measures the prediction margins of crucial tokens, and applies a gating function to identify low-confidence responses that are susceptible to language biases. For selected samples, we integrate the token logits from multiple textual and image perturbation branches with the original ones for debiased decision. More importantly, we selectively restore the most informative corrupted views with sharp prediction distributions for ambiguous samples after debiasing, enabling evidence recovery for discriminative decision-making. We further utilize a calibration dataset to actively identify and prune ineffective branches during contrastive debiasing for cost reduction. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed MAGIC in comparison with extensive baselines.
authors: Shunshun Gu, Enze Zhang, Ming Pei, Hang Zhou, Xiao Luo
bullets: Targets language bias and inefficient inference in test-time robustness scaling for large vision-language models.
Uses token-level prediction margins to gate textual and visual perturbation branches only for low-confidence responses.
Combines logits from selected perturbations with original predictions to enable debiased decisions.
Restores informative corrupted views with sharp prediction distributions to recover evidence for ambiguous samples.
Uses calibration-based branch pruning to reduce redundant contrastive-debiasing cost; experiments on benchmark datasets support its effectiveness against baselines.

papers.abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
authors: Yuval Kansal, Karen Ullrich, Polina Kirichenko, Ilia Kulikov, Niraj K. Jha, Mohammad Pezeshki, Mark Ibrahim
bullets: Addresses the limits of temporary in-context reflection and costly, interference-prone full fine-tuning.
After failure, the agent reflects, extracts a lesson, distills it into a lightweight adapter, and stores it in a retrievable lesson library.
Uses frozen base weights with adapters adding about 0.02% of the base model’s parameters each.
Across GAIA, Claw-Eval, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, success rates improve by 8.9–17.0 percentage points.
Lessons reduce repeated mistakes, nearly double correction reliability, and transfer to new tasks without additional training.

papers.abstract: Indoor radio map estimation (RME) is essential for wireless applications such as coverage planning, localization, and network deployment. However, most existing methods follow a supervised learning paradigm that requires costly labeled data and task-specific model training. Moreover, indoor environments involve privacy-sensitive information, such as building layouts and structures, that often cannot be centralized. To address these challenges, we make the first attempt to formulate indoor RME as a collaborative in-context learning (ICL) problem. We propose Poly-Ripple, a framework in which multiple clients perform ICL using large autoregressive vision models (LAVMs) without model updates. Each client is prompted by its private demonstrations and predicts the radio map for the same scene query. To capture the causal structure of wireless propagation outward from the transmitter (Tx), we adopt ripple-ordered autoregressive modeling. We further introduce importance-aware aggregation to exploit heterogeneous contextual knowledge distributed across clients under the context length constraint. We provide theoretical analysis and conduct extensive experiments on a public indoor RME benchmark. The experimental results show that Poly-Ripple consistently outperforms representative ICL baselines, while aligning with our theoretical analysis.
bullets: Reframes indoor radio map estimation as a collaborative in-context learning task, reducing reliance on centralized labeled data and task-specific training.
Uses large autoregressive vision models without model updates; each client predicts a shared scene’s radio map from private demonstrations.
Applies ripple-ordered autoregressive modeling to reflect wireless propagation outward from the transmitter.
Introduces importance-aware aggregation to combine heterogeneous client context under limited context length.
Theory and experiments on a public benchmark show consistent improvements over representative in-context learning baselines.

The server aggregates the ripple-structured local predictions via A(·) to collaboratively produce the final radio map.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multimodal emotion reasoning systems perform well on standard benchmarks, but improving them through instruction tuning can be computationally expensive. Agentic pipelines built from frozen models avoid this cost, but introduce a different challenge: when a prediction is wrong, the system must identify which agent or stage caused the error. We address this problem with an agentic framework for traceable multimodal emotion reasoning and prompt-space adaptation. Modality-specific perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical inputs and post evidence-cited observations to a shared board. An integration agent combines these observations with retrieved multimodal examples to produce an emotion description, label set, and supporting citations, while an MLLM critic can request one revision before the output is finalized. For incorrect predictions, a separate evidence-grounded verification stage applies deterministic checks to verify that cited evidence and references are valid, and an entailment check to determine whether the final claims are supported by that evidence. Detected failures are then grouped by the responsible component and failure type, converted into targeted prompt patches, and accepted only after validation on a held-out set. This adapts the agent prompts without updating model weights. On the MER2025 dataset, targeted prompt adaptation outperforms the frozen static pipeline on all four MLLMs, ranging from 2B to 38B parameters, and matches or outperforms undifferentiated reflection baselines on each of them: VideoLLaMA3-2B, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and InternVL2.5-38B. It improves F-score by 0.6--2.2 points depending on the backbone, including an increase from 52.3 to 54.5 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
bullets: Frozen perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical signals and post cited evidence to a shared board.
An integration agent combines observations with retrieved examples, while a critic may request one revision.
Deterministic verification checks citation validity and whether final emotion claims are entailed by the evidence.
Failures are attributed to components and failure types, then converted into validated targeted prompt patches.
On MER2025, targeted adaptation improves F-score by 0.6–2.2 points across four MLLMs, including 52.3→54.5 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

papers.abstract: Test-time language models adapt a compact memory while processing the input sequence. This perspective encompasses nonlinear fast-weight learning in LaCT, associative delta-rule updates in DeltaNet, and generalized delta-rule state updates in RWKV-7. Training these models to predict the next token does not explicitly require a fact to remain accessible after many subsequent memory updates. We study delayed supervision for this test-time memory: during post-training, ask a simulator-grounded question only after a long interval of unrelated events, and supervise its answer alongside ordinary next-token prediction. Questions are evaluated on disposable branches, so their answers never enter the continuing event stream. The construction distinguishes retention from revision: a retained fact must remain valid throughout the delay, whereas a revised fact must be answered with its latest value. We evaluate this approach on LaCT-760M and plain DeltaNet-1.3B using TextWorld training trajectories and shared BABILong and RULER evaluation panels, and include a separately reported RWKV-7 comparison. Relative to event-only training, delayed QA improves BABILong by 5.48 percentage points for LaCT and 1.32 points for DeltaNet, and single-needle RULER by 1.45 and 3.27 points, respectively. The RWKV-7 comparison reports gains of 4.60 and 7.00 points on its own panels. These results support delayed semantic supervision as a practical outer training objective for usable test-time memory, while leaving open how much of the benefit derives specifically from delay rather than general question-answering and answer-termination supervision.
bullets: Targets a gap in next-token training: facts need not remain accessible after many memory updates.
Supervises simulator-grounded QA after long delays, using disposable branches so answers do not alter the event stream.
Separately tests retention of unchanged facts and revision to a fact’s latest value.
Improves BABILong and single-needle RULER performance for LaCT and DeltaNet; a separately reported RWKV-7 comparison also shows gains.
The study does not isolate how much improvement comes from delay versus general QA and answer-termination supervision.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework integrating Bayesian physiological modeling with optimal control strategies to achieve uncertainty-aware, personalized hemodynamic regulation during fluid resuscitation. An uncertainty-aware variational autoencoder state-space model (UVAE-SSM) was first developed to capture the dynamical relationship between mean arterial pressure (MAP) and fluid infusion using limited data, while explicitly modeling aleatoric uncertainty (i.e., randomness in the measurements, such as sensor noise). Then, a Bayesian nonlinear state-space model (BNSSM) was developed by utilizing Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to capture epistemic uncertainty arising from physiological and patient-specific variability, enabling the creation of a virtual patient generator (VPG). Building on this uncertainty-aware modeling framework, a stochastic radial basis function model predictive control (sRBF-MPC) algorithm was designed to track the MAP target while satisfying physiological constraints. Finally, an online fine-tuning algorithm was developed to adapt the nominal UVAE-SSM using streaming VPG data, enabling progressive personalization during closed-loop therapy. Simulation results across unseen animal subjects and an independent human clinical dataset demonstrated the strong predictive accuracy and cross-population generalizability of the UVAE-SSM and BNSSM models. Closed-loop evaluations confirmed that the proposed sRBF-MPC framework achieved stable MAP regulation while providing better risk-aware control compared to quadratic MPC (Q-MPC) and stochastic quadratic MPC (sQ-MPC). Overall, the proposed framework accounts for inter- and intra-patient variability through online model adaptation, offering a promising step toward uncertainty-aware, personalized hemodynamic modeling and control in critical care.
bullets: Models MAP–fluid infusion dynamics from limited data while representing measurement noise and physiological uncertainty.
Uses Bayesian neural networks to generate virtual patients and support risk-aware control.
Applies stochastic radial basis function model predictive control to track MAP targets under physiological constraints.
Online fine-tuning adapts the model using streaming virtual-patient data for progressive personalization.
Simulations on unseen animal subjects and an independent human dataset showed predictive generalizability and stable closed-loop MAP regulation versus quadratic MPC approaches.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Proposed uncertainty-aware modeling framework. (a) UVAE-SSM as nominal model: The encoder maps a sliding window of NA MAP measurements and infusion rates (yk−NA:k, uk−NA:k) to the parameters (µx, σx) of a Gaussian latent distribution. A latent state xk is drawn via the reparameterization trick and passed to the deterministic transition network, which predicts the next latent state x̂k+1 given (xk, uk). The probabilistic decoder maps the latent state to a predictive MAP distribution N (µy , σ2 y), explicitly capturing aleatoric uncertainty in the hemodynamic output. Dashed lines indicate training-only connections used to provide supervision targets for the transition loss. (b) BNSSM as VPG: The encoder and decoder form a deterministic autoencoder that maps observations to latent states and reconstructs MAP. The transition function fβ(xk, uk) is implemented as a BNN, where weights β are treated as random variables with variational posterior qη(β), approximated via Bayes by Backprop. At inference, β is sampled once per complete simulation trajectory from qη(β); each distinct draw yields one virtual patient realization.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance, AI agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments to tackle complex sequential tasks (e.g., document processing, cross-application collaboration), relying heavily on actions ranging from GUI operations to semantic APIs. However, three core challenges persist: the "scale dilemma" of massive tool ecosystems exceeding LLM context windows, the "non-stationarity" of tool quality due to updates or outages, and the "heterogeneity" of feedback formats (pixels, text, structured data) creating information silos. To address these, we propose AnyAct, a universal action layer that unifies available capabilities into a self-evolving action space, enabling agents to operate efficiently and reliably in large-scale, dynamic tool ecosystems. AnyAct's core design focuses on two objectives: constructing this action space via hierarchical progressive retrieval (filtering task-relevant actions) and test-time reliability evolution (pruning unreliable actions), and enabling reliability-aware action orchestration through a heterogeneous observation grounding module that unifies multi-modal feedback. Additionally, it defines a hybrid action space (primitive + semantic actions) and optimizes for a balance between task success rate and execution cost. Evaluations on LiveMCPBench and OSMCP (a new benchmark we developed for multi-granularity action collaboration) demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. AnyAct delivers substantial performance gains over baseline methods across various LLM base models on LiveMCPBench and improvements are particularly notable for models with constrained native capabilities. On OSMCP, it achieves 77.27% overall success with only 50 steps, which is half the steps required by most competitors.
bullets: Addresses tool-scale limits, changing tool reliability, and incompatible feedback across GUI, API, visual, textual, and structured interfaces.
Builds a self-evolving action space using hierarchical progressive retrieval and test-time pruning of unreliable actions.
Combines primitive and semantic actions with heterogeneous observation grounding for reliability-aware orchestration.
Balances task success with execution cost in dynamic, multi-tool environments.
Reports state-of-the-art results on LiveMCPBench and 77.27% success on OSMCP using 50 steps, notably benefiting models with limited native capabilities.

papers.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.
authors: Ali Najar, Hosein Hasani, Amir Kooshan Fattah, Yasamin Rajabi, Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah
bullets: Addresses the challenge of inferring unseen tasks from long interaction histories without the quadratic cost of full-trajectory transformer attention.
Uses a causal neural memory for fine-grained, within-episode adaptation and episode-level summaries for long-range task inference.
Supports test-time training and adaptation to unseen tasks and task families.
Achieves over 50% success on held-out Meta-World ML10/45 environments with low training and wall-clock budgets.
Outperforms transformer baselines on long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks through more structured exploration.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning, using neural memory to handle long interaction histories. This fits the Adaptation and Memory topic, specifically test-time learning and embodied memory.
papers.title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: METTA enables efficient long-context meta-reinforcement learning by combining linear-time within-episode memory with compact cross-episode task summaries for test-time adaptation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: \textit{can a VLA's own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution?} Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA $\pi_{0.5}$ and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.
authors: Atiksh Bhardwaj, Edward W. Duan, Junwon Seo, Prithwish Dan, Wei-Chiu Ma, Andrea Bajscy, Preston Culbertson
bullets: Addresses the need for reliable runtime monitoring of VLA policies without continuous human supervision.
Trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate execution progress and flag deviations.
Evaluated with the open-source π₀.₅ VLA on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Competitive with or better than VLM-based monitors and methods trained with failure data for task-failure detection.
Scope: focuses on monitoring execution progress using internal activations rather than preventing failures directly.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Progress Probes (P 2) decode task progress directly from the VLA’s internal activations. Using only successful demonstrations, we assign each timestep a normalized progress ζt and fit a linear probe to predict it from zit, the activation at layer i. At runtime, successful executions follow the expected progression through the task, whereas failed executions cause the decoded progress to lag or deviate from this nominal trajectory. Thus, the policy’s own representations enable us to construct a lightweight runtime monitor without failure data or an external foundation model.

papers.title: Progress Probes $P^2$: Lightweight Runtime Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Progress Probes use lightweight linear probes of a VLA’s internal activations to detect when manipulation tasks are going off-course, avoiding external VLM monitors.

papers.abstract: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.
bullets: Directly estimates a query point’s state, derivatives, and admissible bounds from nearby samples.
Formulates these quantities as latent variables in a constrained local optimisation problem, replacing long global training.
Theoretically provides finite-sample coverage and converges to the true state and derivatives under dense, noiseless sampling.
On six nonlinear benchmark functions, it outperformed Gaussian processes on noiseless data, especially with denser samples.
Prediction after data updates was substantially faster than GP and neural networks, but the advantage applies mainly when few predictions are needed between updates.

papers.abstract: Diffusion trajectory planners with domain-specific experts face a practical question in unseen regions: can they rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the planner itself adapt? We study this question using a planner with a shared adapter and per-domain expert adapters. Across three real-world held-out maps, none of eight test-time routing schemes improves the fleet-mean lateral offset over the static default, which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an oracle that selects the best expert for each scene reduces the mean offset by only 0.9 m. In contrast, reward-based fine-tuning on just 20 target-region scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet-mean offset of 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 m for the static default. Comparisons under the same target-region training budget show that target-region training drives the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine-tuning across training cities also improves open-loop offsets, although closed-loop performance deteriorates. Further diagnostics reveal that two test-time adaptation baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate trajectories. These results show the limited headroom for selecting among existing experts and the greater open-loop gains available from adapting the planner.
authors: Yun Li, Ehsan Javanmardi, Simon Thompson, Jiachen Gong, Qunli Zhang, Zifan Zeng, Shiming Liu, Peng Wang, Yidu Zhang, Manabu Tsukada
bullets: Across three held-out maps, none of eight routing schemes beats the static default in fleet-mean lateral offset.

Target-region training drives the gains, while replay helps limit forgetting on original operating domains.

papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed in high-stakes roles such as therapy, education, and personal assistance, their social cognition must be assessed reliably. Current Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks report aggregate scores that conflate two distinct competencies: explicit ToM (recognizing what someone believes) and applied ToM (using that belief to predict behavior). Building on this distinction, we investigate the gap and its recoverability using four structurally diverse benchmarks. Aggregate reporting obscures uneven competence: on SimpleToM, Llama-3.1-8B scores 51.5 percent overall while recognizing mental states at 99.4 percent and predicting behavior at only 28.9 percent. To assess recovery, we compare structured prompting, matched in-context learning, and our proposed Belief-State Test-Time Training (BSTTT), which adapts lightweight parameters on answered support questions through action reconstruction. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GPT-oss-20B, recovery depends on the model, task, and intervention. On SimpleToM, reminders combined with BSTTT improve Llama's behavior prediction by 40.8 percentage points; reminders account for most of the overall improvement, with BSTTT adding 1.3 to 5.5 points beyond reminders across models. Contextual examples often outperform weight updates, while BSTTT remains stronger in specific model-benchmark settings. Temporal belief tracking remains difficult despite partial recovery. These findings show that aggregate ToM scores can overstate applied competence while hiding performance recoverable through targeted assistance. We recommend decomposed reporting of explicit and applied accuracy alongside intervention comparisons that establish which failures are recoverable and under what conditions.
authors: Prajvi Saxena, Sabine Janzen, Wolfgang Maass
bullets: Aggregate ToM scores can hide a large gap between identifying mental states and applying them to predict behavior.
The study evaluates this gap and its recoverability across four structurally diverse benchmarks.
It compares structured prompting, matched in-context learning, and Belief-State Test-Time Training (BSTTT), which adapts lightweight parameters using action reconstruction.
Recovery varies by model and task: reminders often drive most gains, while BSTTT provides additional improvements in selected settings.
Temporal belief tracking remains difficult, motivating separate reporting of explicit and applied ToM accuracy and intervention effects.

papers.abstract: Domain generalization (DG) aims to improve the generalization of the model to any unseen domains. Targeting this goal, existing DG methods mainly focus on learning domain-invariant features or prompts from the given source domains. However, these methods rely on source-domain data, and collecting and annotating large-scale single- or multi-source datasets is often infeasible, limiting the practical applicability of DG. To tackle this challenge, we propose {\underline{Do}}main \underline{P}rompt Learning (DoP), a method built on a large vision-language model (e.g., CLIP) for zero-shot domain generalization, which recognizes unseen classes in unseen target domains without access to source-domain data. DoP essentially learns the target domain knowledge via prompt both in text and visual modalities to overcome the domain shift in text-visual modalities under the test-time adaptation formulation. Specifically, DoP first takes text domain learning (TDL) to simulate various distribution shifts by learning diverse style tokens implicitly in the text space with inter-style diversity loss and intra-style consistency loss. Subsequently, DoP employs visual domain learning (VDL) to further refine the target-domain-relevant style token generated by TDL by making use of the test visual data with self-supervised learning. Extensive experiments on popular DG benchmark datasets (e.g., PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and DomainNet) and ImageNet show that our DoP consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art DG approaches. Codes are available at: https://github.com/shiming-chen/DoP.
authors: Shiming Chen, Shuhuang Chen, Salman Khan, Fahad Shahbaz Khan
bullets: Addresses the impracticality of source-data-dependent domain generalization when labeled source datasets are unavailable.
Learns target-domain knowledge through text and visual prompt adaptation under a test-time adaptation setting.
Text Domain Learning simulates diverse style shifts using style tokens with inter-style diversity and intra-style consistency objectives.
Visual Domain Learning refines target-relevant style tokens using unlabeled test images and self-supervised learning.
Experiments on PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, DomainNet, and ImageNet report consistent improvements over existing DG methods.

Specifically, TDL first simulates various distribution shifts by learning diverse domain prompts implicitly in the text space with inter-style diversity loss and intra-style consistency loss and implicitly generates the style token S∗ that is relevant to the test image in target domains. Subsequently, VDL explicitly refines S∗ using the test visual data with self-supervised learning. Finally, DoP adopts the refined domain prompt for class prediction following the standard CLIP.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions and navigate to target locations. However, current VLN agents often suffer severe performance degradation in unseen environments due to distribution shifts. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm to bridge this gap, yet existing methods that rely on unsupervised entropy minimization can propagate errors through the trajectory, causing cascading failures in navigation. Recent methods mitigate this by incorporating human feedback, but they apply trajectory-level supervision uniformly across all steps without localizing the actions is truly informative, leading to inefficient feedback utilization and mismatched optimization granularity. To address these limitations, we propose FETA, a Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation method that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization reliability. To reduce unnecessary human interventions, we introduce a hierarchical sample selection strategy to localize informative samples. Specifically, we first filter trajectories whose normalized policy entropy exhibits large fluctuations. Within each selected trajectory, we further select the critical action via an entropy-gradient saliency criterion and query a single binary feedback on its correctness. A discrepancy-aware entropy optimization objective then updates the policy only at the queried step, with adaptive scaling that assigns larger relative weights to samples with greater prediction-feedback discrepancy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FETA achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer human interventions, while remaining robust under noisy feedback and continual adaptation settings.
authors: Zixu Wang, Huaquan Zhang, Shoukai Xu, Jinwu Hu, Zhiquan Wen, Mingkui Tan
bullets: Unseen environments can cause severe VLN degradation, while entropy minimization may amplify navigation errors.
FETA hierarchically selects high-value feedback: unstable trajectories first, then critical actions using entropy-gradient saliency.
It queries one binary correctness signal per selected action and updates the policy only at that step.
Discrepancy-aware entropy optimization adaptively emphasizes actions where predictions and feedback disagree.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance with fewer interventions, including robustness to noisy feedback and continual adaptation.

papers.abstract: Recently, electroencephalography (EEG)-based brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have gained traction as portable neural measurement systems. However, the practical deployment of these instruments is often hindered by nonstationarity and cross-subject distribution shifts, which lead to significant intersubject inconsistency. Existing adaptation methods remain impractical for real-time measurement scenarios, as they typically require offline access to source or aggregated target data. To address these challenges, this article proposes memory-augmented online test-time adaptation (OTTA) with perturbation consistency and confidence calibration (MOPC), a source-free framework designed to enhance the reliability of BCI instrumentation. MOPC enables the measurement system to update its decoding parameters on the fly during the inference stage, facilitating single-pass adaptation without accessing sensitive source data. We introduce random-mask perturbations to enforce prediction consistency against inherent EEG signal noise and acquisition artifacts. Furthermore, a confidence-calibrated reweighting loss is designed to integrate feature-space similarity, effectively mitigating unreliable pseudolabels and class imbalance during continuous signal acquisition. To ensure system stability and prevent the catastrophic forgetting of established neural patterns, a lightweight memory module is incorporated to regularize parameter updates within a tight latency budget. Evaluated on the BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI datasets, MOPC achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods by 2.22~\% and 3.67~\%, respectively, while keeping the per-trial adaptation latency to approximately 40--60 ms. This study provides a robust, recalibration-free solution for real-time EEG decoding, marking a significant advancement in the precision and usability of practical BCI measurement instruments.
authors: Kunkun Zhang, Kehao Wu, Zhitao Chen, Haigen Hu, Qianwei Zhou
bullets: Addresses nonstationarity and intersubject distribution shifts that hinder practical EEG-based BCIs.
Uses random-mask perturbations to promote prediction consistency under EEG noise and artifacts.
Applies confidence-calibrated, feature-similarity-based reweighting to reduce unreliable pseudolabel effects and class imbalance.
Adds a lightweight memory module to stabilize updates and limit catastrophic forgetting within a tight latency budget.
On BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI, it reports improvements of 2.22% and 3.67%, respectively, with approximately 40–60 ms per-trial adaptation latency.

papers.abstract: Object detection models for autonomous driving commonly experience substantial performance drops when deployed under adverse weather due to the domain shift between training data and real-world operating conditions. This degradation is especially evident when models trained on clear-weather images encounter foggy environments with reduced visibility and contrast. To address this challenge, we introduce FogTTA, an online test-time adaptation framework designed to improve the robustness of Transformer-based object detectors in fog. Using RF-DETR as the underlying object detector, FogTTA enables real-time adaptation to the streaming target domain without requiring source data or retraining. The framework follows a teacher-student design, where the deployed model serves as the teacher and generates pseudo labels from weakly augmented target inputs. These predictions are subsequently refined through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering. The student model then learns from strongly augmented target sample using the Varifocal loss to mitigate pseudo-label noise. The teacher is updated via exponential moving averaging to ensure stable and continuous adaptation. Experiments show that FogTTA outperforms prior baselines, delivering improved detection accuracy and stability while maintaining real-time performance.
authors: Ali Abedi, Q. M. Jonathan Wu, Ning Zhang, Shiqi Tian
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by the domain shift from clear to foggy driving environments.
Uses a teacher–student test-time adaptation framework with pseudo-label refinement through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering.
Trains the student on strongly augmented target images with Varifocal loss to reduce pseudo-label noise.
Updates the teacher via exponential moving average for stable, continuous adaptation.
Experiments report improved accuracy and stability over prior baselines while maintaining real-time performance.

papers.abstract: A frozen multi-horizon forecaster can be corrected online from its own residuals. However, under label delay the target of a block arrives only after the whole horizon has passed, and the corrector's retained state grows with the number of channels. Aiming to combine a small retained state with a large error reduction, we propose DRiC (DCT Ridge Corrector), which fits a ridge regression of the leading discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients of the next residual block on those of the frozen forecast and of the latest input block, with sufficient statistics updated recursively. Its local variant, DRiC-L, keeps one such regression per channel; its global variant, DRiC-G, pools all channels into one regression, whose statistics do not depend on the channel count. A guard tracks a running scale of the frozen forecast's residual for each channel; it skips updates on blocks far outside that scale and clips the issued correction. We evaluate on seven datasets (four ETT series, Weather with its missing-value codes filled, Electricity, and Traffic) with DLinear, PatchTST, and iTransformer backbones, against 10 naive, gradient-trained, and closed-form methods. DRiC-L with eight DCT coefficients (DRiC-L8) reduces the mean squared error (MSE) by 14.55% on average over 126 conditions, against 12.98% for ELF, the most accurate comparator, while retaining 15-17 times less state, although ELF is more accurate on Traffic. DRiC-G retains 14.6 kB on the 321-channel Electricity data and 18.9 kB on the 862-channel Traffic data and is the most accurate method at or below its state on both. However, 5 to 7 of the 10 comparators, all with at least 10 times its state, are more accurate there. On the unfilled Weather file, DRiC-L8 without the guard has on average 8.0 times the frozen forecast's MSE, whereas with the guard it reduces the MSE by 7.94%. A residual-scale guard skips anomalous updates and clips corrections to improve robustness.
Across 126 conditions, DRiC-L8 reduces MSE by 14.55% on average, versus 12.98% for the strongest comparator, while using 15–17× less state.
DRiC-G uses only 14.6–18.9 kB on the largest datasets and performs strongly at comparable state, though higher-state methods can be more accurate and Traffic favors the comparator.

papers.title: Local and Global Recursive Ridge Regression for Online Residual Correction of Frozen Multivariate Forecasters under Label Delay

papers.abstract: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.
authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Bozhou Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited coverage of offline demonstrations for contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical deployment states.
Uses provenance-conditioned supervised learning to update policies online from human- and policy-generated data.
Evaluated on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, improving task progress and full-task completion over warm-start policies and matched offline demonstrations.
Performs comparably to a fixed-policy data-collection baseline while providing updated checkpoints during deployment.
Each task-specific post-training session completes in under one hour, with learning and checkpoint handling running asynchronously.

papers.abstract: Vision-based insertion requires correcting alignment errors while retaining useful behavior learned from demonstrations. We present ACT--Flow, an online learning framework that couples an adaptive Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) with a conditional residual flow policy. Following anchor-guided warmup, ACT absorbs successful executed actions through behavioral cloning, while residual targets are recomputed relative to the updated prior. A chunk-level critic learns from successful and failed interactions and evaluates final composed actions. Its estimates weight generated residual candidates for flow matching, complemented by supervision from successful real executions. Candidate scoring is confined to training; deployment uses RGB observations and samples one residual per action chunk. We evaluate the framework on power-plug, USB, and key insertion, together with cable routing and needle threading. Results show a five-task mean success rate of 66% at 20,000 post-initialization interaction steps, exceeding the strongest baseline by 18 percentage points at this checkpoint. Evaluations at matched checkpoints with the residual disabled show ACT's mean success increasing from 16% to 76%. Component ablations further support the complementary roles of behavior absorption, value weighting, and successful-action supervision.
authors: Yiqing Yuan, Zhi Li, Jinrong Yang, Mingshan Sun, Mei Yu Zhi, Yong Zhao, Liangliang Ren, Hui Cheng
bullets: Targets alignment correction in insertion and related manipulation tasks while preserving useful demonstration behavior.
Combines an adaptive Action Chunking Transformer with a conditional residual flow policy after anchor-guided warmup.
A chunk-level critic weights residual candidates during training, with additional supervision from successful real executions; deployment uses only RGB observations.
Achieves a 66% mean success rate across five tasks after 20,000 post-initialization interaction steps, 18 percentage points above the strongest baseline.
With residuals disabled, ACT's mean success rises from 16% to 76%; ablations support behavior absorption, value weighting, and successful-action supervision.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.
authors: Haori Lu, Tianyu Gao, Yaoyao Liu, Yingying Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining future-outcome anticipation with accumulated interaction experience in deployed LLM agents.
Uses a world model to imagine outcomes for multiple candidate actions without executing them in the environment.
Applies MPPI-style cost weighting based on predicted task progress and risk to select actions.
Employs dual-branch experience memory to improve both candidate planning and next-observation prediction.
Shows strong overall performance on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three LLM backbones.

papers.abstract: Trajectory demonstrations show robots how to behave but not why, leaving them to guess which features of the task actually matter. Incorrect guesses produce misaligned internal representations and lead to incorrect robot behaviors. Because task features are often semantically defined, we argue that natural language is better suited for specifying features rather than relying on demonstrations. Although existing representation editing methods have proposed using language to specify new features, only allowing additive edits produces feature sets that are often over-specified or too narrowly scoped, especially in sequential editing tasks. We propose the Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline (FLEX), which uses language models to iteratively refine a robot's internal representation of task features from natural language corrections via three complementary operations: Add missing features, Generalize existing specific features, and Mask irrelevant features. We evaluate FLEX on 2D navigation scenarios, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation tasks, and a real-world study using naturalistic human language corrections and real-robot demonstrations. Comparisons against single-operation and unscaffolded baselines show that all three operations are necessary in interactive scenarios, and that FLEX achieves consistently higher normalized reward compared to other feature editing approaches while maintaining compact, transferable representations. Project available at https://mit-clear-lab.github.io/FLEX/
authors: Audrey Lee, Nathaniel Dennler, Ilia Sucholutsky, Andreea Bobu
bullets: Robot demonstrations show what to do but may not clarify which task features matter, causing misaligned representations.
FLEX iteratively edits representations using three operations: add missing features, generalize overly specific ones, and mask irrelevant ones.
Evaluated on 2D navigation, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation, and real-robot demonstrations with naturalistic language corrections.
All three editing operations are needed for interactive scenarios; FLEX achieves higher normalized reward than compared editing baselines while preserving compact, transferable representations.

papers.abstract: Comparative Process Reward Models (PRMs) provide critical step-level guidance for autonomous web agents by evaluating state-conditioned preferences between candidate actions. However, existing preference training data synthesized via multi-policy sampling suffers from a severe scarcity of Grounded Minimal Contrastive Pairs (GMCPs)-where competing candidates target genuine on-page elements with identical action types. In representative baselines preference data (namely, WebArbiter), GMCPs account for merely 24.19%, biasing PRMs during training to rely on shallow shortcuts (such as element hallucinations and action type mismatches) rather than acquiring genuine contextual decision semantics. To address these challenges, we propose SURFPRM, a graph-guided process preference synthesis framework for comparative Web PRMs. SURFPRM structures web demonstrations into a persistent Interaction Element Graph that acts as an environment-grounded negative action proposal mechanism, systematically synthesizing contrastive negative actions across spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal confusion axes. This elevates the GMCP proportion from 24.19% to 74.60%, producing the curated SURFPRM-DATA dataset. Across six open-source backbones (3B to 9B parameters), PRMs trained on SURFPRM-DATA outperform baseline-trained models on average on WEBPRMBENCH and rival leading proprietary LLMs. In downstream reward-guided trajectory search on WEBARENA-LITE, SURFPRM provides step-level guidance for both GPT-4o (+14.21%) and GPT-4o-mini (+12.83%) policies, yielding substantial improvements in complex web task success rates.
bullets: Existing preference data contains few Grounded Minimal Contrastive Pairs (GMCPs), encouraging PRMs to use shortcuts instead of contextual decision semantics.
SURFPRM builds a persistent Interaction Element Graph to propose environment-grounded negative actions across spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal confusions.
It raises the GMCP share from 24.19% to 74.60%, producing the SURFPRM-DATA training set.
Across six 3B–9B open-source backbones, SURFPRM-trained PRMs outperform baseline-trained models on average on WEBPRMBENCH.
Reward-guided search improves WEBARENA-LITE success rates for GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini by 14.21% and 12.83%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Reusable skills help LLM-based agents solve complex tasks, but the agent must receive guidance before it commits to an ineffective approach. Existing skill mechanisms often expose only metadata and load full content on demand, leaving useful guidance unavailable until the agent decides to retrieve it. General memory methods can incur substantial maintenance overhead, while keeping guidance in conversation context risks repeatedly exposing the agent to irrelevant or harmful advice. We propose TipsWarm, a mechanism that complements existing skill mechanisms by maintaining a budgeted pool of skill-derived keypoints, or \textit{warm tips}, for selective injection into the context of every message turn. By separating event-triggered LLM assessment from inexpensive per-turn screening, it makes transferable skill guidance readily available while controlling maintenance costs. In three coding and iterative task-execution benchmarks, TipsWarm achieves the highest task success rate while remaining time-efficient, compared to recent skill and general memory baselines.
bullets: Existing skill systems may reveal guidance only after an agent commits to an ineffective approach.
TipsWarm selectively injects retained “warm tips” into every message turn.
It combines event-triggered LLM assessment with inexpensive per-turn screening.
Across three coding and iterative task-execution benchmarks, it achieves the highest reported task success rate while remaining time-efficient.
The approach is designed to reduce repeated exposure to irrelevant or harmful advice.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, perception models often struggle to generalize to new environments due to domain shifts. While unsupervised model adaptation offers a feasible solution without labor-intensive manual labeling, existing methods that rely solely on the ego-vehicle's data often lead to inferior pseudo-labeling performance. To address this critical issue, we propose LDE, Learning from Distributed ``Eyes", a novel framework that transforms collaborative perception (CP) into a source of high-quality supervision for model adaptation. This pseudo-labeling approach is hyperparameter-insensitive and relatively reliable, assuming CP often outperforms single-agent's perception. However, naively implementing this approach encounters (1) the communication bottleneck of sharing rich features under time and bandwidth constraints, (2) the view discrepancy between the CP view and the learner's Field of View (FoV), and (3) the unreliability even in CP-generated labels. To address these issues, we design an adaptation-oriented feature sharing mechanism that selectively transmits the most critical information for adaptation, an FoV filtering method that meticulously eliminates mismatched labels, and a curriculum learning strategy to progressively exploit pseudo labels. Extensive experiments on 3D object detection tasks demonstrate that LDE consistently outperforms both the pre-trained models and state-of-the-art unsupervised adaptation methods.
bullets: Addresses domain-shifted 3D object detection without manual labels, improving on ego-vehicle-only adaptation.
Uses an adaptation-oriented feature-sharing mechanism to reduce communication costs while preserving useful information.
Applies field-of-view filtering to remove collaborative labels that do not match the learner’s view.
Uses curriculum learning to gradually incorporate increasingly reliable pseudo-labels.
Experiments show consistent gains over pretrained models and existing unsupervised adaptation methods, without reported numerical results.

papers.abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.
authors: Xinxin Liu, Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Ming Li, Wentao Bao, Chen Chen, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: Addresses reliance on powerful closed-source planners by improving the planner model itself.
Combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning.
Uses harness-specific adapters to unify training across VLA skill invocation and control-code generation while keeping execution components fixed.
On LIBERO-PRO, raises a 9B planner’s success rate from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory.
Framework and trained planner checkpoints are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token. A natural explanation of where it goes wrong is compounding error: the student's mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, so recent methods keep training inside that region, through episode-length curricula, teacher-guided turns, prefix replay, or teacher intervention where the two disagree. We show this explanation is incomplete. From the states where the student departs most from the teacher, the teacher's own takeovers still finish the task, yet the student trained on its token scores keeps running out of turns. We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. The teacher rates each token without seeing where the episode ends, so its scores let through the safe, delaying moves that outcome-based RL would punish with zero reward, a penalty agentic OPD lacks. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout-scorer gap. We propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which repairs the scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states from the untrained student, running teacher takeovers from them, keeping the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training. Across three environments, two teachers and four students, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve teacher-student-environment cells, by 12.8 success points on average over the best of them in each cell. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/r2s/.
bullets: Problem: Token-level teacher scores can reward safe but delaying actions, creating a rollout–scorer gap that causes students to run out of turns even when the teacher can complete the task.
Method: Mine high-disagreement student states, run teacher takeovers, retain states passing consensus or an LLM-based reward-free check, and fine-tune the teacher on takeover-informed token scores.
Training then uses the repaired teacher as the frozen sole scorer in standard agentic OPD, without task rewards or takeover context.
Across three environments, two teachers, and four students, R2S beats three prior agentic-OPD methods in all 12 evaluated cells.
It gains an average of 12.8 success points over the strongest prior method per cell.

papers.abstract: Tactile-visual-language models combine vision and touch through a shared language space to recognize objects and materials. In real-world deployment, changes in lighting, contact quality or sensor hardware can shift visual or tactile inputs and degrade recognition performance. When both modalities contribute to a prediction, an unreliable modality can override correct evidence from the other. Since labeled data are generally unavailable during deployment, test-time adaptation offers a way to recover recognition performance from unlabeled observations. In this setting, we find that comparing accumulated observations with the text embeddings of candidate classes reveals modality reliability differences that confidence can miss. Refining features against competing classes also improves recognition beyond geometric alignment alone. These findings motivate SenseAlign, which uses a common semantic reference for test-time modality weighting and feature correction. Alignment Trust weights each modality according to its support for shared predicted classes. Anchor Realignment uses the same class text embeddings to fit a shared feature correction that separates predicted classes from alternatives. Both modules use the same unlabeled history while keeping all encoders frozen. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate strong recognition performance under both natural shifts and controlled corruptions.
authors: Chuyang Ye, Qinting Jiang, Jingyan Jiang
bullets: Addresses recognition degradation caused by lighting, contact-quality, and sensor-hardware shifts when labeled deployment data are unavailable.
Alignment Trust weights visual and tactile modalities by their support for shared predicted classes, revealing reliability differences that confidence may miss.
Anchor Realignment learns a shared feature correction that separates predicted classes from competing alternatives using class text embeddings.
Both modules reuse unlabeled observation history while keeping all encoders frozen.
Experiments across diverse datasets show strong recognition under natural shifts and controlled corruptions.

papers.abstract: Realistic few-shot adaptation of medical vision-language models (VLMs) can leave low-prevalence classes without any labeled support. The training-free SS- Text+ solver remains operational in this setting, but its zero-support prototypes receive no visual adaptation and fall back to a purely textual class prototype. We in- troduce Gated Knowledge-Guided Prototype Transfer (GProtoT), a pre-repulsion module that transfers supported-class visual residuals to missing classes using VLM similarity and an ontology-based clinical distance. A validation-free evidence gate scales transfer based on semantic relevance and residual agreement, thereby limiting unsupported extrapolation. In 50 paired realistic one-shot trials on MESSIDOR with FLAIR features, severe and proliferative diabetic retinopathy were absent from every support set. Relative to SS-Text+, gated ProtoT improved missing-class recall by 5.23 points, average class accuracy by 1.37 points, and the missing/supported recall harmonic mean by 1.83 points. It reduced negative- transfer frequency from 46-48% for ungated transfer to 2%, while at the cost of reductions of 1.20 percentage points in supported-class recall and 0.45 percentage points in top-1 accuracy. These results indicate that evidence-based gating provides a safety mechanism for the knowledge source. GProtoT is based on SS- Text+ and requires no gradients, validation data, or additional model inference, of- fering a low-compute path toward accountable adaptation under incomplete clini- cal supervision. Code is available: https://github.com/sumaiyaafridi/GProtoT
authors: Sumaiya Fazal, Rizwan Qureshi, Laleh Behjat, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou
bullets: Addresses zero-support classes in realistic few-shot medical VLM adaptation, where textual prototypes lack visual adaptation.
Transfers supported-class visual residuals using VLM similarity and ontology-based clinical distance.
Uses a validation-free evidence gate based on semantic relevance and residual agreement to limit unsupported extrapolation.
Across 50 paired one-shot trials on MESSIDOR, missing-class recall improved by 5.23 points and the missing/supported recall harmonic mean by 1.83 points.
Reduced negative-transfer frequency to 2%, with modest decreases in supported-class recall and top-1 accuracy.
