papers.abstract: Person re-identification (ReID) ranks an image gallery using either an image query or a textual query. In image-to-image (I2I) ReID, viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, and background changes can make distractors appear more similar than the true match. In text-to-image (T2I) ReID, incomplete or ambiguous descriptions may omit key visual evidence. We study this problem for vision-language model (VLM) based ReID, where attributes such as clothing color and carried objects provide useful fine-grained matching cues. However, directly using attribute-prompt similarities as retrieval scores is unreliable because templated prompts can be biased, correlated, and poorly calibrated. We therefore propose \textbf{PR}ompt-guided \textbf{A}ttribute-based \textbf{I}nference-time \textbf{S}imilarity \textbf{E}nhancement (\texttt{PRAISE}), a query-side test-time adaptation framework for VLM-based ReID. Instead of treating prompts as scores, \texttt{PRAISE} uses a transferable attribute-prompt bank to construct an \emph{Attribute-Conditioned Subspace} (ACS): a query-dependent low-rank subspace induced by the most compatible attribute prompts. ACS provides a controlled attribute-conditioned geometry for reshaping query--gallery affinities and guiding lightweight inference-time updates without identity or attribute labels. Experiments across multiple I2I- and T2I-ReID benchmarks show that \texttt{PRAISE} consistently improves VLM retrieval backbones and outperforms both generic and ReID-specific TTA baselines.
authors: Rajarshi Bhattacharya, Aryan Shukla, Shakeeb Murtaza, Christian Desrosiers, Jose Dolz, Maguelonne Heritier, Eric Granger
bullets: Addresses distractor similarity in image-to-image ReID and incomplete or ambiguous descriptions in text-to-image ReID.
Builds an Attribute-Conditioned Subspace from the most compatible prompts in a transferable attribute-prompt bank.
Uses this subspace to reshape query–gallery affinities and guide lightweight, label-free test-time updates rather than treating prompt similarities as direct scores.
Improves VLM retrieval backbones across multiple I2I- and T2I-ReID benchmarks and outperforms generic and ReID-specific test-time adaptation baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Method overview. PRAISE uses attribute prompts to construct a query-specific semantic subspace that stabilizes query-side adaptation under domain shift. At test time, it performs query-side episodic TTA with a fixed source-space gallery index. Gallery and prompt-bank embeddings are computed once and kept fixed; gradients update only the query-side normalization affine parameters.

Figure 1. Motivation and overview of PRAISE. (a) In I2I-ReID, raw visual similarity can retrieve distractors caused by camera, pose, or background bias. (c) PRAISE addresses both cases by selecting query-relevant attribute directions, orthogonalizing them into an Attribute-Conditioned Subspace (ACS), and using this controlled subspace to reshape query-gallery affinities during test-time.

papers.abstract: In object goal navigation (ObjectNav), an embodied agent must find a target object (e.g., "find a bed") in a previously unseen environment, relying on spatial commonsense such as object co-occurrence. Large Language Models (LLMs) encode this commonsense, but deploying them on robots exposes a trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency: cloud-based models incur latency and privacy risks, whereas small on-device LLMs are fast but prone to hallucinated spatial judgments. Hybrid reasoning LLMs offer both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, which raises a key question for embodied agents: when is slow thinking worth its cost? We propose CovNav, a training-free framework that answers this question with Conformal Prediction (CP), turning dual-process (System 1 / System 2) inference into an uncertainty-aware decision. Much like recent decision models such as Jev, CovNav casts each spatial query as a structured binary decision rather than free-form generation: a local LLM in fast mode judges whether the target is likely near an observed object, CP converts its token probabilities into a prediction set, and only ambiguous queries are escalated to slow chain-of-thought reasoning. The object-pair formulation keeps calibration tractable and supports open-set objects through off-the-shelf detectors. Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show that CovNav surpasses the strongest zero-shot baseline by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points in success rate on HM3D v1 and v2, while invoking slow reasoning for only 12.4% of queries and retaining most of the gain of always-on thinking at a fraction of its latency. Real-robot experiments on a TurtleBot 4 further validate the approach. CovNav shows how calibrated uncertainty can decide when an embodied agent should think slowly, offering a principled form of adaptive test-time reasoning for LLM-based robots.
authors: Pengying Wu, Zhejia Wen, Kang Ding, Kangjie Zhou, Chunxuan Jiao, Wei Pan, Xiangli Nie, Chang Liu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between fast, error-prone on-device reasoning and slower, more capable thinking.
A fast local LLM makes binary object-pair proximity judgments; conformal prediction identifies ambiguous cases for escalation to chain-of-thought reasoning.
The training-free design supports open-set objects detected by off-the-shelf detectors and keeps calibration tractable.
On Gibson and HM3D, CovNav improves HM3D success by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points over the strongest zero-shot baseline while using slow reasoning for 12.4% of queries.
TurtleBot 4 experiments further validate the approach in real-robot navigation.

figures.caption: Fig. 6. Visualization of Real World Experiments. The figure depicts the navigation trajectory of the TurtleBot 4 platform (setup shown in top-left) searching for a toy. The system dynamically switches between Fast and Slow modes based on uncertainty. During the initial approach (Steps 11-27), the agent operates in Fast Mode for efficient exploration. At Step 42, high uncertainty at a semantic transition triggers the Slow Mode, enabling the agent to infer the correct path into the bedroom. The agent then reverts to Fast Mode (Step 60) and successfully localizes the target (Step 73). This demonstrates the efficacy of the adaptive fast-slow inference mechanism in handling real-world ambiguities.

Fig. 1. We propose a Conformal Prediction (CP)-guided fast-slow inference paradigm for object goal navigation using Qwen3-8B as the local LLM. Clear Case: When observing a bathtub, Qwen confidently predicts a toilet will be nearby (logits: 0.9 vs 0.1), so CP accepts the fast direct inference. Ambiguous Case: When observing a sofa and querying about a bed, Qwen shows low confidence (logits: 0.6 vs 0.4), so CP triggers its slow deliberative reasoning mode for more reliable spatial analysis.

papers.abstract: Online adaptation of the cornering stiffness keeps a model-based sideslip estimator valid as tires change, but competes with learned model correction for the same filter innovation. A corrector with enough parameters can absorb the innovation pattern that a stiffness change produces, and adaptation is suppressed while the fit improves. We propagate the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted measurements through the vehicle states and construct a corrector orthogonal to them. A null-space parameterization enforces the constraint without a penalty coefficient and preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each identification segment. In full-vehicle simulation, the stiffness response of the unconstrained corrector declines as its parameter count grows, whereas the orthogonal corrector responds at least as fully as the uncorrected filter at all sizes and lowers sideslip error by 12.7% to 22.0%. In a simulated drive with a stiffness step, the orthogonal corrector adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter and lowers sideslip error during and after the transient. On public real-vehicle data, the 430-parameter unconstrained corrector loses most of its response to deliberate offsets of the filter's nominal stiffness, whereas the orthogonal corrector of the same size retains most of it, with a sideslip error slightly above the uncorrected filter's.
authors: Kyoungtae Ji, Dongyeol Won, Kyoungseok Han
bullets: Problem: Flexible learned corrections can absorb the innovation caused by tire-stiffness changes, suppressing stiffness adaptation.
Method: Propagate stiffness sensitivities through the vehicle model and constrain the corrector to their null space using a penalty-free parameterization.
Contribution: The approach preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each identification segment while separating correction from stiffness adaptation.
Results: In simulation, it reduces sideslip error by 12.7%–22.0% and adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter during stiffness transients.
Scope: On public real-vehicle data, it retains most stiffness response for a 430-parameter corrector, though sideslip error is slightly higher than with the uncorrected filter.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language Models (PVLMs) achieve strong zero-shot recognition but often suffer performance degradation under target-domain shift. Unsupervised adaptation provides a practical way to improve target-domain performance without labeled data, but it remains challenging because pseudo-labels generated by the model can be unreliable and no labeled validation set is available for model selection or early stopping. We propose a simple framework for unsupervised PVLM adaptation that combines progressive margin-based subset selection with cascaded consistency learning. The subset selection strategy constructs a class-balanced pseudo-labeled set using prediction margins and gradually expands it during training, enabling adaptation to start from reliable supervision anchors before incorporating broader target-domain data. Cascaded consistency learning further exploits unlabeled samples by using temporally smoothed teacher predictions on weakly augmented views to supervise student predictions on strongly augmented views, with confidence filtering to reduce the influence of uncertain pseudo-labels. To preserve the pretrained embedding structure, the framework updates only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts. Experiments across multiple recognition benchmarks with both CLIP and SigLIP backbones show consistent improvements over zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against recent unsupervised PVLM adaptation methods. These results suggest that progressive pseudo-label selection and teacher-guided consistency provide an effective and lightweight strategy for adapting PVLM classifiers without labeled target data.
bullets: Addresses unreliable pseudo-labels and the lack of labeled validation data during target-domain adaptation.
Builds a class-balanced pseudo-labeled subset from prediction margins, starting with high-confidence samples and expanding it progressively.
Uses cascaded consistency learning with temporally smoothed teacher predictions, strong/weak augmentations, and confidence filtering.
Updates only visual-encoder normalization parameters and text-initialized class prototypes to preserve pretrained representations.
Across multiple benchmarks with CLIP and SigLIP, consistently improves over zero-shot baselines and remains competitive with recent unsupervised methods.

The teacher parameters are updated as an exponential moving average of the student parameters, producing stabilized pseudo-labels that progressively improve subset selection and consistency learning.

papers.abstract: Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.
authors: Stella Kombo, Masih Haseli, Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala, Peter I. Renn, Morteza Gharib, Joel W. Burdick
bullets: Addresses model mismatch from unmodeled, spatially varying aerodynamic disturbances during deployment.
Learns an offline nominal Koopman Control Family model, then updates only a lightweight, low-dimensional residual correction online.
Uses causal state-command-state transitions and evaluates disturbance corrections across the MPC prediction horizon.
Hardware tests on a nano-quadrotor in uniform wind and a spatially varying wake show improved multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbances increase.
Designed to satisfy real-time control requirements while preserving the nominal model.

papers.abstract: Although deep learning-based point cloud denoising methods have demonstrated impressive results in recent years, their effectiveness usually degrades substantially in real-world scenarios where the noise distribution of test point clouds deviates from that of the training set. To address this challenge, we propose a test-time adaptive denoising (TTAD) framework that enables existing denoising approaches to adapt to unknown noise patterns at test time without relying on additional supervision or retraining from source data. Taking a pre-trained denoising model and a test noisy point cloud as input, TTAD first employs a residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module to estimate the sample-specific noise distribution through analyzing the deviation between the noisy input and its pseudo-clean version denoised by the initial model. Then, a noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module is designed to build sample-specific noisy-noisier test-time training pair from the denoised point cloud, and update the model parameters over a few adaptation steps per sample at test time through contrastive learning. Furthermore, TTAD naturally extends to a continual TTAD (CTTAD) setting, facilitating efficient progressive refinement across sequential test samples with consistent noise distributions, while reducing the computational cost per sample. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the generalization ability of existing denoising models under unseen noise, achieving superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics.
authors: Kun Jiang, Shida Fu, Fanhao Yi, Weiqing Li, Zhiyong Su
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when test-time noise differs from training noise.
Uses residual-driven noise modeling to estimate each input’s sample-specific noise distribution.
Constructs noisy–noisier training pairs for noise-aware contrastive adaptation over a few test-time steps.
Extends to continual TTAD for efficient progressive refinement on sequential samples with consistent noise.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report improved generalization across multiple metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed TTAD framework. (a) The input noisy point cloud Xt is first denoised by a pre-trained model fθ to produce a pseudo-clean output Ỹ . (b) The residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module utilizes the residual noise N̂t = Xt − Ỹ to estimate the test-time noise distribution p(n) of Xt via a lightweight Gaussian mixture model (GMM). (c) The noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module generates a sample-specific noisy-noisier pair (X̃(1) t , X̃ (2) t ) of Ỹ . Within each test-time adaptation step, we first use the reconstruction loss Lrecon, identity loss Lid, and consistency loss Lconsist to update the online model fθonline via gradient descent at each iteration step. After that, the target model’s parameters θtarget are updated as an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online model’s parameters θonline. Finally, we can use the final θtarget to obtain the adapted denoised result Yc = fθtarget (Xt).

papers.abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. This creates two challenges: estimating the downstream value of long reasoning and deciding when that value is worth using the remaining budget. We propose Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation (PORA), which learns this decision by comparing short and long reasoning from the same interaction state. During training, \method{} completes the task twice from each selected state, once with a short reasoning allowance and once with a long allowance, and compares their final quality and total processing to estimate when longer reasoning is valuable. During inference, a controller weighs this estimate against learned prices on remaining-budget pressure and chooses either short or long reasoning without running both alternatives. We evaluate PORA across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks, achieving strong results across all settings. On BFCL memory, it exceeds the strongest existing method by 17.4--32.9 percentage points. Within the same agent, it matches or exceeds always using long reasoning on code and mathematics with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.
authors: Bo Yan, Qi Zhang, Zhen Tan, Tianlong Chen, Song Wang
bullets: LLM agents must balance deeper reasoning against saving budget for later decisions.
PORA learns the value of longer reasoning by comparing short- and long-reasoning outcomes from the same state.
At inference, a controller combines this value with remaining-budget pressure to select one reasoning length without running both.
It performs strongly across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks.

On BFCL memory, it improves over the strongest existing method by 17.4–32.9 percentage points; on code and mathematics, it matches or exceeds always-long reasoning with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PORA. 1⃝ From one checkpoint (si, bi, Ni), a PRESERVE branch and a SPEND branch continue under the same policy ρk; their differences in terminal quality and complete processing give the paired targets (qi, gi). 2⃝ The controller learns to predict these targets from the visible history and learns the prices on the pressure terms (Oi, Hi) through the direction label di. 3⃝ At inference, the predicted gain is weighed against the priced pressure, and native rules map the proposal to a feasible grant κt. The dashed arrow repeats collection and training under the updated policy. The calendar case is illustrative.

Figure 3: Task success against total tokens. Each marker is one method with a recorded token total; hollow markers are lower bounds. The dotted line marks PORA, and each subtitle gives its difference from the best external method in Table 1. The logarithmic horizontal axis differs across panels.

papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users. Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations. We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities. At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.

bullets: Addresses pluralistic alignment when user preferences are heterogeneous and annotators are anonymized.

Across embodied control tasks, generalizes to out-of-distribution users and supports variable adaptation-query budgets.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.
authors: Haonan Zhao, Jiaxuan Chen, Qingyang Liu, Shuochen Chang, Siyu Sun, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of re-encoding or retrieving video evidence for every question.

Evaluated on LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, achieving data-efficient video-free QA with fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods.
Scope: memory is adapted separately for each video, so it is not a universal video memory.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

Demonstrates reliable few-shot adaptation on a full-size autonomous race car with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.

papers.abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $\pi_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.
authors: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang, Maggie Wang, Fangneng Zhan, Manling Li, Qianqian Wang, Mac Schwager, Zhuang Liu, Li Fei-Fei, Mengyu Wang, Paul Pu Liang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving robot policies from limited test-time experience while keeping pretrained weights fixed.
Uses a sparse autoencoder and a shared temporal descriptor of feature activation-order patterns to select a task-specific feature without timestep alignment.
Builds reference banks offline from successful and failed rollouts, then online determines when and how strongly to adjust the feature activation.
With 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, improves success by approximately 10% across simulated and real-world manipulation evaluations.
Scope: requires labeled successful and failed reference rollouts and focuses on steering a selected feature during execution.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling of diffusion models with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) has become a promising strategy for sampling under user-specified rewards, such as human preference scores. However, the standard SMC framework typically relies on stochastic proposals and therefore does not directly transfer to flow matching models, in which inference is governed by deterministic ODEs. In this work, we introduce noise-rejuvenated SMC, an inference-time scaling method tailored for text-to-image flow matching models. Our key idea is to perturb each resampled particle by changing its source noise and constructing a new intermediate state using its current endpoint estimate. This moves the particle to another state that remains representable under the flow-matching interpolation form, enabling particle exploration without converting the sampler to an SDE. We further introduce a look-ahead mechanism to refine resampled particles before weighting. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image demonstrate consistent improvements in reward-guided generation, while ablation studies validate the contributions of noise rejuvenation and look-ahead refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/shermanlian/NR-SMC.
authors: Wenyi Lian, Zheng Zhao, Thomas B. Sch{\"o}n
bullets: Addresses the challenge of applying standard SMC to flow-matching models, whose ODE-based inference uses deterministic proposals.
Perturbs resampled particles by changing their source noise and reconstructing an intermediate state that remains compatible with flow-matching interpolation.
Adds look-ahead refinement to improve resampled particles before reward weighting.
Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image show consistent reward-guided generation improvements.
Ablations support the roles of noise rejuvenation and look-ahead refinement.

papers.abstract: Decision models answer typed questions, such as multiple-choice or yes/no questions, with a probability for each option. We add test-time search to frozen decision models, with no training: we show the model a complete proposed answer, read off its probability of saying "Yes" to the proposal's correctness, and search for answers that it rates higher. The search is done either by editing one answer at a time or by joint optimization, which changes several answers at once. Search raises accuracy for every model and test set we tried, and the gains are largest for exact correctness on logic puzzles, where every answer in a task must be right. On 128 such puzzles, it takes Qwen3.8-27B from 2 to 30 exactly correct puzzles ($15\times$) and its per-blank accuracy from 27.8% to 48.5%. On a shared set of 47 puzzles, searching over each model's own Yes/No score raises the per-blank accuracy of StartLux Instant, Perplexity Decider, Clef, and JEV, which we reach only through its public API, by 4.0 to 13.0 percentage points, and raises the number of puzzles they get exactly correct, out of 47 and averaged over three search seeds, from 10 to 35, 9 to 26, 2 to 11, and 9 to 31.7 respectively.
bullets: Targets typed-answer tasks such as multiple-choice and yes/no questions without additional training.
Evaluates complete proposed answers and searches for alternatives rated more likely correct by the model.
Uses either single-answer editing or joint optimization to revise multiple answers simultaneously.
Improves accuracy across all tested models and test sets, with the largest gains on exact logic-puzzle solving.
On 128 puzzles, Qwen3.8-27B’s exactly solved tasks rise from 2 to 30, while per-blank accuracy increases from 27.8% to 48.5%.

papers.abstract: Pedestrians differ in whether they respond to a robot, yet many RL policies assume all are non-reactive to prioritize safety. Policies trained without conditioning on local pedestrians' reactivity may therefore be unnecessarily conservative or rely on cooperation that does not occur. We propose RCRA, an online adaptation framework that modulates a learned residual around a frozen conservative navigation policy according to estimated pedestrian reactivity. A Transformer-based estimator infers latent pedestrian reactivity from motion histories and robot context, providing a more accurate signal for navigation adaptation and improving scenario-averaged simulation accuracy by $12.62$ percentage points over the Bayesian baseline, which assumes known pedestrian goals. These estimates are spatially aggregated into an adaptation scale that gates LoRA modules, enabling cooperative behavior near reactive pedestrians and conservative behavior near non-reactive pedestrians. Among baselines achieving SR above $90\%$ in every scenario, RCRA reduces scenario-averaged path length by $16.7\%$ relative to the conservative backbone and by $7.3\%$ relative to randomized-training baselines. It improves mean SR by $14.88$ percentage points over the reactive-trained policy.
authors: Immanuel R. Santjoko, Benedictus C. G. Cinun, Jing Chen, Bin Hu
bullets: Addresses the conservatism and coordination failures caused by assuming all pedestrians are non-reactive.
Uses a Transformer to infer latent pedestrian reactivity from motion histories and robot context.
Aggregates local reactivity estimates to gate LoRA-based residual adaptations around a frozen conservative policy.
Improves scenario-averaged simulation accuracy by 12.62 percentage points over a Bayesian baseline.
Reduces scenario-averaged path length while maintaining high success rates, and improves mean success rate over a reactive-trained policy.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained rectification of existing generations under a limited additional budget remains a key problem in test-time optimization (TTO) for image generation. As for prior approaches, they could identify residual errors, but could not directly ensure that the model acts on the feedback during reasoning. Such errors stem from multiple sources, such as the initial noise or text prompt, and ultimately induce an execution gap of failing to handle potential deviations along the trajectory generating. However, classic models generally cannot remedy this gap. To narrow it, we propose Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification (RGDR), which turns reflections on completed outputs into corrective interventions on the process of sampling dynamics at the trajectory level. Specifically, RGDR could impact every sampling step by adapting to instantaneous intervention. Moreover, RGDR generates flexible candidates while adjudicating between them and the reference. As experiments show, rectification from RGDR starts from the existing base trajectory and reflection, and RGDR is substantially more effective than former trajectory exploration. Under matched budgets for additional image generation, RGDR's gain in the cross-model average final checklist score over the reference is $1.51\times$ that of TIR prompt refinement and $1.81\times$ that of Dynamic CFG.
authors: Shuo Xu, Hanrui Ying, Debin Liu, Jianjun Li, Zhiyuan Ma
bullets: Addresses test-time optimization when existing generations contain errors from noise, prompts, or trajectory deviations.

Adapts interventions at each sampling step and evaluates generated candidates against a reference.

Scope: focuses on fine-grained rectification starting from an existing base trajectory and reflection.

papers.abstract: Multiobject tracking (MOT) is a fundamental capability in autonomous navigation, radar and sonar systems, as well as 6G integrated sensing-and-communication (ISAC) networks. In this paper, we propose a neural-enhanced track-before-detect (TkBD) framework that operates directly on complex-valued raw signals and learns a latent representation of unmodeled propagation effects during runtime. We introduce an environment-dependent latent intensity variable that characterizes the signal power of each object in the shared propagation environment. The probability density function of this intensity variable is represented by a normalizing flow and trained online in an unsupervised manner within the sequential Bayesian inference procedure. The learning objective is derived from a variational Bayes formulation by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO), thereby accounting for the uncertainties inherent in the Bayesian TkBD problem. To enable scalable inference, we make use of a recently introduced Bayesian TkBD framework that combines belief propagation, which avoids high-dimensional operations, with sequential Monte Carlo methods for efficient low-dimensional updates.
authors: Shaoxiu Wei, Bhaskar Rao, Florian Meyer
bullets: Targets multiobject tracking in autonomous navigation, radar, sonar, and 6G ISAC settings.
Operates directly on complex-valued raw signals while modeling unmodeled propagation effects through a latent representation.
Represents each object’s environment-dependent signal intensity with a normalizing flow trained online and unsupervised.
Optimizes the flow using an ELBO-derived variational Bayes objective to capture inference uncertainty.
Combines belief propagation with sequential Monte Carlo for scalable Bayesian inference.

papers.abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.
authors: Chuan Liu, Tianya Zhao, Xuyu Wang

An LLM planner selects diagnostic actions under evidence, trust, cost, and budget constraints.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.
authors: Boyi Liu, Yite Wang, Xinyu Lian, Fan Shu, Sida Li, Feng Yan, Mingjia Zhang, Yuxiong He, Zhewei Yao
bullets: Targets the difficulty of separating algorithmic gains from an under-tuned RL baseline for long-horizon agents.
Uses small-pool overfitting to expose failures hidden by early reward gains and integrates gated rewards, importance-weight control, aligned training/inference engines, and consistent policy state.
Reaches 62.0% pass@1 with Qwen3.5-4B on raw R2E-Gym data, comparable to FrogNano while using about one-sixth as many rollouts.
Filtering and refining multiple datasets improves Qwen3.5-4B to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% and Qwen3.5-9B to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2.
Controlled comparisons find that curation and stronger tests improve held-out performance, while stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery.

papers.title: Arctic-SWE: Revisiting the Long Horizon Agent Training by Modeling-System Co-Design
papers.tldr: Arctic-SWE co-designs asynchronous RL infrastructure and training practices to provide a reproducible long-horizon software-engineering baseline, achieving strong SWE-bench performance without new algorithms.

papers.abstract: Recovering metric 3D geometry from images is fundamentally ill-posed due to perspective projection ambiguity. Current geometry models incorporate supplied or predicted intrinsics during inference, but do not use them to supervise model adaptation. To refine these predictions, test-time adaptation (TTA) typically relies on external depth measurements. In this paper, we instead use camera intrinsics as an output-side geometric verifier. Comparing the point cloud's viewing rays with those defined by the known intrinsics yields a direct measure of geometric inconsistency. We propose \textit{IntriAdapt}, a TTA framework that minimizes this closed-form geometric residual. By optimizing a lightweight LoRA adapter on a frozen geometry foundation model, our method aligns the prediction with the specific camera model without depth sensors or external priors. We further extend this approach to video sequences, demonstrating that adapting a short sequence generalizes to other sequences captured by the same camera. The adapted model processes held-out images in a feed-forward pass, without repeating optimization for each frame. Experiments on ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks across multiple base models show that \textit{IntriAdapt} consistently outperforms both unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.
authors: Jiaxing Chen, Zizheng Yan, Jingyu Zhuang, Jinwei Chen, Shuguang Cui, Guanying Chen, Qingnan Fan
bullets: Addresses perspective ambiguity in image-based metric 3D geometry estimation.
Minimizes a closed-form residual between predicted point-cloud viewing rays and rays implied by the camera intrinsics.
Optimizes a lightweight LoRA adapter while keeping the geometry foundation model frozen.
Sequence adaptation generalizes across images from the same camera, enabling feed-forward inference on held-out frames.
Across ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks, it outperforms unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
authors: Sizhe Tang, Zuyuan Zhang, Zeyu Fang, Tian Lan
bullets: Addresses the coupled problem of choosing research assignments while learning from the resulting experiences.
Uses a hierarchical framework: a Coordinator organizes search branches and directives, while Scientists generate hypotheses and execution plans.
Alternates GRPO-style updates for both hierarchy levels under a shared best-of-budget objective; execution uses a frozen shared Executor.
Provides theoretical results on objective alignment, coordination gains, private adaptation, and finite-budget regret.
On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD was best on 20 and achieved the highest aggregate normalized MLGym scores; comparisons involve mostly proprietary Scientist baselines.

papers.abstract: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. Preserving its value over time is also difficult: our accumulation baseline without consolidation initially improves but eventually performs below a no-memory baseline. Our key idea is to compare attempts at the same task to identify reusable decisions and refine when they apply. We introduce Hippo, a memory framework inspired by selective hippocampal encoding and replay that learns from these comparisons when shortcomings are diagnosed. It compares the resulting experience with existing memory to merge overlaps and resolve conflicts through explicit applicability conditions. This allows prior guidance to be revised without storing every lesson as a separate entry. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web show performance gains in all three settings and substantially fewer retained experiences than the accumulation baseline. The gains extend across the evaluated base models of varying capabilities, indicating that memory-based adaptation remains useful even for highly capable models.
authors: Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Yuxuan Ren, Tony Qin, Baoyuan Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of extracting reliable lessons from flawed or mixed-quality attempts.
Uses selective hippocampal-style encoding and replay to diagnose shortcomings and compare attempts on the same task.
Merges overlapping memories and resolves conflicts with explicit applicability conditions instead of storing every lesson separately.
Improves performance on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web while retaining substantially fewer experiences than simple accumulation.
Benefits persist across base models with varying capabilities, including highly capable models.

papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) beat classifiers lose accuracy on new patients and devices, and source-free adaptation methods that assume class-balanced target batches fail on real recordings, whose label-free prefix is 87.9--98.6% normal beats. We propose Normal-Anchored Geometric Transport (NAGT, GA_NS), which estimates a closed-form symmetric positive-definite congruence map from label-free normal anchors in the first 5 min of each recording and applies it only to the normal and supraventricular prototypes, keeping the ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed. The score offsets and decision rules were set on MIT-BIH only; the rate-invariant RR head (relA) was adopted after the development databases (INCART, SVDB) had been opened; the frozen model was then evaluated once on Icentia11k chest-patch recordings under a pre-registered protocol. In 493 patients (973 recordings, 3,615,388 evaluated beats), NAGT reached an arrhythmia macro-$F_1$ $J = \frac{1}{2}(\text{S-}F_1 + \text{V-}F_1) = 48.7\%$ [95% CI 42.1, 54.7] versus 34.5% without adaptation ($\Delta J = +14.1$ [+8.6, +19.3] pp; 59.8% versus 43.9% in non-AF) and outperformed all five Holm-adjusted comparators, including AdaBN, Tent and T3A. In the 75-patient test subgroup of the historical split (73 analyzed), the gain was not significant (+6.1 [-8.5, +23.4] pp). Adaptation takes a median of 5.8 ms per record without back-propagation.
bullets: Addresses patient/device domain shift when target recordings are heavily dominated by unlabeled normal beats.
Uses a closed-form symmetric positive-definite transport map estimated from normal beats in each recording’s first 5 minutes.
Adapts only normal and supraventricular prototypes while keeping ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed.
On 493 patients and 973 Icentia11k recordings, macro-F1 rose from 34.5% to 48.7%, outperforming five adjusted comparators.
The gain was not significant in a small 73-patient historical test subgroup; median adaptation time was 5.8 ms per record.

From the label-free 5-min prefix, U1 normal anchors (non-premature beats with p(N) ≥ 0.5 under the four-dimensional RR head, 80% core of the patient’s own covariance cloud) define the AIRM mean M̂N and the closed-form congruence map Ap (Eq. papers.abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. ID-TAP combines a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley-Terry explorer, and transfers comparison evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts. The neural model shares statistical strength across queries while preserving query-specific scores, and efficient BT updates score hypothetical challengers. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks under reference- and model-based preference simulators, ID-TAP achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a fixed ten-round comparison budget. These results support information-directed challenger selection as an effective design for test-time persona adaptation.
authors: Jie Mao, Pingchen Lu, Xiangyi Wang, Hengquan Huang, Shuang Qiu, Min Zhang, Zhongxiang Dai
bullets: Targets query-dependent user preferences when only binary comparisons between candidate responses are available.

Transfers evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts while retaining query-specific scores.
Evaluated on seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks with reference- and model-based preference simulators.
Achieved the strongest aggregate performance among evaluated baselines under a fixed ten-round comparison budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of ID-TAP. Historical context induces a shared persona space and each new query inherits similarity-weighted BT statistics from prior queries (1–2). At every interaction round, the neural utility model selects the champion and estimates utility gaps, while the query-local BT explorer computes a plug-in entropy-reduction proxy; their acquisition ratio selects the challenger (3). The agent generates the resulting response pair, obtains one binary preference, and updates both systems (4–5). After T rounds, the highest-scoring persona produces the personalized response, and the query-local BT increments are retained for later warm starts.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) adapts pretrained models to distribution shifts encountered during deployment. However, most existing methods rely on the weight representations of the final layer or signals derived from the model's output probability distribution. We study hidden trajectories: the ordered sequence of intermediate representations produced across a deep neural network. We observe that clean and corrupted trajectories become more separable as corruption severity increases. We introduce Drift-TTA, which adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen backbone and trains them to align corrupted hidden trajectories with those from cleaner inputs. The approach supports two variants: a source-dependent version trained with clean targets, and a source-free setting that learns from corrupted images at different severities. We develop an online TTA approach that freezes the backbone and adapters while updating a scalar gate to control adaptation strength. We further cast trajectory alignment as MAP inference under a Gaussian observation model and derive a KL-based transfer bound characterizing test-time trajectory misalignment in terms of offline residual error, residual dimensionality, and distribution shift between offline and test corruptions. We evaluate Drift-TTA on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C using supervised ViTs and CLIP models. On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, our source-free online approach improves accuracy over no TTA by 13.3 percentage points with ViT-B/16 and 11.6 percentage points with CLIP ViT-B/16, reaching 74.9% and 47.4%, respectively. Under the same setting, prior TTA baselines yield ECEs of 18.00% for ViT and 14.70% for CLIP, while our approach reduces them to 9.53% and 5.77%, respectively. These results demonstrate that hidden trajectory alignment provides an effective signal for both offline correction and lightweight online test-time adaptation.

An online variant updates only a scalar gate to control adaptation strength, keeping the backbone and adapters frozen.
On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, source-free online Drift-TTA improves accuracy by 13.3 points for ViT-B/16 and 11.6 points for CLIP ViT-B/16, while also reducing calibration error.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly operate in open-ended environments, where they are expected to continually adapt to evolving tasks and distributions, often without access to external supervision. Existing continual learning approaches rely on external supervision, such as labeled data, demonstrations, or reward signals, which can be costly or unavailable in practice. Test-time adaptation removes this dependence by learning from self-generated supervision, but existing methods derive that supervision from the single policy being updated, so once the policy drifts, its own learning signal drifts with it, leading to policy collapse, degraded reasoning, and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Evolution Strategy Reinforcement Learning (ESRL)}, a continual test-time learning framework that draws its self-generated supervision from a population of policies instead of the single policy being trained. ESRL perturbs an anchor policy in parameter space to form a population of nearby policies, samples one trajectory from each, and aggregates their answers into label-free group-relative learning signals for the central student. The anchor is held fixed within each block and refreshed from the student at block boundaries, so the population stays centered on a stable yet current policy and continues to supply diverse and reliable supervision as the student moves. In single-task test-time adaptation across mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and medical domains, ESRL improves average accuracy by up to 31.7% relative to the base model and 16.6% relative to the strongest test-time adaptation baseline. Notably, ESRL substantially reduces catastrophic forgetting and achieves the strongest final performance in continual learning.

papers.abstract: Reliable fetal brain biometry on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosing congenital brain anomalies, but artificial intelligence models often lose accuracy under domain shifts. We developed BioTTA, a backbone-agnostic, source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation framework that adapts pretrained models online to individual unlabeled target volumes. This retrospective multicohort study included 394 reconstructed 3D fetal brain MRI volumes at 20-39 gestational weeks, with 11 biometric measurements annotated by radiologists. BioTTA was developed on single-center turbo spin-echo MRI and evaluated on three datasets representing cross-sequence, cross-center, and cross-nation shifts. Biometry accuracy was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE) and the percentage of correct measurements within 4 mm. A web-based reporting platform mapped measurements onto normative growth trajectories and was evaluated against radiologists in four multicenter disease cohorts covering germinal matrix-intraventricular hemorrhage, ventriculomegaly, and cerebellar abnormality. Across all three target datasets, BioTTA outperformed auto-SVRTK, source-only models, and FetalSynthGen, while matching models finetuned with target labels. MAEs ranged from 1.10 to 1.46 mm with a convolutional backbone and from 1.46 to 2.25 mm with a transformer backbone. Diagnostic accuracy ranged from 82.1% to 95.0%, comparable to a senior radiologist. BioTTA supports accurate, generalizable fetal brain biometry and standardized prenatal brain growth assessment across heterogeneous MRI sources.

papers.abstract: LLM agents accumulate valuable task-specific information through their actions, observations, and environmental feedback during multi-turn task execution. When effectively used, this information can help agents refine subsequent decisions and improve task performance. However, the learning value of an interaction depends on its context and subsequent feedback, making it challenging to extract reliable, actionable lessons and revise them as the task unfolds. In this paper, we introduce ReTTT, which enables experience-driven self-adaptation through test-time training on lessons constructed and continually revised within an episode. ReTTT lets the agent reflect on interaction feedback, maintain the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and learn from them by updating an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen. The adapted model then performs both subsequent actions and reflection, coupling policy adaptation with the construction of future learning experience. We evaluate ReTTT on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite using two model families. ReTTT outperforms trajectory-based test-time training across all six model--benchmark settings, improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points. A frozen-reflection comparison further shows a 7.14-point benefit from adapting the reflection policy, while trajectory analysis illustrates how adapted reflection derives more task-specific guidance from failed attempts. These findings suggest that learning to reflect on its own behavior can boost agents' performance on long-horizon tasks.
authors: Kangcong Li, Hangfan Zhang, Shuyue Hu, Shengji Tang, Tao Chen

papers.abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.
authors: Junyu Cao, Ruijiang Gao, Maytal Saar-Tsechansky, Mingzhang Yin
bullets: Reframes targeted AI deployment as multiple testing: select individuals whose policy-induced outcomes are unlikely to exceed a user-defined harm threshold.
Uses weighted conformal p-values to address distribution shift between observed behavior and the target policy.
Applies a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure with finite-sample FDR control.
Provides a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee when either the outcome or propensity model is correctly specified.
Synthetic and semi-synthetic studies support the guarantees and demonstrate use as a safety gate for high-risk subgroups.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FDR and power with correctly specified scores and weights on synthetic data (n = 500, m = 100, 400 replications). The FDR remains well below the nominal level q (dashed line) across all target levels, while power increases steadily.

papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are trained predominantly on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images but are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for immunohistochemistry (IHC), where cross-hospital differences can impair grading. However, systematic comparisons of correction methods for cross-hospital IHC grading remain limited. To address this gap, we benchmark label-free transformations applied to input images before frozen-FM encoding and to features after frozen-FM encoding using UNI and Virchow2, three IHC markers, and six directed cross-hospital transfers, yielding 12 settings. Among the evaluated input-space methods, our proposed method FIX achieved the largest macro-F1 improvement over no correction, outperforming well-known stain normalization techniques. Among feature-space methods, a simple feature-wise standardization achieved the best improvement over no correction, outperforming CORAL. Under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation, combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) by 0.181 and 0.208, respectively, and reduced ordinal error by 0.209 relative to no correction. These results show that input- and feature-space transformations can provide complementary benefits for cross-hospital IHC grading with frozen pathology FMs.
authors: Jongwoon Lee, Jhair Gallardo, Christopher Kanan
bullets: Cross-hospital variation can impair IHC grading when H&E-trained foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors.
The study benchmarks input-space corrections and feature-space corrections with UNI and Virchow2 across three IHC markers and six directed hospital transfers.
FIX achieved the strongest improvement among input-space methods, while feature-wise standardization outperformed CORAL in feature space.
Combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and QWK and reduced ordinal error under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation.

papers.abstract: The web is not static or uniform. Websites that serve the same purpose can look and navigate very differently. Even within a single site, successive redesigns can change how familiar features are presented and accessed. Humans adapt to this by recognizing familiar interaction patterns and reusing what they already know. We give web agents a similar ability with WebMix, a mixture hypernetwork that adapts them to unseen interfaces by composing previously trained low-rank adapters. WebMix begins with a bank of adapters trained on source interfaces. At deployment, a scout agent explores the target interface and summarizes its observations into a compact manual. A lightweight router uses this manual to predict mixing coefficients over the adapter bank, which combine the existing adapters into a new one for inference. Adapting to a new interface takes only a scouting run and a forward pass, without gradient updates on the target. With Qwen and Llama models, we evaluate domain transfer on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2, and version transfer on TimeWarp. In all three settings, WebMix matches or outperforms in-context learning and LoRA baselines, often matching the average success of specialists trained directly on those interfaces. On TimeWarp domain transfer, it gains about 8 percentage points on average over the best baseline with both models. These gains do not come at the cost of seen interfaces, where WebMix keeps its lead, and extend to version transfer. Adapting to a new interface can therefore rely on exploration and composition instead of retraining.
authors: Md Farhan Ishmam, Minh Pham Dinh, Kenneth Marino
bullets: Web interfaces vary across sites and redesigns, motivating reusable adaptation mechanisms.
A scout agent creates a compact manual of the target interface, and a router selects adapter-mixture weights.
The resulting adapter is composed from previously trained adapters and used in a single forward pass without gradient updates.
Evaluated with Qwen and Llama on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2 for domain and version transfer.
WebMix matches or exceeds in-context learning and LoRA baselines, with about an 8-point average gain over the best baseline on TimeWarp domain transfer.

Websites vary across versions (v1–v5) and domains.

papers.abstract: Automated fundus-based diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading can substantially expand screening capacity, but source-trained models degrade sharply across different cameras, clinics, and patient populations. Existing test-time adaptation methods depend on entropy minimization or target information accumulated from image batches and streams. These mechanisms can reinforce confidently incorrect predictions and break down when clinical images arrive independently. We introduce CF-NODE, a novel counterfactual test-time adaptation framework for cross- domain DR grading. Instead of trusting prediction confidence or estimating a target distribution, CF-NODE asks how each prediction responds under a controlled intervention on the evidence supporting it. CF-NODE ranks internal spatial nodes using model-derived attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, progressively attenuates the highest-ranked nodes, and uses the stability of the resulting expected-grade response to apply a bounded calibration of the predicted grade distribution. The framework is fully frozen and adapts every image independently using only geometric views and a fixed source-derived prior, requiring no target-derived information or model updates. We evaluate CF-NODE on five external DR datasets under repeated-seed evaluation against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A. CF-NODE outperforms all four methods with statistically significant improvements over the second-best method, improves AUC on every target domain, and attains the highest average AUC and macro-F1, delivering stronger grade discrimination together with more balanced recognition across DR severity levels. These results demonstrate that counterfactual intervention sensitivity provides consistent and deployment-ready domain robustness for single-image clinical inference.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation across cameras, clinics, and patient populations, where batch- or confidence-based adaptation can reinforce errors.
Ranks internal spatial nodes using attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, then attenuates selected nodes to measure prediction stability.
Calibrates each image’s predicted grade distribution using intervention sensitivity, geometric views, and a fixed source-derived prior.
Evaluated across five external DR datasets against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A; it achieved the highest average AUC and macro-F1 and improved AUC on every target domain.
Supports independent, deployment-oriented inference, but its scope is limited to the evaluated DR cross-domain settings.

papers.abstract: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter-updating test-time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation-valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot-matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre-relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never-seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning-savings
bullets: Tests whether later relearning reflects the specific fact previously learned, rather than familiarity with its components or query format.
Compares matched histories: correct binding (LEARNED), exposure without the binding (CONTROL), and a competing answer in the same slot (WRONG).
In Qwen2.5-1.5B, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL after rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning and partial forgetting.
WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, supporting binding-specific savings, though competitor interference may affect this comparison.
A secondary descriptive analysis estimates roughly 18% fewer optimizer updates for restoration after prior learning, using an unpaired never-seen pool.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns from rewards has to trust whatever reports those rewards. When the reports suddenly change, either the world changed or the reporter broke. From the reports alone these are indistinguishable, and reinforcement learning theory shows that no amount of further experience separates them. The prescribed escape is richer data about the reporter itself. We ask whether a frozen language model, handed exactly that data, uses it. We build a two-option game in which a payout swap and a lying reporter produce byte-identical histories. Then we add one verified record: an independent check of one round's real result, printed beside what the reporter said about that round. That single line settles the case. We ask three large models, from two families, to answer one question with one letter. Is the reporter honest or lying? They catch a lying reporter almost perfectly. At the 70B class that holds in every condition we tried; the 32B model slips in one wording. They clear an honest reporter far less often, and how often depends on things that should not matter. Averaged over rounds, letters, and wordings, a 72B model calls an honest reporter a liar 38% of the time when nothing has changed at all, and 58% of the time when the payouts moved. A 70B model from a second family calls an honest reporter a liar 26% and 48% of the time. The failure is not one of reading, because in the situation where nothing changed the same models score 0.96 to 1.00 with the answer printed in the prompt. Which surface feature drives it differs by family. For the Qwen models it is which round the record names, and for Llama it is which letter stands for "honest." Adding the record to a prompt that already states the answer makes Llama less likely to give that answer. We had registered a prediction for that 58% before the run: 35%. The failure is larger than we expected.
bullets: A payout change and a lying reporter can generate identical reward histories, making them indistinguishable from reports alone.
The study tests whether one verified comparison between the reporter’s claim and the real outcome resolves this ambiguity for language models.
Models nearly always identify lying reporters, but their accuracy for honest reporters varies substantially with wording and other irrelevant surface features.
False accusations are especially frequent when payouts changed, reaching 58% for one 72B-class model and 48% for another 70B-class model.
Providing the verified record alongside an answer can sometimes reduce, rather than improve, the likelihood of selecting that answer.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-guided Bayesian optimization (BO) uses past observations to guide search, but proposed directions and their revision can remain implicit. We propose Feedback-Guided Search State (FGSS), a structured hypothesis-management interface connecting language-based guidance to observed evidence, executable parameter interventions, and comparative support updates. An LLM reflector proposes and revises hypotheses; a deterministic curator validates them and maintains identities and test records. The evolving state guides candidate construction and priorities. Instantiated on LLAMBO, FGSS-BO retains its surrogate and default expected improvement selection, with a bounded testing policy. On two retrospective protocol/media tasks with nearest-neighbor response oracles, it attains higher sample mean final best and search AUC than the matched LLAMBO baseline and evaluated non-LLM baselines. Prose-reflection and EI-only controls show mixed component effects. Six direct-training hyperparameter-optimization tasks show task-dependent transfer, strongest on diabetes SVM; exact-grid and reaction controls examine other settings. FGSS exposes hypotheses, their execution, and cross-round revisions for inspection while supporting search gains in selected settings.
bullets: Addresses the implicit nature of proposed directions and their revisions in LLM-guided BO.
Uses an LLM reflector to propose/revise hypotheses and a deterministic curator to validate, track, and record tests.
Integrates the evolving hypothesis state into candidate construction and search priorities while retaining LLAMBO’s surrogate and expected-improvement selection.
Outperforms matched LLAMBO and evaluated non-LLM baselines on two retrospective protocol/media tasks, with mixed component effects and task-dependent transfer elsewhere.
Provides inspectable records of hypotheses, executions, and cross-round revisions; gains are strongest only in selected settings.

papers.abstract: Reliable fault detection is crucial for industrial machinery in large-scale facilities, where unexpected failures can cause costly downtime and production interruptions. Although acoustic monitoring provides a scalable solution for machine condition monitoring, its deployment is often constrained by high false-positive rates. We propose a two-step approach to automatic anomalous sound detection: first, when only normal operating audio samples are available, a regularized unsupervised model is deployed; then, after the first machine fault, a few-shot adaptation strategy exploits the anomalous samples acquired during the fault to improve the system. This adaptation increases the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) from 23.0 to 64.0 and improves detection in the low false-positive-rate region, with the partial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (pAUROC) increasing from 39.6 to 72.8. We also show that covariance regularization improves both prediction accuracy and training stability in the unsupervised model. These results provide a practical strategy for acoustic anomaly detection systems, enabling improved accuracy and reduced false alarms.
bullets: Targets costly false alarms in scalable acoustic monitoring of industrial machinery.
Initially trains a regularized unsupervised model using only normal operating sounds.
Adapts the detector with a few anomalous samples collected after the first machine fault.
Adaptation raises AUPR from 23.0 to 64.0 and low-false-positive pAUROC from 39.6 to 72.8.
Covariance regularization improves prediction accuracy and training stability.

papers.abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
