papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder's final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification.
authors: Zhipeng Ye, Feng Jiang, Qiufeng Wang, Hao Li
bullets: Addresses the underuse of complementary intermediate-layer information and differing feature dimensions in few-shot adaptation.

Evaluated on 11 datasets with ViT and ResNet backbones, LAMP and LAMP-F consistently improve over global-feature-only baselines across support budgets.
At 16 shots, LAMP-F reaches 83.57% on ViT-B/16 and 79.10% on ResNet-50; multi-layer integration is identified as the main improvement source.

papers.abstract: Test-time context optimization adapts frozen language models through textual feedback, but ordinary conditional generation provides no separate control over how strongly to reinforce the distributional changes induced by a context update. We introduce EMO, a training-free framework inspired by expectation--maximization that alternates question-specific context estimation (E-step) and distribution refinement (M-step). The E-step revises a system context using textual gradients from an external judge without access to gold answers. The M-step contrasts next-token distributions under the revised and preceding contexts at a shared prefix to construct a confidence-constrained logit correction. Feedback on the steered response drives the next context update, coupling adaptation across rounds with intervention within each generation. Theoretically, we connect parameter and context optimization through a shared target-KL objective and additive logit representations, and derive the steering vector from context-induced logit displacements. Under context-improvement and faithful-steering assumptions, we prove a one-round decrease in target KL divergence for sufficiently small steering strength. Under greedy decoding across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging $+9.10$ percentage points. With the same judge, it adds $+1.53$ points on average over context-only optimization (TextGrad), with consistent MMLU-Pro gains across models. At matched target-model generation budgets, accuracy advantages over best-of-$N$ are strongest on Llama, while oracle coverage is higher in most comparisons despite fewer candidates. The coverage--selection gap motivates allocating test-time computation jointly to candidate generation and verification.
authors: Wei Xia, Yehui Tang, Zhi-Hong Deng
bullets: Addresses the lack of independent control over how strongly context updates alter a language model’s output distribution.
Uses an expectation–maximization-style loop: an external judge revises question-specific context, then logits are corrected by comparing revised and previous contexts.
Derives steering from context-induced logit changes and theoretically shows reduced target KL divergence under stated assumptions and sufficiently small steering strength.
Across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging +9.10 percentage points.
Outperforms context-only optimization on average and can surpass best-of-N at matched generation budgets, while highlighting a remaining candidate-generation versus verification trade-off.

papers.abstract: Neural networks offer critical adaptability for controlling complex systems where nominal modeling proves intractable. However, when offline-trained neural networks are deployed within closed-loop control systems, their actions fundamentally alter the state distribution upon which they were trained. This paper introduces a unified taxonomy to categorize these sequential failure modes: the initial Closed-Loop Identification Error, the deployment-induced Action Error, and the continuous Tracking Error. Through discrete-time sensitivity analysis, this work formalizes how offline-learned parameters locally guarantee a trajectory divergence upon deployment, degrading performance due to local loss geometry. To mitigate this distribution shift, we propose actionable design policies centered on time-scale separated online adaptation. These mechanisms are validated through ablation studies on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator, demonstrating that bounded continuous learning successfully mitigates trajectory divergence whereas static deployments fail, offering concrete guidelines for practitioners deploying machine learning components in safety-critical feedback systems.
bullets: Identifies three sequential failure modes: Closed-Loop Identification Error, deployment-induced Action Error, and continuous Tracking Error.
Uses discrete-time sensitivity analysis to formalize how local loss geometry can cause deployment trajectories to diverge from those seen during training.
Proposes time-scale-separated online adaptation policies to mitigate deployment-induced distribution shift.
Ablations on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator show bounded continuous learning mitigates trajectory divergence, unlike static deployment.
Targets safer deployment of learned control components in safety-critical feedback systems.

In this generalized architecture, the “Plant” represents the target physical system or dynamical environment (e.g., the 1-DOF nonlinear Duffing oscillator in Section 6), which outputs physical state variables xk+1 (such as position and velocity). The z−1 block denotes the standard discrete-time unit delay operator mapping the next state to the current state xk, and xre f represents the desired reference trajectory or setpoint.

Figure 4: Evaluation of proposed baselines on the 1-DOF nonlinear Duffing oscillator. While the MRAC bounds the trajectory via its linear-in-the-parameters Lyapunov formulation, it suffers from a persistent tracking lag due to its inability to capture the unmodeled cubic stiffness. Conversely, the Dual IOP model, despite achieving unbiased closed-loop identification in Phase 1, distorts the amplitude upon static deployment, demonstrating the persistence of the Action Error independent of calibration bias.

Figure 2: Experimental Evaluation Phases: The three-phase deployment strategy utilized in Section 6 to explicitly isolate and quantify the proposed error taxonomy. While practical deployments may initialize directly into online adaptation, this staged experimental approach is necessary to independently evaluate the Closed-Loop Identification Error (Phase 1), the Action Error induced by static deployment (Phase 2), and the continuous Tracking Error mitigated by time-scale separated learning (Phase 3).

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes deployment-time distribution shift in closed-loop neural control and proposes online adaptation, fitting test-time and continual learning.
papers.title: Learning Changes the World and Then What Was Learned has Changed: Training and Deploying Neural Networks in the Control Loop
papers.tldr: Offline-trained neural networks can destabilize closed-loop control by changing the data distribution they encounter, while bounded online adaptation helps prevent trajectory divergence.

papers.abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.
authors: Bruno Arcanjo, Zhaoxing Li, Sebastian Stein
bullets: Addresses preference elicitation when no user choices are yet available.

A Bayesian learner updates these priors as user choices accumulate.

Its benefit is concentrated among early users, with performance comparable to information from roughly 6–40 surveyed users in log-loss terms.

papers.abstract: Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy. We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining. Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions. Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy. DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space. This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies. Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone.
bullets: Expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in a few dimensions, with important directions varying across regions of state space.
DHS learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states replayed through the frozen policy.
It suppresses low-variance coordinates more strongly than high-variance ones, then maps states back while retaining all coordinates.
Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over unmodified Transformer policies.
Nonlinear coordinates outperform linear alternatives in controlled comparisons; combining DHS with action smoothing helps on some tasks.

papers.abstract: We adapt the diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN architecture for longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge. The method combines affine pre-registration, multi-modal deformable registration, and test-time instance optimization. We further introduce PET biomarker preservation losses for metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG), including Jacobian-based constraints, and a per-structure rigidity regularization for skeletal structures. The submitted configuration achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with MTV and TLG errors of 3.3% and 3.3%, respectively, on our evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/koegl/psmareg.
authors: Fryderyk K\"ogl, Anna Reithmeir, Daniel M. Lang, Emily Chan, Rickmer Braren, Julia A. Schnabel
bullets: Targets longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration for the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge.
Adapts a diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN pipeline with affine pre-registration, multimodal deformable registration, and test-time optimization.
Adds MTV and TLG biomarker-preservation losses with Jacobian constraints, plus rigidity regularization for skeletal structures.
Achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with 3.3% errors for both MTV and TLG under the reported evaluation protocol.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

Finally, after the LapIRN stage, we refine this field per pair by instance optimization (IO) and resample the moving scan with it into the fixed space (warped PET/CT). Both stages are driven by the same objective, a weighted sum of three groups of terms: registration accuracy, PET quantification, and deformation regularization (Sec. 2.3).

papers.abstract: Learning from interaction experience is essential for enabling large language models to continually improve during deployment. Context distillation offers a promising path: privileged information extracted from experience is provided to a teacher, whose behavior is then distilled into a student model that has no access to it. However, both existing forms of context distillation have limitations. Off-policy context distillation trains the student on teacher-generated trajectories and thus suffers from exposure bias; whereas on-policy context distillation trains on the student's own rollouts, whose states are often uninformative and fail to convey behaviors the student cannot yet produce. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Localized Context Distillation (LoCD). LoCD first localizes the critical spans of a student trajectory that require revision. The teacher then regenerates only these spans from the student's own prefix, and the student is trained on the regenerated segments. LoCD thereby concentrates learning on the most informative states while keeping exposure bias low. Extensive experiments across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks demonstrate that LoCD consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves more stable training with smaller and sparser parameter updates.
authors: Zhezheng Hao, Yongkang Yang, Xilin Xia, Jiarui Yu, Yi Liu, Fanjunduo Wei, Peijie Dong, Tianfu Wang, Qiang Lin, Can Wang, Hande Dong, Jiawei Chen

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.
authors: Inseok Kong, Geunyoung Jung, Jiyoung Jung
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in 3D point clouds without source data or backpropagation.

Uses Otsu-based separability to derive each sample’s retained/pruned token partition.
Routes to the pruned prediction only when keep-ratio-penalized entropy favors it.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C.

A sample-specific token partition is then derived directly from the fused score distribution via sorted-split Otsu thresholding, eliminating iterative purge-size search. A keep-ratio-calibrated routing mechanism selects between the original and pruned token sequence predictions, accounting for the keep ratio in the routing criterion.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model's own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.
authors: Wenqiu Tang, Zhen Wan, Yihui Wang, Takahiro Komamizu, Ichiro Ide
bullets: Targets implicit emotional states that must persist across topic shifts from sparse conversational cues.
Uses causal localization on synthetic minimal pairs to find affective attention heads.
Boosts, at the answer position, tokens already attended to by those heads—without externally specified target spans.
Improves prompt-matched baselines by up to 10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and 5.5 on GoEmotions across three LLMs.
Combining SIAB with external supervision yields further gains, while analyses link effects to sparse emotion-enriched heads and layer proximity.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.
authors: Tanush Kalhan, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Sriram Ranga, Amritendu Mukherjee
bullets: Lower LP variance predicts correctness in SFT models, but the relationship weakens with scale and reverses in RL-distilled models.
Training paradigm influences density behavior more strongly than model size, while models show an intrinsic preference for complexity-favoring distributions.
Directly forcing density patterns during inference sharply reduces accuracy, suggesting natural density structure is important for reasoning.
Pre-generation hint injection plus contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points across both density metrics.
Entropy-Gated Density Routing improves accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without external guidance.

papers.abstract: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.
authors: Sheldon Yu, Tong Yu, Nikki Lijing Kuang, Zhendong Chu, Zhenwei Tang, Sungchul Kim, Lina Yao, Julian McAuley, Junda Wu
bullets: GRPO learns nothing when all attempts for a problem fail because there is no successful exemplar or nonzero group-relative advantage.
RSHD has the policy write a corrective note, re-solve with that note, and admit it only when fresh replay succeeds more often than the original group.
Answer-stating notes are screened out; admitted replays are distilled into the ordinary plain-prompt policy.
The method uses only policy training and outcome verification, with no reference solutions, and requires no notes or extra inference at deployment.
It consistently improves over GRPO across model families, sizes, and two training domains, with gains also transferring out of domain.

papers.abstract: Safety in agentic systems is inherently sequential: whether an action is safe depends on prior actions, tool outputs, information disclosures, and interactions among agents. Recent work has shifted agent safety guardrails from post-hoc trajectory-level assessment toward step-level action diagnosis and proactive risk prediction, yet existing training objectives provide limited supervision for how step evidence accumulates over time and when it becomes sufficient to justify intervention. We propose \methodlong~(ASPO): a training framework for step-level timely intervention. Pre-fix level stage alignment allows crediting each decision at its own step: it compares each response with the other responses sampled at the same prefix and rewards the action that fits the stage, continuing before the risk is visible, asking while clarification can still avert harm, and stopping before harm is irreversible. Adaptive feedback self-distillation further credits the reasoning behind each decision, with the model itself as a teacher that sees the step annotations on intervention steps and rules mined from its own false alarms on safe steps. Its training data carry a violation taxonomy and an intervention window at every step and are extended through self-evolving multi-agent red-teaming. Finally we present \textsc{StepSafe}, a step-level reasoning guardrail with timely intervention, that achieves the state-of-the-art peformance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks on safety-utility pareto curve with Youden's $J$ of 53.0 (4B) against 46.2.
authors: Siyi Gu, Kunhan Gao, Chao Peter Yang, Sukanta Ganguly, Rex Ying, Arman Cohan
bullets: Targets limited supervision for how step-level safety evidence accumulates and when intervention becomes necessary.
Uses pre-fix level stage alignment to evaluate each action against alternatives from the same interaction prefix.
Applies adaptive feedback self-distillation to teach decision reasoning from intervention annotations and false-alarm rules.
Builds training data with violation taxonomies and per-step intervention windows, expanded through multi-agent red-teaming.
Reports state-of-the-art performance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks, with a Youden’s J score of 53.0 for the 4B model versus 46.2.

papers.abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
authors: Anutam Srinivasan, Siddhant Panse, Glen Chou
bullets: Addresses conservative robust adaptive control that ignores guaranteed future parameter learning and struggles with high-dimensional robots.
Uses system-level synthesis to forecast parameter uncertainty and preserve correlations among disturbances, parameter errors, and estimate updates.
Builds tighter guaranteed reachable sets that incorporate expected information gain during planning.
Demonstrates real-time scalability on nonlinear robots, including whole-body control for a 61-state quadruped.
Validates online dynamics learning and stabilization on a physical Crazyflie drone.

papers.abstract: Damage-recovery algorithms often rank gaits from short trials, yet a gait that performs well briefly may not remain effective during continued execution. In reset-free recovery, each trial also changes the physical state inherited by the next. We introduce persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR), which predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait execution and uses conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and slot-averaged recovery quality (SRQ) by 0.044 relative to an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final-quality gains occur in all three damage classes. Against no adaptation, PGRR also improves final quality and reduces low-quality failures, whereas the aggregate SRQ difference is inconclusive. Development ablations identify conservative uncertainty handling as the clearest supported contributor to the observed gains. These results show that PGRR can identify stronger post-damage gaits under continuous physical state and that final-gait quality and recovery-summary performance provide complementary evidence for evaluating reset-free recovery.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between short-trial gait rankings and long-term gait effectiveness after irreversible leg damage.
Uses persistent outcome profiles and conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot.
Evaluated across 108 MuJoCo tasks involving leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock.
Improved final gait quality and reduced low-quality failures versus an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline; gains appeared across all damage classes.
Ablations most strongly supported conservative uncertainty handling, while aggregate SRQ improvement versus no adaptation was inconclusive.

papers.abstract: The closed world asks AI for specialized competence and lets it manufacture the iid data its theory assumes: a fixed criterion licenses collecting examples until the task is covered. The open world asks for versatility --- taking up tasks a machine was not built for, from few examples and with little prior from a human designer --- and offers data that is grouped, not shuffled. Its tasks are not known in advance, so a machine must do inference-time learning (1st requirement). Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, we derive two more: a *rich representation*, retaining more than iid generalization requires, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low-dimensional groups. The analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner, and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. We test these claims on language models up to 8B, asking whether a model has a property (qualitative) rather than how much it wins (quantitative). Models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates; the rest degrade, and neither scale nor layer-type interleaving repairs this.
bullets: Open-world settings involve unknown tasks, few examples, and grouped rather than iid data.
The analysis identifies three requirements: inference-time learning, representations richer than iid generalization needs, and aligned low-dimensional input–output groups.
A consistent inner learner and long contexts spanning related tasks are also predicted to help.
Experiments with language models up to 8B find that models meeting these requirements improve as related-task data accumulates, while others degrade.
Neither model scale nor interleaving different layer types fixes failures to meet the requirements.

papers.title: Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements
papers.tldr: Open-world AI requires inference-time learning, rich representations, and predictive disentanglement to improve across previously unseen related tasks.

papers.abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
authors: Yingfa Chen, Xingyu Shen, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han
bullets: Targets the memory and attention costs of large KV caches during generation.
Initializes compact caches using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity.
Distills attention outputs and log-normalizers from the full cache, then jointly optimizes the cache while freezing model weights.
Uses only generic document prompts, without downstream questions or answers.
Achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32× compression on a RULER task versus 40.0% for KVZip+, with gains across RULER, LongBench, Phonebook Lookup, Qwen3, and MiniCPM5.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents. A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%. Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.
authors: Peidong Wang, Ying Chang, Zhiming Ma, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng, Daqi Liu, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Daling Wang
bullets: Targets failures in pretrained vision-language-action models on unseen long-horizon tasks.
A coding agent first improves skills and the execution harness, then diagnoses persistent sub-step failures by retrying from saved states.
Fine-tunes only unreliable executor sub-steps using self-collected demonstrations and experience reused across tasks.
On 50 RoboCasa365 target tasks, success on unseen composite tasks increases from 4.6% to 13.8% without human demonstrations.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, uses 28% of GPU time and 22% of self-collected demonstrations while achieving slightly higher success.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning policies for robot locomotion can fail at deployment when operating conditions shift (e.g., rough or slippery terrain, payload changes, sensing degradation), and retraining or manual recalibration is often infeasible under on-device latency and memory constraints. We study test-time adaptation (TTA) for robotic control: adapting a pretrained policy online and in a self-supervised manner during execution, without access to rewards. Our starting point is a lightweight baseline that updates only the actor using a frozen pretrained critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate. Building on this, we introduce TEMPO, a test-time entropy-regularized, memory-guided policy optimization method that stabilizes critic-driven updates under severe shift. TEMPO combines (i) an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic's predictive distribution to mitigate overconfident extrapolation, and (ii) a score-based memory, inspired by prioritized replay, that prioritizes low-value ("hard") observations and applies importance sampling to focus limited computation on the most informative deployment conditions. Across Go1, Go2, and G1 in MuJoCo Playground under four representative shifts and multiple architectures, TEMPO yields consistent gains, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting. We further validate on a physical Unitree Go2 with an added calf payload, where fully on-device adaptation improves performance over the non-adapted baseline across real-world episodes.
authors: Motasem Alfarra, Pietro Mazzaglia, Markus Peschl, Daniel Dijkman, Christos Louizos
bullets: Addresses failures from terrain, payload, and sensing shifts when retraining or manual recalibration is impractical.
Adapts only the actor online using a frozen critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate.
TEMPO regularizes the critic’s predictive distribution to reduce overconfident extrapolation.
A score-based memory prioritizes hard, low-value observations and uses importance sampling under limited compute.
Improves performance across simulated robots and shifts, with gains up to 80%, and transfers to a physical Go2 with added payload.

papers.abstract: An agent can improve its behavior within an unresolved problem by changing how it acts and which experience it retains. We propose MMLA-RSI, a recursive self-improvement scheme with two implementations in Memory-Mediated Learning Architecture: Reasoning-Time Training (RTT) changes the policy state $\Phi$, while Reasoning-Time Memory Adaptation (RTMA) changes authoritative memory $M$. Each route also makes its adaptation method an object of improvement. A current numerical updater trains the policy proposing its successor; a current memory manager chooses the records available to the process proposing its successor. An independently admitted successor takes over the same role in the next generation. We give bounded executable rule languages, shared task/proposal interfaces, and one algorithm for either route or their composition. The RTT instance changes scalar schedules in a clipped-momentum update. The RTMA instance chooses NULL or a complete-row write with possible eviction. A fixed interpreter, trusted committer, and independent evaluator bound what can change. State versions, read closures, and conditional properties describe causal execution, accepted transitions, and finite work. Existing numerical-component studies motivate the construction. In four-candidate program selection, retaining LARC feedback updates reduces expected error by 24.65 and 36.65 percentage points for two trained initializations. In chronological continuous-integration replay, feedback binding is positive while retention increases loss. Completed SQL studies improve substantially over an unadapted substrate but do not establish the required additional online benefit. These results characterize their declared components. The two recursive routes and their joint realization are specified here; their beneficial recursive chains and discovery efficiency remain to be evaluated.
bullets: RTT adapts the policy state, while RTMA adapts authoritative memory and its retention decisions.
Each route recursively improves the mechanism that proposes the next policy or memory-manager successor.
A shared framework uses bounded rule languages, fixed interpreters, trusted commits, independent evaluation, versioned state, and causal execution controls.
Component studies show mixed outcomes: feedback retention helps in program selection, while retention increases loss in continuous-integration replay; SQL studies improve over an unadapted substrate.
The paper does not yet establish the benefit or discovery efficiency of complete recursive chains or their combined realization.

papers.abstract: Nanosatellites (e.g., CubeSats) have the potential to carry out useful science and exploration activities for outer solar system exploration, but their small size leads to tradeoffs between attitude control and science capabilities. Magnetorquers offer a unique compromise as compact actuators that enable three-axis attitude control, but suffer from a loss of control authority and require full knowledge of the planetary magnetic field. In this work, we present a learning-based adaptive model predictive control (MPC) algorithm that plans rotational trajectories for the satellite while accounting for this loss of control authority. Key to our approach is the inclusion of a learned magnetic field model that is trained in simulation using low-fidelity magnetic field data. Using measurements collected online, our proposed algorithm adapts this learned magnetic field model using a simple last-layer update scheme, allowing the MPC controller to quickly adapt to the true planetary magnetic field model and more effectively plan attitude trajectories. We demonstrate the results of our proposed approach for two use cases, (1) Earth-orbit and (2) Uranus-orbit, and show that our learning-based adaptive MPC algorithm improves controller success for these system simulations by 5% and 61%, respectively.
bullets: Magnetorquers enable compact three-axis control but have limited authority and depend on accurate planetary magnetic-field knowledge.
The method combines trajectory-planning MPC with a learned magnetic-field model trained from low-fidelity simulation data.
Online measurements update only the model’s last layer, enabling rapid adaptation to the true magnetic field.
Simulations show controller-success improvements of 5% in Earth orbit and 61% in Uranus orbit.
Evaluation is limited to Earth- and Uranus-orbit system simulations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models suffer significant accuracy drops under common corruptions. While test-time adaptation (TTA) successfully mitigates these shifts in CLIP-like contrastive models, its application to generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains underexplored and uniquely challenging due to their sequential token generation. In this work, we demonstrate that representation-based TTA fails to recover performance in MLLMs. Our experiments reveal that even when violating standard TTA assumptions by leveraging target data offline, sample-blind feature alignment recovers only marginal accuracy. We attribute this failure to the nature of corruption shifts: unlike CLIP-like architectures, which benefit from a shared domain-shift direction within a single pooled classification embedding, MLLM visual token sequence shifts are nearly orthogonal and span the full embedding space.These findings bound what any sample-blind, position-shared correction at a single encoder site can achieve, establishing that representation-space interventions alone might be insufficient to ensure corruption robustness in MLLMs.
authors: Miko{\l}aj Pi\'orczy\'nski, Wojciech Masarczyk, Damian S\'ojka, Sebastian Cygert, Bart{\l}omiej Twardowski
bullets: MLLMs experience substantial accuracy drops under common corruptions, and standard TTA strategies do not transfer reliably from CLIP-like models.
Even with offline access to target data, sample-blind feature alignment provides only marginal recovery.
MLLM corruption shifts are nearly orthogonal across visual tokens and span the embedding space, unlike the shared shift direction in pooled CLIP representations.
These results limit the effectiveness of position-shared, single-layer representation corrections for MLLM robustness.
The findings suggest that representation-space interventions alone may be insufficient for corruption robustness in generative MLLMs.

papers.title: On the Limits of Representation-Based Test-Time Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Representation-based test-time adaptation is fundamentally limited for improving corruption robustness in multimodal LLMs because their visual-token shifts are diverse rather than aligned.

papers.abstract: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test-Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length-conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine-tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length-based and confidence-based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model-agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.
authors: Fiorenzo Parascandolo, Enver Sangineto, Xiaoyi Yu, Wenhui Tan, Jipei He, Ruihua Song, Rita Cucchiara
bullets: Targets the tendency for longer chain-of-thoughts to be less likely correct.
Models this length-dependent correctness prior with a simple logistic function.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of continual adaptation in conventional pretrained VLA policies.
Adds a reinforcement-learning module that uses past observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals.
Refines action generation during deployment without updating the underlying model parameters.
Designed to support diverse history-construction strategies and VLA training pipelines.
Experiments in simulation and real-world deployment demonstrate adaptation to unseen scenarios.

papers.abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.
bullets: AIF and Bayes-UCBVI are compared under the same tabular-MDP state abstraction, differing only in exploration bonuses.
Uncalibrated AIF information gain decays too quickly, causing greedy agents to miss optimal actions.
Square-root calibration gives AIF order-$\sqrt{T}$ regret under an exact abstraction.
For fixed rewards, calibrated AIF offers no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI.
For rewards chosen from the agent’s data, calibrated AIF remains effective with a $\sqrt{S}$ factor, while Bayes-UCBVI can be locked out.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.
bullets: Addresses failures whose causes occur several steps before the observed error, beyond local reflection or backtracking.
Maintains relational beliefs over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints; execution and diagnostic evidence guide priorities and actions.
Uses an implicit world model to evaluate repair hypotheses, predict progress, and identify relationships among exploration frontiers.
Across three terminal-based benchmarks, it raises aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive exploration-efficiency trends.
A distilled 9B student gains 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline and reduces matched teacher API cost by 54.8%.

papers.abstract: Deep graph learning models deployed in real-world systems often need to cope with non-stationary environments, where the underlying graph distribution drifts continually over time. Prevailing solutions rely on training auxiliary generative modules to synthesize memory graphs for cross-domain adaptation, which incurs substantial computational overhead and scales poorly under prolonged distribution shifts. We argue that a more economical path exists: rather than generating memory, one can crystallize it. To this end, we propose Efficient Memory Crystallization (EMC), a training-free test-time framework that distills each incoming graph domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory through a closed-form solution to a memory-oriented distribution-matching objective, thereby eliminating redundant domain information under continual covariate shifts. To preserve both generalizability and adaptability as the model traverses a long sequence of target domains, EMC further models inter-domain dependencies through state-evolving memories and admits a theoretically grounded, tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of EMC over state-of-the-art baselines on graphs under non-stationary distribution shifts, while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory consumption by 92.4% relative to the recent competitor, making continual graph adaptation practical at scale.
bullets: Addresses the computational and scalability costs of synthesizing memory graphs during prolonged graph distribution shifts.
Uses a training-free, test-time framework with a closed-form distribution-matching objective to distill each incoming domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory.
Models inter-domain dependencies with state-evolving memories to balance generalizability and adaptability across target domains.
Provides a theoretically tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation.
Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory use by 92.4% relative to a recent competitor.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous driving requires more than accurate planning at a single frame: it demands reliable closed-loop execution in dynamic environments. Although end-to-end driving policies have advanced rapidly, the accumulated closed-loop errors, especially in unseen scenarios, can push vehicles into states from which the same policy struggles to recover. We address the challenge by treating closed-loop driving safety as a test-time execution problem. We introduce AutoAgent0, an agentic runtime and harness framework that augments existing driving experts with complementary detection skills, rule-based action verification, and feedback-driven recovery. To address inaccurate scene perception, an independent detection module constructs scene context using complementary perception skills, and a rule-based verifier checks proposed trajectories against this context before execution. When the nominal trajectories are unreliable, the orchestrator of the runtime activates Recovery Planning, where an agentic loop constructs alternative action proposals from action primitives and iteratively refines them using verification feedback. This design combines independent scene assessment with feasibility checks and online recovery, addressing both perception errors and the limited recovery capabilities of individual experts. Evaluations on Fail2Drive and NavSafe-$\infty$ demonstrate improved closed-loop robustness over single-expert execution in long-tail and safety-critical scenarios. These results demonstrate that runtime supervision can improve closed-loop robustness across multiple driving experts without retraining the underlying policies.
authors: Jiageng Liu, Seth Z. Zhao, Zewei Zhou, Alejandro Huerta, Aidan Bayer-Calvert, Yuxin Bao, Haotian Lin, Robert Spataru, Zijun Cui, Yining Hong, Bolei Zhou, Jiaqi Ma
bullets: Targets accumulated execution errors and poor recovery in dynamic, unseen, and safety-critical scenarios.
Uses complementary detection to build an independent scene context and verify proposed trajectories before execution.
When nominal actions are unsafe or unreliable, an orchestrator generates and iteratively refines alternatives from action primitives.
Evaluations on Fail2Drive and NavSafe-$\infty$ show greater closed-loop robustness than single-expert execution.
Scope: the framework augments existing driving experts at test time rather than changing or retraining their underlying policies.

papers.selection_reason: Agentic runtime for closed-loop driving safety with test-time recovery; fits robot navigation and test-time learning.
papers.title: AutoAgent0: An Agentic Runtime for Safe Closed-Loop Driving
papers.tldr: AutoAgent0 improves closed-loop autonomous-driving safety by supervising existing policies with independent perception, rule-based verification, and online recovery—without retraining them.

papers.abstract: Language model systems repeatedly make test-time decisions by comparing similarity: they retrieve exemplars, rank candidates, and revise responses. Yet similarity is not unique: lexical, semantic, structural, and stylistic resemblance can point to different candidates, and the task-aligned notion can change across instances. We introduce BASIS (Bayesian Axis Selection via Interactive Signals), a training-free Bayesian method that uses weak test-time feedback to infer which criterion in a supplied, task-specific library governs the current decision. It maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria, updates it from scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs, and selects probes by expected information gain. In a finite noisy model, we characterize when the target-criterion pair is recoverable and show why fixed-criterion and fixed-mixture rules can fail under criterion shift. Across concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement, BASIS improves six-probe concept-recovery Success@1 from 56.0% to 68.1%, reasoning accuracy from 72.3% to 73.1%, and refinement win rate from 61.4% to 63.8% over tuned static mixtures. It also exceeds compute-matched best-of-N selection on reasoning (72.1%) and refinement (61.2%). Gains are largest under criterion mismatch and with larger candidate pools, and matched controls indicate that adaptive criterion weighting explains much of the benefit, with joint target-criterion inference adding further value. BASIS selects only among supplied criteria and does not discover new ones.
bullets: Addresses criterion shift: lexical, semantic, structural, or stylistic similarity may be task-dependent.
Maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria using scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs.
Chooses informative probes via expected information gain without additional training.
Improves concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement over static mixtures; gains are largest under criterion mismatch.
Scope: selects among supplied criteria and cannot discover new similarity dimensions.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning
authors: Jason Ken Adhinarta, Raina Wu, Ashutosh Sharma, Avinash Balakrishnan, Rameswar Panda, Polina Golland, Yoon Kim, Zhang-Wei Hong
bullets: Evaluates SDPO and OPSD across code, science, tool-use, and math reasoning tasks.
Finds reported improvements do not consistently transfer to unseen problems.

Shows self-distillation gradients align weakly with reward-optimizing policy gradients.
Concludes that effectively using privileged information for reasoning remains unresolved.

papers.title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
papers.tldr: Self-distillation methods may improve in-distribution reasoning, but their gains often fail to generalize and do not clearly result from privileged information.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric. DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.
authors: Haotian Liu, Yingjian Chen, Xiaohang Xu, Lang Huang, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo, Irene Li
bullets: Targets unresolved intermediate errors that final-answer voting in self-consistency cannot correct.
Builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier.
Applies one focused repair only when verifier-supported refutation connects to the majority answer’s supporting path; otherwise preserves the SC vote.
Across five benchmarks, zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 points for Qwen2.5-7B and 15.83 points for Llama3.1-8B.
Outperforms the evaluated CoT, GoT, GoV, and self-consistency baselines without expanding the initial trace bank.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based test-time scaling enhances LLM reasoning by aggregating multiple reasoning paths for the same query. Existing methods use answer frequencies or path confidence to compute candidate scores, which do not explicitly characterize comparisons between competing answers. Inspired by the Condorcet principle in social choice theory, we introduce pairwise confidence comparisons between paths supporting different answers to capture answer-level comparative advantage. We combine this comparative evidence with voting support through a KL-regularized objective. Theoretically, we show that this comparative-advantage is equivalent to the adjustment to the traditional voting logits. In this way, our proposed Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment (PGLA) framework allows comparative evidence to compensate for weaker voting support and correct voting-based ranking errors. Experiments on 10 challenging benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, knowledge reasoning, and code generation with 7 models ranging from 1.7B to 32B parameters speak to the effectiveness of this plug-and-play term. Additional evaluations with external reward scores and online sampling further demonstrate its applicability.
authors: Cong Hua, Qianqian Xu, Zitai Wang, Zhiyong Yang, Shilong Bao, Linchao Zhang, Qingming Huang
bullets: Existing methods rank candidate answers mainly by frequency or path confidence, missing direct comparisons between alternatives.
PGLA adds pairwise confidence evidence for paths supporting different answers, inspired by the Condorcet principle.
A KL-regularized objective combines comparative evidence with voting support and yields an equivalent logit adjustment.
The framework is evaluated across 10 reasoning and code-generation benchmarks with 7 models, plus external-reward and online-sampling settings.
The method is presented as a plug-and-play way to compensate for weaker vote counts and correct ranking errors.

papers.abstract: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target tasks, or uses open-ended agents that discover task-specific choices but leave them implicit in trial-level edits, limiting their systematic reuse and recombination across trials. To fill this gap, we introduce optimization over a task-adapted recipe space, a novel paradigm that can adapt the recipe space itself to the target tasks while representing its choices explicitly for systematic reuse, recombination, and joint optimization. We instantiate this paradigm with Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO), comprising an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer that constructs the task-adapted recipe space and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer that uses structured trial evidence to guide LLM candidate construction and multi-objective Bayesian trial selection. Extensive experiments show that SRO achieves the highest average score in all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations. In joint post-training across three capability domains and six benchmarks, SRO reaches 41.1 versus 15.4 for the strongest baseline on Qwen3-1.7B with GPT-5.4, and 53.8 versus 40.8 on Qwen3-4B with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuohLiuq/SRO.
authors: Ruohong Liu, Bohan Tang, Lekang Jiang, Jack Umenberger, Yiwen Guo
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of predefined recipe spaces and the implicit, hard-to-reuse edits of open-ended agents.
Introduces task-adapted recipe-space optimization, with explicit choices that support reuse, recombination, and joint optimization.
Uses an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer guided by structured trial evidence and multi-objective Bayesian selection.
Reports the highest average score across all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations.
In joint post-training across three domains and six benchmarks, scores 41.1 vs. 15.4 and 53.8 vs. 40.8 for the strongest baselines in two evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) aims to improve large language model reasoning by exposing agents to alternative solutions and enabling iterative revision. However, standard broadcast-style MAD makes peer answers visible without requiring agents to engage with a particular peer claim. As a result, reliable reasoning may be suppressed by conflicting or majority responses, limiting achievable performance, while erroneous reasoning may persist and degrade final predictions without actionable feedback. We propose TrueMAD, a backbone-agnostic test-time plug-in that introduces one-to-one, free-form peer advice between answer broadcasting and self-revision. Each source agent responds to a target's current reasoning through support, rebuttal, refinement, or further questions, while the target retains control over how to revise. The same mechanism can augment standard MAD and its improved variants without parameter updates. Across AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and TruthfulQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B, TrueMAD improves agent-level and strict-majority accuracy over MAD by 3.62 and 3.52 percentage points on average, while TrueDMAD improves DMAD by 4.72 and 4.06 points, respectively. Analyses at the utterance, agent-transition, and group levels further show more peer-specific deliberation, more correction-oriented revisions, and more favorable consensus dynamics.
authors: Dezheng Bao, Sihang Du, Renhong Huang, Zhizhang Yuan, Yifei Sun, Yang Yang
bullets: Standard broadcast debate can leave agents disengaged from peer claims, allowing errors or majority influence to persist.
TrueMAD adds one-to-one, free-form peer advice—including support, rebuttal, refinement, or questions—between answer sharing and self-revision.
It is a backbone-agnostic, parameter-free test-time plug-in that can augment standard MAD and improved variants.
On AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and TruthfulQA using Qwen3-30B-A3B, TrueMAD improves agent-level and strict-majority accuracy over MAD by 3.62 and 3.52 percentage points on average.
The method produces more peer-specific deliberation, correction-oriented revisions, and favorable consensus dynamics.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards. Together, these components establish a reward-driven policy optimization loop in which multiple attempts jointly inform reusable context updates. We evaluate TextualRL with five target agents on six benchmarks. Averaged over the six benchmarks, TextualRL improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 and 15.3 percentage points for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B, respectively.
authors: Tianyu Huai, Jie Zhou, Bo Mao, Qin Chen, Liang He, Xipeng Qiu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting execution rewards into generalizable context edits from limited, task-specific evidence.
Uses Groupwise Policy Critique to compare successful and failed rollouts within the same task and context.
Uses Cross-Group Policy Update to refine proposed edits against evidence pooled across tasks, including cases with no proposed edit.
Builds bounded textual patches and adopts candidate contexts based on held-out validation rewards.
Across six benchmarks, improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 points for GPT-5.5 and 15.3 points for Qwen3.8-27B.

papers.abstract: Cross-domain few-shot action recognition (CD-FSAR) aims to recognise unseen action classes in a target domain from a handful of labelled videos. Despite advances in representation learning, CD-FSAR inference still relies on prototypes estimated from extremely limited support examples. To assess this bottleneck, we perform an oracle analysis with the representation fixed. Constructing oracle prototypes and decision boundaries from ground-truth query labels improves 5-way 1-shot accuracy by 7--20 percentage points across five target datasets. This reveals a substantial estimation gap: the representation contains useful discriminative information, but prototypes and boundaries estimated from scarce supports fail to capture each episode's true class structure. Motivated by this, we propose TRACE, a training-free transductive inference framework that improves episode-level estimation without modifying the backbone. TRACE comprises two complementary stages. Confidence-Thresholded Transductive Prototype Refinement (CTPR) refines support-based prototypes using confidently predicted queries. The refined prototypes initialise a lightweight per-episode classifier, which Transductive Classifier Refinement (TCR) further adapts by encouraging confident, class-balanced predictions over all queries. Together, the two stages improve prototype and boundary estimation, enabling better use of information in the unlabelled queries. Across five target datasets (HMDB51, UCF101, SSv2, Diving48, and RareAct) in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong CD-FSAR baseline, including gains of more than six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot, while recovering much of the oracle-estimated gap. These results suggest that improving test-time estimation is a powerful, broadly applicable complement to representation learning for CD-FSAR under extreme support scarcity.
authors: Changyi Li, Zeyu Yang, Yu Xiao
bullets: An oracle analysis shows that scarce-support prototype and decision-boundary estimation is a major bottleneck, despite useful learned representations.
TRACE uses two training-free transductive stages: confidence-based prototype refinement (CTPR) and class-balanced classifier refinement (TCR).
The method leverages confidently predicted unlabelled queries to better estimate each episode’s class structure.
Across five target datasets and both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong baseline, with gains exceeding six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot.
The approach recovers much of the oracle-estimated gap, but its scope is limited to test-time transductive settings with available unlabelled queries.

papers.title: Closing the Estimation Gap: Training-Free Transductive Inference for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Action Recognition
papers.tldr: TRACE improves cross-domain few-shot action recognition without retraining by refining prototypes and episode-specific classifiers using unlabelled queries.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations. However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths. We propose TRACESTEER, a trace-driven activation steering framework that uses preceding denoising predictions as feedback to jointly adapt steering direction and strength. Specifically, Denoising Feedback Steering (DF-Steering) constructs step-specific steering vectors from preceding predictions and current hidden states. Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate (TS-Gate) regulates their strength using prediction uncertainty and the denoising timestep. With the backbone frozen, factual supervision and magnitude regularization jointly guide the learning of adaptive steering interventions, promoting factual reliability and stability throughout denoising. Experiments on two dLLMs show improved factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalization across five downstream benchmarks.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yili Wang, Yue Tan, Xin He, Rui Miao, Yixin Liu, Yi Chang, Xin Wang
bullets: Targets dLLM-specific challenges: changing denoising states and time-varying hallucination risk.
Uses Denoising Feedback Steering to derive step-specific steering vectors from prior predictions and current hidden states.
Uses a Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate to adjust intervention strength based on uncertainty and denoising timestep.
Learns adaptive interventions with the backbone frozen, combining factual supervision and magnitude regularization.
Improves factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalizes across five downstream benchmarks in experiments on two dLLMs.
