papers.abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.
authors: Yue Wang, Qizhou Wang, Feng Liu, Gang Niu, Masashi Sugiyama, Bo Han
bullets: Long-context inference is costly, motivating test-time encoding of context into model weights.
Weight-encoded information can be confused with the model’s pre-existing knowledge and ignored as context.
The method associates each encoded context with an identifier, enabling the LLM to recite it later.
A prompting framework further guides the model to use the recalled information for subsequent inference.
It outperformed a baseline across controlled tasks and practical benchmarks using off-the-shelf LLMs.

papers.title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?
papers.tldr: The paper makes context encoded into temporary LLM weight updates usable by assigning it an identifier and prompting the model to apply the recalled information as context.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled plausible interactive environments, yet long-horizon generation places a fundamental demand on visual memory: the previously observed world must remain consistent as the model continues to generate. Existing autoregressive approaches often implicitly rely on the generative model itself to retain such information, leading to spatial memory decay beyond the active context. We introduce World-T3, a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training memory that consolidates past observations into dedicated model parameters. To robustly update this memory, we propose a recursive least-squares rule that incrementally absorbs novel visual features via online pose-keyed memory updates. Our TTT memory reads out previously observed scene features from the fast-weight state by camera pose, enabling consistent generation with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length. To facilitate real-time interactive generation with this robust memory, we further distill the autoregressive model into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching. On a long-horizon revisit benchmark, World-T3 raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and reduces absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075 relative to the strongest baseline on both metrics, while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.
authors: Junyi Wu, Zekun Li, Chenhongyi Yang, Chen Guo, Lingchen Yang, Yongan Zhang, Xinyi Zhang, Hongbing Hu, Bartek Rymkowski, Srinath Sridhar, Yan Yan, Xijie Huang
bullets: Addresses spatial memory decay when autoregressive world models generate beyond their active context.
Uses recursive least squares to update fast-weight memory with newly observed visual features keyed by camera pose.
Reads stored scene features with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length.
Distills the autoregressive model into a few-step generator using dual-teacher distribution matching for interactive speed.
Improves revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075, while reaching 20.6 FPS at 1280×704 on one NVIDIA B200 GPU.

papers.selection_reason: Camera-controlled video world model with test-time training as persistent memory, fitting video world models, interactive world models, and test-time learning.
papers.title: World-T3: Test-Time Training as Persistent Memory for Real-Time Video World Models
papers.tldr: World-T3 gives real-time video world models persistent, pose-keyed test-time memory to preserve scene consistency during long-horizon generation.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery with language models requires finding the best valid solution within a finite computational budget. We study how feedback from this search can improve the procedure used to conduct it. We introduce HarnessTTT, a test-time learning framework that trains a harness proposer while keeping the executor frozen. The proposer generates executable harnesses comprising system prompts, reusable skills, tools, middleware, and execution controls. Each harness guides a budgeted discovery rollout, whose outcome provides feedback for updating the proposer. A discovery-oriented policy-gradient objective combines gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages (RLOO), and max-sharpening to favor high-performing proposals. Generated components are validated before execution, and the search retains the best valid solution and selected harnesses across rounds. Across fourteen discovery tasks in mathematics, systems, GPU kernels, heuristic programming, astrodynamics, and biology, HarnessTTT with a frozen 9B executor improves on OpenEvolve with the same executor on all eleven benchmark tasks (e.g., from 1.17 to 2.64 on circle packing), improves on the discovery-fine-tuned Finch-9B by up to 92%, holds the best open-weight sub-10B result on nine, and reaches 0.380919 on Erd\H{o}s minimum overlap, better than the best human reference of 0.380927. Scaling the proposer and frozen executor to 27B improves on eleven of fourteen tasks, and transferring the learned harnesses to GPT-5.5 matches or exceeds the strongest reported system of any backbone on nine of fourteen tasks. Together, these results show that harness search can itself be learned at test time: a trained proposer lets a small frozen executor search effectively, and the harnesses it finds carry over to stronger executors.
authors: Yingzi Ma, Yulong Cao, Nanxi Li, Fang Wu, Yizhe Zhang, James Zou, Yejin Choi, Chaowei Xiao
bullets: Addresses how to find high-quality valid solutions under a fixed computational budget for scientific discovery.
Trains a harness proposer while keeping the solution-generating executor frozen; harnesses combine prompts, skills, tools, middleware, and execution controls.
Uses rollout feedback with gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages, and max-sharpening to improve proposed harnesses, while validating components and retaining strong results.
Across 14 tasks, it improves over OpenEvolve on all 11 benchmark tasks and transfers effectively to larger executors, including GPT-5.5.
Scope: results cover mathematics, systems, GPU kernels, heuristic programming, astrodynamics, and biology; performance gains vary across tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time learning framework that updates a harness proposer from search feedback directly matches test-time learning.
papers.title: HarnessTTT: Learn to Optimize Harness at Test-Time for Scientific Discovery
papers.tldr: HarnessTTT learns better search procedures at test time, enabling a small frozen language model to solve diverse scientific discovery tasks more effectively and transfer its learned harnesses to stronger models.

papers.abstract: Humans expand their locomotion capability by wearing appropriate footwear, such as hiking boots for mountains or skates for ice. Footwear changes the ground-contact interface and enables traversal of otherwise difficult terrain. In contrast, locomotion controllers are typically trained for a fixed morphology, and their performance can degrade when shoes alter foot geometry, mass, and friction. We propose SHOES, a sample-efficient framework for adapting locomotion policies to footwear-induced morphology changes. SHOES freezes a simulation-trained nominal policy and fine-tunes only lightweight, identity-initialized modulation modules on the robot, preserving the initial behavior while enabling efficient hardware adaptation. We also introduce SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that constrains online adaptation within a user-defined workspace. The simulation results with a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 show that SHOES substantially recovers locomotion performance after footwear-induced morphology changes using limited additional adaptation. Under the same adaptation budget, SHOES outperforms FiLM-only, Linear Adapter-only, and residual-RL baselines. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 fitted with human shoes further evaluate the effectiveness of SHOES for hardware deployment.
authors: Kota Tsuruhara, Tsung-Yuan Chen, Kento Kawaharazuka
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by changes in foot geometry, mass, and friction from added footwear.
Freezes a simulation-trained nominal policy and fine-tunes identity-initialized modulation modules for sample-efficient adaptation.
Introduces SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that keeps online adaptation within user-defined limits.
Simulation on a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 substantially recovers locomotion performance and outperforms several adapter and residual-RL baselines under the same adaptation budget.
Real-world experiments with human shoes further assess deployment on a Unitree Go2.

papers.selection_reason: Adapts locomotion policies to morphology changes via lightweight online modules, combining embodied control with test-time adaptation.

papers.tldr: SHOES efficiently adapts legged-robot locomotion policies to footwear-induced morphology changes through safe, lightweight on-robot fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.
authors: Yike Wu, Keyan Chen, Qixiong Wang, Xi Xiang, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses redundant, noisy, or disruptive computation in MLLMs during video spatial reasoning.
Uses a training-free multiagent framework that plans steps to gather missing spatial evidence and combines it with native evidence.
Applies stage-aligned verification to identify whether failures arise from planning, perception, or reasoning.
Uses dependency-based recovery to recompute affected states while preserving valid intermediate results.
Achieves the highest overall score among compared methods across three MLLMs and two benchmarks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback--response cycles elicited by replay in the target model. Our training-free framework, $\textbf{REVEAL}$ ($\textbf{REV}$erse $\textbf{E}$ngineering $\textbf{A}$gentic $\textbf{L}$atents), uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match and select local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task and source model. Their response-transition contrasts yield a target-specific steering direction, applied before each response. Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy than unmodified agents across three targets. Representation analyses and behavioral case studies support reusing frontier-model experience as local activation control.
authors: Yuetian Du, Meng Wang, Yucheng Wang, Zhangzhe Chen, Wei Wang, Boyu Yang, Weiqi Zhai, Bing Zhao, Ming Kong, Zhan Zhou, Jie Liu, Qiang Zhu
bullets: Addresses the cost of transferring frontier-agent experience when target training or source-model internals are unavailable.
Constructs agentic latents from replayed feedback–response cycles, including anchored states and dynamic profiles.
Matches local events across successful and failed trajectories to derive response-transition steering directions.
Applies the resulting control before each target-agent response.
Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity’s Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy across three target agents; analyses support local activation control as the mechanism.

papers.abstract: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.
bullets: Analyzes prediction-derived updates in released test-time-training (TTT) implementations.
For dot-product objectives, finds no explicit prediction-error residual and shows ascent/descent equivalence under reparameterization in certain conditions.
For LayerNorm-based TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP objectives, derives the inner gradient and identifies a component that cancels at initialization in the zero-epsilon limit.
Removing the component reduces gradient norms to 0.25–0.32 of the original and modestly increases perplexity, while freezing all fast-weight updates causes much larger degradation.
Synthetic tests show that plain delta-rule overwriting depends on step size.

papers.abstract: Time series (TS) anomaly detection (AD) lacks a universal detector, with the best choice determined by the series rather than by the algorithm. Existing methods therefore either select one detector for each series or average a pool of them. However, both assume that no label ever arrives, while a deployed monitor does receive them, since an operator confirms the alarms it raises. In this paper, we propose ONESHOT, which uses a single confirmed anomaly to weight the pool rather than to choose one detector from it. Specifically, we score each detector on the confirmed anomaly, and those scores become the weights of a soft mixture over the whole pool. We show that a single confirmed anomaly is enough to come close to the best detector for the series. Across 152 univariate and 73 multivariate series, ONESHOT outperforms the strongest single detector, averaging the whole pool, and even picking the best detector on the confirmed event. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/one_shot.
authors: Seunghan Lee, Jun Seo, Jaehoon Lee, Junhyeok Kang, Sangjun Han, Sungdong Yoo, Minjae Kim, Tae Yoon Lim, Dongwan Kang, Hwanil Choi, Soonyoung Lee, Wonbin Ahn
bullets: Addresses detector selection when deployed monitors receive operator-confirmed anomaly labels.
Scores every detector on the single confirmed anomaly and uses the scores as soft-mixture weights.
Evaluated on 152 univariate and 73 multivariate series.
Outperforms the strongest single detector, uniform pooling, and selecting the detector that best detects the confirmed event.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: An agent can retain successful trajectories without learning which part of an experience should repair a new discrepancy. We formulate passive imitation (PI) as an architectural loop that localizes a violated contract, extracts a local goal, proposes an effect-matched skill, tests a small patch, and retains evidence after full-task verification. We instantiate this loop as a deterministic symbolic controller and analyze its finite repair-query complexity under explicit identifiability and noninterference assumptions. Across ten simulated tool worlds, PI solves all 600 cold held-out composition tasks with three allowed small trials, compared with 6.17% for a whole-trajectory control, while an equally expressive compositional repair control matches PI. On an unseen tool revision, PI achieves 70.0% success versus 24.0% without small trials and 79.0% with self-trial enumeration; an exploratory 24-task adaptation stream subsequently raises first-submission success to 100%, supporting a limited correction-and-retention mechanism rather than a unique incentive advantage or general intelligence. The CPU-only implementation, integrity checks, and reproducible results are available at https://github.com/FriendOfYishan/PI.
bullets: Frames imitation as a loop that localizes violated contracts, extracts local goals, proposes effect-matched skills, tests small patches, and retains evidence after full-task verification.
Implements the approach as a deterministic symbolic controller and analyzes finite repair-query complexity under identifiability and noninterference assumptions.
Solved all 600 cold held-out composition tasks with three small trials, while whole-trajectory control solved 6.17%; an equally expressive compositional repair control matched it.
On an unseen tool revision, success was 70.0% with small trials, versus 24.0% without them and 79.0% with self-trial enumeration.
Results support a limited correction-and-retention mechanism, not a unique incentive advantage or general intelligence.

Right: first-submission success after separate C acquisition tasks in the exploratory follow-up. Lines show means over ten worlds; PI and compositional repair overlap. Repeated evaluations use the same frozen final C tasks. Learning C changes the interpretation from unseen-revision transfer to retention within a learned revision.

A local trial pass permits a tentative patch. Full-task acceptance contributes evidence for later proactive reuse. Candidate sources may include other executions or the controller’s own trials.

papers.selection_reason: Localized repair, test-time skill patching, and evidence retention fit adaptation and memory interests.
papers.title: Imitation Holds a Key to Evolution: Localized Repair and Verified Skill Acquisition for Adaptive Agents
papers.tldr: Passive imitation enables adaptive agents to repair localized failures and retain verified skills, achieving strong performance in simulated tool-composition tasks under stated assumptions.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) enables large language models to adapt directly on unlabeled test problems by constructing pseudo-labels from multiple sampled responses. However, existing TTRL methods typically apply the same expensive sampling and optimization procedure to all test problems, despite substantial differences in their training utility. In this paper, we study whether such problems can be identified before costly test-time training, without access to ground-truth answers. We uncover a stable relationship between internal response representations and problem-level empirical accuracy. Specifically, we define COS as the cosine similarity between a model's response representation and a correctness-related direction constructed from an independent question-answering dataset. COS consistently correlates with problem solvability across different models, datasets, and experimental settings, and we further provide a theoretical analysis explaining this relationship. Building on this finding, we propose SelectTTRL, a representation-guided data selection method that ranks test problems using COS and applies TTRL only to a selected percentile interval. SelectTTRL leaves the standard TTRL pipeline unchanged for the selected problems, while avoiding unnecessary multi-response sampling and reinforcement learning updates on the remaining ones. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SelectTTRL substantially reduces test-time computation while maintaining or improving the performance of standard TTRL. Code is available at https://github.com/heyiliyi/SelectTTRL-public.
authors: Yi Li, Linan Yue, Weibo Gao
bullets: TTRL can waste costly sampling and optimization on problems with limited training utility.
A cosine similarity score (COS) between response representations and a correctness-related direction estimates problem solvability without ground-truth answers.
COS is reported to correlate consistently with problem-level empirical accuracy across models, datasets, and settings.
SelectTTRL ranks problems by COS and applies standard TTRL only within a selected percentile interval.
Experiments on multiple reasoning benchmarks show substantially lower test-time computation with maintained or improved TTRL performance.

papers.abstract: Movable agents, such as autonomous vehicles and robots, should be able to autonomously adapt their pre-trained object recognition models to new environments without human annotations. While existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods address label-free model adaptation, they typically treat test data as independent snapshots, without constructively exploiting a rich, unique source of supervision: the significant variance in prediction quality as an agent observes the same object from different distances and viewpoints. To capitalize on this, we propose \texttt{MoCaFe}, a model-agnostic and hyperparameter-insensitive paradigm that leverages motion-induced prediction variance for unsupervised adaptation. Specifically, we first develop mobility-calibrated filtering of pseudo-labels, which constructs reliable pseudo-labels by fusing cross-view predictions using inverse-variance weights. The filtered pseudo-labels then guide the selection of ``hard samples'' for effective learning. To further suppress pseudo-label corruption, we introduce \texttt{p-MoCaFe}, an optional extension that uses a public dataset to assign weighting factors to data samples, yielding an estimator of the clean loss with bounded bias. Extensive experiments on autonomous driving (nuScenes, KITTI) and embodied-agent datasets show that \texttt{MoCaFe} significantly outperforms state-of-the-art TTA schemes, achieving up to approximately 20% accuracy gain.
authors: Yanan Ma, Yihang Tao, Zhengru Fang, Senkang Hu, Xianhao Chen, Yuguang Fang
bullets: Targets autonomous vehicles and robots adapting pre-trained recognition models to new environments without human annotations.
Fuses predictions across distances and viewpoints with inverse-variance weighting to create mobility-calibrated pseudo-labels.
Uses filtered pseudo-labels to select hard samples for more effective test-time adaptation.
p-MoCaFe optionally uses a public dataset to weight samples and reduce pseudo-label corruption with bounded bias.
Experiments on autonomous-driving and embodied-agent datasets report gains of up to approximately 20% in accuracy over existing TTA methods.

In the p-MoCaFe extension, an additional public dataset is used to calibrate debiasing weights, yielding an unbiased empirical risk for robust model adaptation.

papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal foundation models are increasingly capable of directly controlling robots, yet improving their manipulation capabilities through autonomous interaction remains challenging. A key challenge to such self-improvement is learning from failures in complex manipulation tasks involving cross-stage dependencies, where an action may succeed locally but cause a later stage to fail. To address this challenge, we introduce ReTrace, a self-improvement framework for robotic manipulation through autonomous physical interaction and retrospective reasoning, without provided demonstrations or model-parameter updates. ReTrace retrospectively traces downstream failures to earlier decisions, proposes targeted corrections, and evaluates them through subsequent interactions. Across attempts, ReTrace progressively consolidates validated corrections into a reusable manipulation skill that guide subsequent execution. We evaluate ReTrace on four real-world manipulation tasks using a Franka Research 3 robot. On the two tasks with strong cross-stage dependencies, GPT-6 Astra-low improves from 0% to 80% success on plug insertion and from 0% to 100% on ball pouring, while GPT-6 Sol-xhigh improves from 0% to 10% and 0% to 90%, respectively. The learned skills also transfer across model and reasoning configurations and reduce inference-time decision cost in most evaluated settings.
authors: Yue Yu, Bin Zhu, Junhui Li, Jiayu Wang, Shijie Zhou, Jingjing Chen
bullets: Addresses failures caused by dependencies across stages of complex manipulation tasks.
Uses retrospective reasoning and physical interaction without demonstrations or model-parameter updates.
Consolidates validated corrections into reusable skills for subsequent executions.
Evaluated on four real-world tasks with a Franka Research 3 robot; reported gains on plug insertion and ball pouring.
Learned skills transfer across model and reasoning configurations and usually reduce inference-time decision cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the framework. The Executor plans and executes robot actions using current observations and accumulated experience. Across attempts, the Attributor diagnoses problems, proposes corrections, and refines them based on execution feedback. The Experience Memory stores skill, pending corrections, and execution history to guide subsequent attempts.

Figure 3. Real-world task settings. From left to right: banana picking, block stacking, plug insertion, and ball pouring. The latter two tasks require earlier grasping decisions to support later operations.

Figure 4. Learning process through cross-stage failure attribution and correction refinement. Top: Plug insertion improves over three attempts by attributing the collision risk to an unfavorable grasp pose and progressively refining the gripper tilt before grasping. Bottom: Ball pouring succeeds in the second attempt by shifting the grasp position to prevent scoop instability during lifting.

Figure 5. Inference-time decision counts with and without learned skill. Bars show the mean over 10 trials per configuration. The per-trial decision budget is 35 for plug insertion and 25 for each of the other tasks. Unsuccessful trials are assigned the full task-specific decision budget.

Figure 1. Cross-stage dependencies and failure attribution in robotic manipulation. Top: Plug insertion involves grasping, lifting, rotating, and inserting the plug. Although the grasp succeeds, the resulting relative pose between the gripper and plug leaves insufficient clearance for subsequent insertion, causing a collision. Bottom: Retrospective reasoning traces the insertion collision back to the earlier grasp pose, identifying the decision to revise.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ReTrace, a self-improving framework for robotic manipulation that attributes cross-stage failures and proposes corrections through autonomous physical interaction without model updates.
papers.title: ReTrace: Cross-Stage Failure Attribution for Self-Improving Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: ReTrace enables robots to improve manipulation autonomously by tracing later failures back to earlier decisions and validating targeted corrections.

papers.abstract: Bitemporal remote sensing change detection requires representations that preserve spatial detail while capturing contextual information relevant to changes between acquisitions. Visual test-time training offers an alternative to explicit token-to-token attention by adapting a compact inner model to each image. This letter describes ChangeT$^3$, a vanilla Siamese configuration combining the existing hierarchical ViT$^3$-Tiny encoder with the multiscale ChangeFormer decoder. The two image streams share learned encoder parameters, while their fast weights are computed independently from their respective spatial features. Each encoder block retains the inherited global simplified SwiGLU and local adaptive depthwise-convolution branches. Temporal comparison is performed by the decoder through learned fusion of paired features at four resolutions, followed by coarse-to-fine aggregation and binary prediction. This separation provides a direct setting for examining image-conditioned inner updates without introducing an additional temporal interaction module. Trained from scratch on LEVIR-CD+ with the same decoder, recipe, and budget as a ChangeFormer control, ChangeT$^3$ reaches an F1 of 80.61$\pm$0.90 against 78.84$\pm$0.21 for ChangeFormer (three seeds each); as in the standard protocol for this dataset, checkpoints are selected on the test split. Trained with both inner updates disabled, the same encoder reaches 78.63$\pm$0.20. Neither model transfers zero-shot to SYSU-CD, DSIFN-CD, or WHU-CD, and ChangeT$^3$ is the slower of the two at small inputs despite similar parameter and operation counts.
authors: Sharukshan Niranjan, Oshadha Samarakoon, Nichula Wasalathilaka, Roshan Godaliyadda, Parakrama Ekanayake, Vijitha Herath
bullets: Uses a vanilla Siamese architecture with shared hierarchical ViT$^3$-Tiny encoders and independently computed fast weights for each image.
A multiscale ChangeFormer decoder compares paired features at four resolutions and produces coarse-to-fine binary change maps.
On LEVIR-CD+, ChangeT$^3$ achieves 80.61±0.90 F1 versus 78.84±0.21 for the ChangeFormer control across three seeds.
Disabling inner updates reduces the encoder’s F1 to 78.63±0.20, supporting the value of test-time adaptation in this setup.
Neither model transfers zero-shot to SYSU-CD, DSIFN-CD, or WHU-CD; ChangeT$^3$ is also slower at small inputs despite similar parameter and operation counts.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates vision test-time training for remote sensing change detection; directly fits test-time learning.
papers.title: ChangeT$^3$: Evaluating Vision Test-Time Training for Remote Sensing Change Detection
papers.tldr: ChangeT$^3$ evaluates image-conditioned vision test-time training for remote-sensing change detection, improving LEVIR-CD+ F1 over a matched ChangeFormer control but showing limited cross-dataset transfer and slower inference at small inputs.

papers.abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries real-data evaluator feedback, and updates a retained factor pool across turns. This design jointly leverages market text, LLM financial knowledge, real data, and evaluation feedback. At inference time, AlphaPilot performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to shifting market regimes. Across three independent runs in out-of-sample rolling backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, AlphaPilot achieves mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively. It attains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes.
authors: Peiqi Jiang, Fan Zhang, Xin Xu, Tianhao Chen, Can Yang
bullets: Addresses alpha mining by jointly using unstructured market descriptions, financial knowledge, historical data, and quantitative factor evaluation.
Agents propose factor expressions, query a real-data evaluator, and update a retained factor pool over multiple turns.
Performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to changing market regimes.
In rolling out-of-sample backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, it reports the highest mean total return, Sharpe ratio, and RankIC among evaluated methods.
Mean total returns were 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively, across three runs.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to hardware-dependent 3D sensing modalities, yet predicting precise metric depth remains a persistent challenge due to intrinsic scale ambiguity, edge bleeding, and limited zero-shot generalization in unseen environments. Recent multi-modal approaches incorporate 1D/3D Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) data to resolve these ambiguities, but they mainly treat SPAD noise as a harmful artifact required for denoising or leave the noise ignored. In this paper, we present an essentially different insight: native SPAD noise is an informative prior that implicitly encodes deterministic environmental characteristics. Driven by this paradigm shift, we introduce a novel, lightweight Test-Time Gated Attention framework by Harnessing SPAD Noise, therefore dubbed HSN. Tailored for indoor scenarios, HSN leverages the synergistic combination of 1D SPAD histograms and Gate Adapters (GAs). Through three complementary optimization phases, it generates channel-wise gated attention vectors to dynamically adjust encoder feature maps at inference time, effectively resolving ambiguous scale and boundary challenges without the heavy computational overhead or dense 3D modalities that other TTA methods suffer from. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world indoor benchmarks show that HSN achieves state-of-the-art metric depth accuracy in in-domain settings, while exhibiting even greater potential under zero-shot generalization to unfamiliar environments. Furthermore, interpretability analysis reveals that the proposed gated attention mechanism adaptively shifts attention toward deeper semantic layers under intensifying SPAD noise. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Targets scale ambiguity, edge bleeding, and weak zero-shot generalization in monocular depth estimation.
Combines 1D SPAD histograms with Gate Adapters that dynamically recalibrate encoder features at inference time.
Uses three optimization phases to produce channel-wise gated attention without dense 3D sensing or heavy computation.
Reports state-of-the-art metric-depth accuracy on challenging real-world indoor benchmarks, with stronger potential in zero-shot settings.
Interpretability analysis shows attention shifts toward deeper semantic layers as SPAD noise increases.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the proposed Test-Time Gated Attention framework (HSN). (a) illustrates how Gate Adapter (GA) modules are embedded between the selected encoder map and its corresponding decoder map, where the targeted encoder map is routed to the subsequent decoding layer. Conversely, encoder maps not routed to decoding layers bypass GA modulation entirely. (b) details the architectural design of the GA module and the TTA workflow. During inference, the pre-trained encoder-decoder network θ remains frozen to preserve its inherent structural priors, restricting optimization strictly to the GA parameters ϕ. These modules leverage the SPAD noise signal to dynamically generate a channel-wise gated attention vector g, thereby calibrating the selected encoder maps prior to decoding.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.
authors: Yi Ge, Kangrui Ruan, Jifan Chen, Manish Prajapat, Christian Bock, Xiaoyang Wang, Rein Houthooft, Aritra Sengupta, Varun Kumar
bullets: Coding agents often act reactively, making early mistakes that can irreversibly damage repository state before terminal feedback arrives.

On SWE-bench Verified, ANTE improves Qwen3-32B pass@1 from 25.0% to 57.2%; its world-model accuracy rises from 44% to 69% and transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains.

papers.abstract: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $\Delta S_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the lack of test-time sequential memory in predictive coding while avoiding BPTT’s large memory demands.
Treats each per-step memory update as a latent variable rather than a slowly learned weight.
Derives a predictive-coding-native update rule from a probabilistic model and connects it to DeltaNet-style linear attention updates.
Evaluates scaling, memory footprint, contextual inference, single- and multi-sequence storage, and key-value associative memory.
Reports perfect recall for the tested sequence and associative-memory tasks.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after an update minus success before. That difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. We introduce Trace Evolution Bench (TEB), a protocol that separates that rescore from a context or weight update, together with three frozen 80/20/40 packs. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out identifiers never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The primary scoreboard is coding, graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace. On that pack (40 held-out tasks, one family), DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds. Of nine text-update cells inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, seven have positive excess above that seed's own band, and one gepa_llm seed moves down by the width of its band (-12.5, regression 0.48). GLM and MiniMax do not reproduce that seven-of-nine pattern. No method stays above its own band on every seed of all three models: GLM has two paired cells above their own bands, and MiniMax expel_llm seed 44 is a third (regression 0.30). The methods were fixed on a validation screen before held-out was read. Office, graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA are separate packs: office DeepSeek does not exceed its own bands (widest 17.5 points), and manufacturing has no paired positive excess beyond its seed band.

bullets: Introduces TEB, which distinguishes frozen rescoring from context or weight updates using validation gates and held-out tasks.

Positive excess was not consistent across all seeds and models; office and manufacturing packs showed no comparable robust improvement.

papers.abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.
authors: Kounianhua Du, Jianxing Liu, Kangning Zhang, Wenxiang Jiao, Yuan Lu, Jiarui Jin, Jianghao Lin, Weiwen Liu, Yong Yu, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Targets personalization with sparse, heterogeneous, evolving user histories and query-dependent preferences.
Generates sample-level interference vectors and injects them into the model’s forward pass.
Combines match contrast, attention/MLP activation steering, and query-conditioned signal aggregation.
Validated across text generation and web function-calling scenarios, with reported gains especially in fast-changing and data-sparse settings.
Designed to avoid training cycles while adding limited storage and inference overhead, though specific quantitative results are not provided.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Overview of FleetPilot. 1) Steering Vectors Preparation. During this stage, we construct contrastive prompts from user logs, where relevant context retrieved from personal corpus is concatenated with target query to form the positive sample and irrelevant context sampled from other users is concatenated with target query to form the negative sample. For each positive sample, we generate K negative samples. Each pair is then fed into the LLM in the teacher forcing mode, during which the response tokens’ activations of attention and MLP blocks are hooked. We store the difference between two sample activations of a pair to serve as the steering vector, with the text of each pair being the key for indexing convenience. 2) Instance-Tailored Personalized Adaptation and Inference. During this stage, we sample from target user’s steering vectors set to interfere model for personalized output. Concretely, we rank the similarity between query text and sample pair text to select the top-k steering vectors, which are then aggregated and injected into LLM for personalized adaptation.

Fig. 1 Personalization paradigms and the design of FleetPilot. Left: prompt-based personalization supplies retrieved history through a context window, where noisy evidence and limited model capacity constrain its use. Middle: parametric adaptation and personalized reward modeling introduce optimization or candidate-scoring stages, with challenges in sparse-data fitting, model updates, storage, and best-of-N inference. Right: inference-time steering modifies intermediate activations in a frozen LLM, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis. FleetPilot adapts this principle to personalization through three design changes: response contrast to matched contrast, whole-layer hooking to fine-grained hooking, and user-tailored to instance-tailored steering.

papers.abstract: Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can execute impressive motions, but downstream applications such as loco-manipulation demand high whole-body positional accuracy. Existing BFMs suffer from a systematic command-execution gap, where executed motions deviate from desired ones. We show that additional test-time compute can improve execution without retraining the BFM. First, we introduce Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO), which adapts the input command to the specific BFM to produce an executed trajectory closer to the desired motion. TTCO finds such commands by sampling-based optimization through closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. Across three BFMs on the AMASS dataset, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79-84% in simulation. Second, we analyze test-time compute scaling and derive an approximate compute-optimal strategy that can sustain performance gains as the compute budget increases. Third, TTCO can generate BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories without requiring the original teleoperation body-motion commands. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that these labels are effective for training high-level loco-manipulation policies. This method also supports reusing existing demonstrations across BFMs.
authors: Weiji Xie, Junsong Wu, Zibo Zhou, Yueru Chen, Xingyi Wang, Zhenhua Xiong, Weinan Zhang, Chenjia Bai
bullets: Addresses the command-execution gap that limits whole-body accuracy in downstream loco-manipulation.
Introduces TTCO, which uses sampling-based optimization over closed-loop BFM and robot-dynamics simulations to adapt input commands.
Across three BFMs on AMASS, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79–84% in simulation.
Derives an approximate compute-optimal scaling strategy to preserve gains with larger test-time budgets.
Generates BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories, validated in simulation and on a real robot for high-level policy training.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution. We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. A fixed verifier scores candidates generated by a flow-matching VLA, the weighted aggregate is executed, and the observations and aggregated chunks from successful adaptation episodes are distilled directly into LoRA parameters with the standard flow-matching loss. This reuses supervision that TTC has already produced during execution, without additional reinforcement learning or rollouts dedicated to teacher generation. On the 40 LIBERO tasks with a SmolVLA 5k checkpoint, distilling from only 10 episodes per task raises the mean success rate of verifier-free single-candidate generation from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of the improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates. Applying the same aggregation to the distilled policy further raises the success rate from 76.4% to 82.3%, with a particularly large gain on LIBERO-Long (44.0% to 57.8%), and the single-candidate policy also improves on LIBERO-plus, which contains distribution shifts. These results show that using verification as a learning signal, rather than only as an execution-time selector, both retains the improvements of TTC and re-amplifies the effect of subsequent TTC.
authors: Kaneyoshi Hiratsuka, Satoshi Yamamori, Jun Morimoto
bullets: Existing TTC improves execution by selecting among candidates but requires recomputing this selection at every execution because the policy remains frozen.

The framework uses a fixed verifier to score flow-matching VLA candidates, executes their weighted aggregate, and distills successful episodes into LoRA parameters using the standard flow-matching loss.
It requires no additional reinforcement learning or teacher-generation rollouts, reusing supervision produced during TTC.
On 40 LIBERO tasks, distilling from 10 episodes per task raises verifier-free single-candidate success from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of eight-candidate aggregation’s improvement.
Applying aggregation after distillation further increases success from 76.4% to 82.3%, with gains also observed on LIBERO-Long and distribution-shifted LIBERO-plus.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation under uncertain object dynamics and geometry remains a core challenge in real-world robotics. Policies trained under fixed assumptions often degrade when object mass, friction, scale, or shape vary. Embedding-based adaptation methods such as Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) address this by conditioning actions on latent representations of environment dynamics inferred from interaction history. We investigate whether this paradigm scales from single arm settings to coordinated bimanual manipulation, where higher dimensional control, coupled contacts, and shared object forces introduce additional complexity. We evaluate bimanual RMA on three contact-rich ManiSkill tasks with randomized YCB object properties. Bimanual RMA, using observation-action history and dual wrist depth images, retains privileged policy performance on bimanual picking and lifting, while an otherwise matched stationary PPO policy without latent conditioning achieves low success; all methods remain limited on long-horizon stacking. We further demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer on a dual Franka lifting task without real-world finetuning. Together, these results suggest that latent conditioning provides useful structure for scaling robust control to coordinated bimanual systems, while longer horizon tasks require additional temporal structure.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.
authors: Tianle Liu, Gongbo Cheng, Chenggong Ni, Minming Gu, Tao Zhou, Fuyuan Hu, Fan Lyu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing TTD methods discover novel classes only with anonymous labels.
Uses an LLM to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and builds an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space.
At test time, Relational Semantic Grounding compares unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors to propose and rerank candidate concepts.
Applies confidence-guided semantic stabilization to refine discovered concepts over the test stream.
Experiments show improvements over TTD baselines, though the abstract does not report specific numerical results.

During testing, we discovers unknown classes, retrieves their semantic relations to known class anchors, and queries the LLM to generate candidate category names. The candidates are then grounded and filtered by the RSG module, and the selected prediction is used to guide confidence-aware test-time updates.

(b) Pre-known semantic discovery handles unknown sample by matching visual features to a predefined category vocabulary, but it is unrealistic and its discovery ability is limited. (c) Our method aims to more meaningful and open-ended test-time discovery where unknown classes are grounded with visual and semantic relations to known classes, and interpreted through concept generation.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones while the model is already deployed, operating directly on a continual unlabeled test-time stream. Existing TTD methods are overly conservative, making known and unknown features collapse together and difficult to separate during test-time adaptation. In this paper, we revisit TTD from an energy perspective and find that the natural energy gap between known and unknown classes is unstable and easily collapses. We therefore propose Energy Ring to stabilize this gap by anchoring the two types of classes on separate energy rings. A lightweight adapter enlarges the norm-based gap while preserving known-class directions, and a perturbation consistency module forms compact clusters for unknown classes. During testing, energy-guided confidence weighting improves prediction, and a stability-based rectification mechanism corrects unreliable updates. Experimental results show that Energy Ring significantly improves TTD performance against existing TTD methods.
authors: Tianle Liu, Fan Lyu, Tingliang Feng, Chenggong Ni, Tianqi Wang, Zhang Zhang, Fuyuan Hu, Rui Yao, Tao Zhou
bullets: Targets the collapse of known and unknown feature representations in continual, unlabeled test streams.
Anchors known and unknown classes on separate energy rings to preserve a stable energy gap.
Uses a lightweight adapter to enlarge norm-based separation while retaining known-class directions.
Applies perturbation consistency to compact unknown-class clusters and energy-guided confidence weighting for prediction.
Adds stability-based rectification to correct unreliable test-time updates and reports significant gains over existing TTD methods.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Method Schema. ERA projects features onto concentric energy rings: high-energy ring for known classes and low-energy ring for unknowns, together with perturbation-consistency during training. During testing, we conduct energy-weighted prediction, while selectively rectifying highperturbation samples to refresh memory queues and update ERA to rectify energy rings.
Figure 3: Comparison of norm and angular prediction for test samples. Our method further expands the differences of energy in both intensity and direction.

Figure 1: Energy comparisons among existing TTD methods and our method. HM keeps the backbone frozen and classifies based on fixed spatial energy. DAA collapses the original energy intensity onto a single hypersphere. Energy Ring compresses known and unknown classes onto different energy rings, yielding spatial-energy difference and retaining separability.

Figure 2: Task setting of TTD. In TTD, a model is pretrained on data containing only known classes. During deployment, the test data may include both known and unknown classes, requiring the model to predict known classes and discover novel ones.

papers.title: Energy Ring: Stabilizing Feature Energy for Reliable Test-Time Discovery
papers.tldr: Energy Ring improves test-time discovery by stabilizing the energy separation between known and unknown classes during adaptation.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) enables time series forecasters to update after deployment as new observations become available. However, adaptation objectives that focus primarily on prediction errors at individual time steps do not fully address the needs of financial time series forecasting. In addition to pointwise return fitting, return direction and the price trajectories reconstructed from sequences of returns are also important. To better account for these properties, we introduce Direction- and Price-Aware Adaptation Loss (DPAL), which combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms. We apply DPAL within existing TSF-TTA frameworks without modifying the source forecaster or the adapter architecture. Across a diverse collection of financial datasets, DPAL reduces reconstructed-price mean squared error in most evaluated settings.
authors: Wuzhou Lian, Haochun Wang, Yuefan Deng
bullets: Financial TTA objectives based only on pointwise prediction errors may miss directional and price-trajectory quality.
DPAL combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms.
It can be applied within existing TSF-TTA frameworks without changing the forecaster or adapter architecture.
Across diverse financial datasets, DPAL reduces reconstructed-price MSE in most evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve through repeated cycles of modification and evaluation. However, existing methods receive feedback on modifications only after costly evaluations, and aggregate scores may obscure distinctions between failures that require different repairs. We introduce predictive self-evolution through an editable Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM). Before evaluation, the IDM predicts task-level outcomes of a proposed modification and guides an optional revision. After evaluation, past modifications and their observed outcomes are used to improve the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations. The system can thus improve how it solves tasks, proposes modifications, and predicts their effects. Building on HyperAgents, we evaluate this approach across multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level mathematical grading. Our approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with up to 46% higher average performance over generations. Gains also persist under matched token budgets that include both agent evolution and task evaluation, and extend to held-out tasks. Forecast accuracy improves as the IDM evolves, and the learned predictive knowledge transfers to improve evolution in a new domain.
authors: Zixuan Xie, Chang Xu, Yuhua Jiang, Li Zhao
bullets: Existing self-evolving agents learn from modifications only after evaluation, while aggregate feedback can hide failure-specific repair needs.
The Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM) predicts task-level effects of proposed changes and can guide revisions before evaluation.

Evaluated on multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level math grading using HyperAgents as a baseline.
The approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with gains of up to 46% in average performance; forecast accuracy also improves over time.

papers.abstract: We propose a linearized Physics-Informed Neural Network (lPINN), a reduced-order neural basis method for forward and inverse differential equations. In an offline stage, lPINN learns operator-compatible continuous neural basis functions from an ensemble of numerical solutions. The basis functions are differentiable through automatic differentiation and are pretrained using solution data together with either derivative information or physics residuals. For each new problem instance, the basis functions are frozen and the solution is obtained by minimizing the governing-equation residual together with applicable initial, boundary, regularization, and observational terms. Unlike surrogate and operator-learning methods, the training data define the trial space offline, while the instance-specific solution is computed online by enforcing the governing physics. Relative to vanilla PINNs, lPINN pretrains the nonlinear hidden-layer representation offline and performs online inference only in the final linear layer. We evaluate lPINN on forward and inverse problems for the advection-diffusion equation, Burgers' equation, and the nonlinear pendulum equation. Compared with vanilla PINNs, lPINN achieves lower solution and parameter errors while reducing online inference times by approximately one to more than three orders of magnitude, with the largest gains generally observed for limited residual or measurement data. Cross-resolution experiments show that the learned continuous representation can be evaluated on finer meshes without retraining and with nearly unchanged accuracy.
bullets: Targets faster and more data-efficient solution of forward and inverse differential equations than vanilla PINNs.

Compared with vanilla PINNs, reports lower solution and parameter errors and online speedups of roughly one to over three orders of magnitude, especially with limited residual or measurement data; supports finer meshes without retraining.

papers.abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is increasingly used to evaluate whether neural networks can infer task-specific transformations from few demonstrations. Recent ARC models differ in architecture, but also in broader training and evaluation protocols, including pretraining data, data augmentation, test-time setup, and optimization budgets, making conclusions about architecture benefits debatable. In this work, we study how the performance of the vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM models is affected by pretraining and test-time training (TTT) budgets under a common inductive protocol on ARC-AGI-1. We cross five pretraining budgets with four TTT budgets for each test task. Each budget specifies a task-variant count and total sample presentations, defining the controlled training budgets. We observe that increasing TTT sample presentations improves the standard ARC pass@2 metric in all settings for both models. Increasing the TTT task-variant count consistently helps only TRM, whereas VARC often performs better with fewer variants. VARC also remains competitive without pretraining, while TRM benefits much more from it. These results show that pretraining and TTT budgets affect ARC evaluation and motivate reporting at comparable budgets.
bullets: Evaluates vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM under a common protocol.
Crosses five pretraining budgets with four per-task test-time training budgets.
More test-time sample presentations improve pass@2 for both models.
More task variants consistently help TRM but can hurt VARC; TRM benefits more from pretraining.
Findings support reporting ARC results at comparable training and evaluation budgets.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T$^2$Mem extracts lightweight episode-level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query-specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T$^2$Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.
authors: Zijun Wang, Yifan Ji, Haidong Xin, Zhenghao Liu, Yukun Yan, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu, Maosong Sun

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are increasingly used to improve language model systems without human intervention through either weight updates or harness improvements. Existing approaches typically pursue these directions separately: some methods update model weights using self-generated experience, while others rewrite the harness that defines how an agent uses prompts, tools, context, and execution feedback. However, these approaches overlook the relationship between model weights and the agent harness. To connect these processes and ensure effective and smooth agent self-evolving, we propose Evo$^2$, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. For harness updates, we design a unified dual-role pipeline that a single policy serves as both a Proposer, which writes harness edits, and a Reflector, which diagnoses their effects and guides revision. For weight updates, harness modifications and their execution outcomes guide the training of both the Proposer and the Reflector. We further develop EvoTIDE, a training pipeline that recovers usable trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, then combines SFT with interleaved GRPO across the two roles. Extensive experiments across three coding benchmarks demonstrate that Evo$^2$ significantly outperforms existing self-evolution methods. It achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, compared with 62.6% and 41.0% for the strongest baseline, respectively. We also show that the evolved harnesses transfer to different tasks without further evolution and rank first in cross-benchmark evaluations. Our dual-role harness improvement framework is also able to extend to self-evolution with proprietary models, improving a GPT-5-mini agent's performance from 24.4% to 48.3%. These results demonstrate the applicability of the framework Evo$^2$ across domains and its broad transferability across models and tasks.
authors: Chejian Xu, Shujian Zhang, Wenxuan Zhou, John Lambert, Beck Chen, Bo Li, Andrew Hard, Rajiv Mathews
bullets: Addresses the gap between approaches that separately update model weights or agent harnesses.
Uses a dual-role policy as both a Proposer of harness edits and a Reflector that diagnoses outcomes and guides revisions.

Achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, exceeding the reported strongest-baseline results of 62.6% and 41.0%.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving LLM agents typically improve how they act through accumulated experience, reflection, or skills. Yet even procedurally capable agents can fail when their beliefs about environment dynamics are incomplete, incorrect, or outdated. We study a complementary axis of self-evolution: evolving those beliefs during deployment. Such beliefs can support multiple tasks, but incorrect ones can also propagate across them. We introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model that represents environment knowledge as falsifiable hypotheses. Unexpected outcomes and decision-relevant unknowns trigger hypothesis formation. Later observations and controlled experiments provide independent validation before a rule can guide predictions or plans within its supported scope. Counterexamples narrow or retire rules as the environment changes. The language model remains frozen, and each rule remains linked to its evidence and the decisions it changes. Across four benchmarks spanning static dynamics, hidden drift, and scientific discovery, EvoBelief improves task performance and reuses learned rules across tasks. On ALFWorld without actor-side transition memory, it improves success over the matched Frozen World Model by 23.9% and 31.3% with Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4, respectively. On MiniGrid, it revises stale rules and recovers after unannounced dynamics changes. In DiscoveryWorld's Reactor Lab, it discovers and validates quantitative laws, completing 83.3% of Normal-tier and 58.3% of Challenge-tier instances, versus 0% for each evaluated baseline. These results demonstrate self-improvement through testable, revisable environment knowledge rather than model-parameter updates.
authors: Janet Wang, Jiang Guo, Yi Xiang, Jiaqing Yuan, Mingwen Dong, Hideo Kobayashi, Shuaichen Chang, Chandan K. Reddy, Jiarong Jiang
bullets: Targets failures caused by incomplete, incorrect, or outdated beliefs about environment dynamics.
Creates hypotheses from unexpected outcomes or decision-relevant unknowns, then validates them through observations and controlled experiments.
Links each rule to supporting evidence and affected decisions; counterexamples narrow or retire stale rules.
Across four benchmarks, it improves task performance, reuses rules across tasks, adapts to hidden dynamics changes, and discovers quantitative laws.
Reported gains include 23.9% and 31.3% higher ALFWorld success than a matched Frozen World Model, and nonzero DiscoveryWorld completion where baselines achieved 0%.

papers.abstract: Distribution operators need visibility of behind-the-meter photovoltaic (PV) generation, yet most residential customers are observed only through net smart meters. Deep-learning-based PV disaggregation can restore this visibility, but its operational value depends on whether the model serves known customers, new customers, future periods, or new regions. We quantify this dependence using four deployment regimes that separate household transfer from temporal extrapolation, applied to Ausgrid smart-meter data with cross-dataset adaptation to the Pecan Street data. Using a fixed training protocol, we benchmark representative deep sequence architectures for PV disaggregation under regime-matched evaluation. At a fixed 48-hour context length, daylight mean absolute error (MAE) of the best model rises from 0.104~kW on seen households in the future test period to 0.185~kW on unseen households over the same period, and under a fixed training contract the deployment regime explains far more of the error variation than model choice. Under target-domain normalization, fine-tuning on five target-region households reduces source-model transfer error by 28\%--36\%. Long input windows help known-customer extrapolation, while their new-customer benefits vary by model. These findings suggest regime-matched error budgets, limited target supervision for model adaptation in new regions, and use-case-dependent context selection for energy data analytics.

Under a fixed training contract, deployment regime explains substantially more error variation than architecture choice.
Five target-region households reduce source-model transfer error by 28%–36%; longer windows help known-customer forecasting, but benefits for new customers vary by model.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves code generation by spending additional inference budget (e.g., calls or tokens) on direct sampling, feedback-conditioned repair, and reasoning-guided implementation. Search-based methods can allocate this budget adaptively, but two challenges remain. First, tree-structured search treats each generation history as a separate state even when trajectories converge to the same program, duplicating evaluation and preventing statistics from being shared. Second, sampling, repair, and reasoning have complementary and state-dependent payoffs, making online allocation among them difficult under a finite budget. To address these challenges, we propose an adaptive graph search method with heterogeneous actions (GraphAHA). GraphAHA organizes the test-time code generation in a typed directed acyclic graph. Equivalent programs are merged into a single code node, allowing their downstream search statistics to be reused across all discovery paths. Hierarchical Thompson sampling then selects whether to generate a new state or follow an existing successor and, for generation, chooses among the type-valid sampling, reasoning, implementation, and repair operations. Evaluated on LiveCodeBench and CodeContests with Qwen2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder, GraphAHA achieves the best score in 18 of 20 cases. For Pass@1 measured using visible tests, it outperforms the strongest baseline for both models on both benchmarks by 4.1 percentage points on average, demonstrating more effective use of a fixed inference budget.
bullets: Merges equivalent programs in a typed directed acyclic graph, avoiding duplicated evaluation and sharing search statistics across discovery paths.
Uses hierarchical Thompson sampling to decide between generating new states, following existing successors, and selecting valid sampling, reasoning, implementation, or repair actions.
Evaluated on LiveCodeBench and CodeContests with Qwen2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder.
Achieves the best score in 18 of 20 cases and improves visible-test Pass@1 over the strongest baseline by 4.1 percentage points on average for both models and benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces GraphAHA, a graph-based adaptive search method for test-time code generation that optimizes inference budget allocation.
papers.title: GraphAHA: Graph-Based Adaptive Search with Heterogeneous Actions for Test-Time Code Generation

papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of machine learning in network and distributed security systems has created an urgent need for mechanisms that can selectively and efficiently remove the influence of specific training data to eliminate compromised or adversarial data points from production models. Privacy regulations such as GDPR's \emph{right to be forgotten} also pose similar requirements. However, existing approximate unlearning techniques remain computationally prohibitive for deployment in real-world security systems, as they require repeated expensive Hessian-inverse-vector computations for each data point removal, creating a bottleneck when processing multiple related requests in scenarios such as intrusion detection systems, spam filters, and threat intelligence platforms. Thus, we introduce a computationally efficient unlearning framework that identifies correlated data points in the training set and applies a theoretically derived closed-form parameter update rule, achieving an $82\times$ wall-clock speedup over standard influence function unlearning while preserving model utility with a $10^{-2}$ improvement in accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines. Our method establishes theoretical guarantees and ensures numerical stability through Hessian damping. Our evaluation across seven diverse dataset architecture combinations, including large-scale CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50, demonstrates superior forgetting effectiveness, with membership inference attack success rates of 0.660 and tug-of-war scores of 0.950.
bullets: Targets efficient removal of compromised, adversarial, or privacy-sensitive training data in security systems.
Identifies correlated training points and uses a theoretically derived closed-form parameter update instead of repeated Hessian-inverse-vector computations.
Uses Hessian damping to improve numerical stability and provides theoretical guarantees.
Evaluated across seven dataset–architecture combinations, including CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50.
Reports an 82× wall-clock speedup, a 10⁻² accuracy improvement over stated baselines, and strong forgetting metrics.
